title: Recursive and Recursively Enumerable Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A language is recursive if a Turing machine halts on every input and accepts exactly its members; it is recursively enumerable if a machine halts and accepts exactly on its members. A language is decidable precisely when both it and its complement are recursively enumerable.
short: Decidability promises an answer either way; semi-decidability only promises a yes answer eventually.
long: Decidability promises an answer either way; semi-decidability only promises a yes answer eventually. Every recursive language is recursively enumerable, but a recognizer for a recursively enumerable language may run forever on nonmembers. Dovetailing two recognizers decides a language whose complement is also enumerable.
proof: Run the recognizer for L and the recognizer for its complement in parallel; one of them eventually accepts.
consequence: This distinction separates problems with certifiable negative answers from those with only positive certificates.

title: Halting Set Is Enumerable but Undecidable
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The halting set can be enumerated by dovetailing all simulations, yet no Turing machine decides it.
short: We can list all halting computations, but we cannot decide in general whether a given computation halts.
long: We can list all halting computations, but we cannot decide in general whether a given computation halts. Enumerate pairs of machine descriptions and inputs by increasing simulation time. Turing's diagonal argument shows that any proposed decider fails on a specially constructed input.
proof: Dovetail the simulation of every pair (M,w). Undecidability follows by defining D(x) to loop when the alleged decider says x halts and to halt otherwise, then inputting D's own description.
consequence: It is the archetypal undecidable problem from which most other undecidability proofs are derived by reduction.

title: Post Correspondence Problem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Given a finite set of dominoes with a top and bottom word on each, deciding whether some nonempty sequence makes the two concatenations equal is undecidable.
short: A child's domino puzzle encodes arbitrary computation.
long: A child's domino puzzle encodes arbitrary computation. The problem is undecidable even with a small constant number of dominoes over a binary alphabet, although it is decidable for a single domino pair in some restricted variants.
proof: Reduce the halting problem by constructing dominoes whose successful matches trace a valid accepting computation history of a Turing machine.
consequence: It is a standard starting point for proving undecidability of grammar and morphism problems.

title: Rice–Shapiro Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A property of recursively enumerable languages has a recursively enumerable index set exactly when it is witnessed by some finite subset from a computable list of finite sets.
latex: Wₑ ∈ P iff ∃ i : Fᵢ ⊆ Wₑ
short: Rice's theorem has a positive converse: semicidable semantic properties are exactly those with finite witnesses.
long: Rice's theorem has a positive converse: semicidable semantic properties are exactly those with finite witnesses. The theorem refines Rice's theorem by characterising which nontrivial semantic properties are even semi-decidable. Finite subsets are the only positive evidence a recognizer can use about an enumerable language.
proof: Finite witnesses are checked by dovetailing enumeration; conversely, the recursion theorem shows a semicomputable index set must admit such a computable family of finite witnesses.
consequence: It describes the exact boundary between properties that are semi-decidable and those that are not.

title: Kleene's Recursion Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: For every computable function on program indices there exists an index e such that the programs e and f(e) compute the same partial function.
short: A program can effectively obtain its own description without an explicit fixed-point construction.
long: A program can effectively obtain its own description without an explicit fixed-point construction. The theorem is a fixed-point result for Gödel numberings and is the rigorous basis of self-referential programming tricks such as quines.
proof: Use the s-m-n theorem to build a program that applies f to its own index, then show the resulting index is a fixed point.
consequence: It simplifies many undecidability proofs and enables programs that reason about their own code.

title: The s-m-n Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: For every computable function of two arguments there is a computable function that, given one argument, returns a program computing the resulting unary function.
short: Fixing an input is itself a computable operation on program descriptions.
long: Fixing an input is itself a computable operation on program descriptions. Also called the parametrization or translation theorem, it formalizes the compiler trick of embedding constants into a program.
proof: Write a program that contains x as a hard-coded constant and simulates the machine i on (x,y).
consequence: It is indispensable for the recursion theorem and for reduction-based undecidability proofs.

title: Kleene's Normal Form Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Every partial computable function can be written as U applied to the least t such that the primitive recursive predicate T holds of the program, input, and t.
short: All computation can be reduced to a primitive-recursive check plus unbounded search.
long: All computation can be reduced to a primitive-recursive check plus unbounded search. The predicate T verifies that t codes a halting computation, and U extracts the output from that code.
proof: Code finite computation histories arithmetically; the verification predicate is primitive recursive, and minimization searches for a valid history.
consequence: It shows that Turing computability can be expressed inside first-order arithmetic.

title: Oracle Turing Machines
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: An oracle Turing machine is a Turing machine with a distinguished query state that, in one step, learns whether a given string belongs to a fixed oracle set A.
short: Relative computation treats a set as a black box that answers membership questions for free.
long: Relative computation treats a set as a black box that answers membership questions for free. Different oracles give different notions of relative computability and relative decidability; every machine becomes trivial relative to its own halting oracle in a suitable sense.
proof: Extend the transition function with a query tape and two branches depending on the oracle answer.
consequence: Oracle machines define Turing reducibility and the Turing degrees.

title: The Turing Jump
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The jump A′ is the halting problem relative to oracle A; it is computable from A but strictly more powerful than A.
latex: A′ = { e : φₑᴬ(e) halts }, A <ₜ A′
short: Every oracle has a strictly harder halting problem attached to it.
long: Every oracle has a strictly harder halting problem attached to it. Iteration of the jump generates an infinite strictly increasing hierarchy of degrees and mirrors the arithmetical hierarchy.
proof: Simulate φₑᴬ(e) using A to answer queries, establishing A′ ≤ₜ A′; diagonalization shows A′ ≰ₜ A.
consequence: The jump is the fundamental operation for measuring noncomputability.

title: The Arithmetical Hierarchy
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: First-order arithmetic formulas are classified by the number and type of alternating blocks of quantifiers into the levels Σₙ, Πₙ, and their intersection Δₙ.
short: Quantifier alternation measures how far a set is from being computable.
long: Quantifier alternation measures how far a set is from being computable. Σ₁ sets are exactly the recursively enumerable sets, and Π₁ sets are their complements; Δ₁ sets are the computable ones.
proof: Put formulas in prenex normal form and count alternations; the classification is invariant up to logical equivalence.
consequence: It connects definability in arithmetic with relative computability.

title: Strictness of the Arithmetical Hierarchy
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: For every n the class Σₙ contains sets that are not in Πₙ, so the arithmetical hierarchy never collapses.
short: Each additional quantifier alternation really buys new descriptive power.
long: Each additional quantifier alternation really buys new descriptive power. The n-th iterated Turing jump is Σₙ-complete and hence cannot be Πₙ.
proof: Iterate the jump and use the fact that each jump strictly exceeds the previous degree, translating jump levels into arithmetical levels.
consequence: It yields a rigorous scale of unsolvability beyond the halting problem.

title: Many-One and Turing Reducibility
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A many-one reduction maps inputs of A computably to inputs of B preserving membership; a Turing reduction is a computation with oracle access to B that decides A.
latex: A ≤ₘ B via f with x ∈ A iff f(x) ∈ B
short: Many-one reductions translate instances; Turing reductions ask questions.
long: Many-one reductions translate instances; Turing reductions ask questions. Many-one reducibility is stricter and is used for m-completeness, while Turing reducibility underlies the degree structure.
proof: Immediate from the definitions; any many-one reduction can be implemented as a single oracle query.
consequence: The choice of reduction determines what completeness means.

title: m-Completeness of the Halting Set
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The halting set is complete for the recursively enumerable languages under many-one reductions.
short: Every semi-decidable problem reduces to the halting problem.
long: Every semi-decidable problem reduces to the halting problem. Given a machine M recognizing A, map x to the pair (M,x); membership is equivalent to halting.
proof: Define f(x) = ⟨M,x⟩ where M recognizes A; then x ∈ A iff M(x) halts, and f is computable.
consequence: It makes the halting set a universal representative of semi-decidability.

title: Undecidability of First-Order Validity
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The set of valid sentences of first-order logic is recursively enumerable but not decidable.
short: Proof search can find valid formulas but cannot always refute invalid ones.
long: Proof search can find valid formulas but cannot always refute invalid ones. Gödel's completeness theorem yields enumeration by exhaustive proof search; undecidability follows because satisfiability of arbitrary machines can be encoded.
proof: A complete proof system enumerates all valid sentences. Reducing the halting problem, or using Trakhtenbrot-style arguments, shows no decision procedure can exist.
consequence: It sets a fundamental limit on automated theorem proving in full first-order logic.

title: Gödel's Completeness Theorem for First-Order Logic
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A first-order sentence is semantically valid if and only if it is provable in a standard deductive system.
short: Syntax and semantics agree for first-order logic.
long: Syntax and semantics agree for first-order logic. Completeness is distinct from incompleteness: it concerns logical truth, not truth in a particular theory such as arithmetic.
proof: Assume a consistent theory and extend it to a maximal consistent Henkin theory, then build a term model satisfying it.
consequence: It justifies proof search as a complete method and enables the compactness theorem.

title: Compactness Theorem of First-Order Logic
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset of it has a model.
latex: T satisfiable iff every finite T₀ ⊆ T is satisfiable
short: Infinite consistency is already visible in all finite fragments.
long: Infinite consistency is already visible in all finite fragments. Compactness fails in second-order logic and is responsible for nonstandard models of arithmetic and analysis.
proof: If T were inconsistent, a finite proof of contradiction would use only finitely many premises by completeness.
consequence: It transfers finite satisfiability to infinite structures and underpins many model-theoretic constructions.

title: Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: If a first-order theory in a countable language has an infinite model, it has a countable model, and models of all larger infinite cardinalities.
latex: infinite model implies countable elementary submodel
short: First-order logic cannot force a unique infinite size of a model.
long: First-order logic cannot force a unique infinite size of a model. Skolem's paradox arises because a countable model of set theory can contain only countably many sets from the outside while satisfying the axioms saying there are uncountably many.
proof: Use Skolem functions and take a countable closure of terms for downward direction; add constants and apply compactness upward.
consequence: It limits the expressive power of first-order axiomatizations.

title: Decidability of Presburger Arithmetic
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The first-order theory of the natural numbers with addition and order but without multiplication is decidable.
short: Linear arithmetic is decidable, though its worst-case complexity is very high.
long: Linear arithmetic is decidable, though its worst-case complexity is very high. Presburger arithmetic admits quantifier elimination after adding divisibility predicates. Its decision problem has doubly exponential worst-case complexity.
proof: Eliminate quantifiers by introducing congruence predicates and using Cooper's or Fourier–Motzkin-style elimination.
consequence: It is the theoretical basis of decision procedures for linear integer arithmetic in verification tools.

title: Tarski's Decidability of Real Closed Fields
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The first-order theory of real closed fields with addition, multiplication, and order is decidable by quantifier elimination.
short: Nonlinear arithmetic over the reals is decidable even though integer arithmetic is not.
long: Nonlinear arithmetic over the reals is decidable even though integer arithmetic is not. Quantifier elimination replaces every formula by an equivalent quantifier-free Boolean combination of polynomial inequalities.
proof: Eliminate one existential variable at a time, splitting on signs of polynomial coefficients; cylindrical algebraic decomposition gives a constructive procedure.
consequence: It enables exact reasoning about polynomial constraints in hybrid-system verification.

title: Undecidability of the Word Problem for Groups
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: There is no algorithm that decides, for an arbitrary finite group presentation and two words, whether the words denote the same element.
short: Equality in a finitely presented group can be as hard as the halting problem.
long: Equality in a finitely presented group can be as hard as the halting problem. Some finitely presented groups have unsolvable word problem, although many important classes, such as finite and free groups, are decidable.
proof: Novikov and Boone encoded Turing machine computations into group relations so that equality of words corresponds to halting.
consequence: It shows that even algebraic questions can encode universal computation.

title: Hilbert's Tenth Problem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: No algorithm decides whether an arbitrary polynomial equation with integer coefficients has a solution in integers.
short: Diophantine equations can simulate any computation.
long: Diophantine equations can simulate any computation. The DPRM theorem characterizes recursively enumerable sets exactly as projections of Diophantine equations, and Matiyasevich supplied the final missing step.
proof: Show that every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine; decidability of solvability would then decide the halting problem.
consequence: It closes Hilbert's famous question and links number theory with computability.

title: Undecidability of the Word Problem for Semigroups
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Equality of words in an arbitrary finitely presented semigroup is undecidable.
short: Even associativity-only algebra can encode a Turing machine.
long: Even associativity-only algebra can encode a Turing machine. The result predates and is simpler than the corresponding group result, using presentations that directly mimic machine transitions.
proof: Reduce the halting problem by writing relations so that a word equality holds exactly when a configuration sequence reaches a halting state.
consequence: It demonstrates that undecidability appears in very weak algebraic structures.

title: Two-Counter Machines Are Turing Complete
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A finite-state machine equipped with two integer counters that can be incremented, decremented, and tested for zero can simulate any Turing machine.
short: A single natural number can store an entire tape.
long: A single natural number can store an entire tape. One counter encodes the tape content in a mixed-radix or prime-exponent representation, and the other assists in arithmetic and head movement.
proof: Represent a Turing machine configuration by a code number, then implement the transition function by arithmetic on the two counters.
consequence: It shows that surprisingly minimal machines suffice for universal computation.

title: Rule 110 Is Turing Complete
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The elementary cellular automaton known as Rule 110 is capable of universal computation.
short: A one-dimensional array of binary cells with a simple local rule can simulate any algorithm.
long: A one-dimensional array of binary cells with a simple local rule can simulate any algorithm. Cook proved universality by identifying structures in Rule 110 that emulate a cyclic tag system.
proof: Show that glider-like periodic patterns and collisions implement the storage and rewriting steps of a cyclic tag system, which is Turing complete.
consequence: Minimal dynamical systems can exhibit maximal computational power.

title: The Chomsky Hierarchy
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Formal languages are stratified into regular, context-free, context-sensitive, and recursively enumerable classes, matched by finite automata, pushdown automata, linear bounded automata, and Turing machines.
short: Each step up the hierarchy adds a more powerful memory mechanism.
long: Each step up the hierarchy adds a more powerful memory mechanism. The inclusions are strict: for instance, balanced parentheses are context-free but not regular, and copying a string is context-sensitive but not context-free.
proof: Each machine class accepts exactly its associated grammar class; pumping-style arguments separate the levels.
consequence: It organizes the study of parsing, compiler design, and decidability.

title: Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: For every regular language there is a pumping length p such that any word of length at least p splits as xyz with |xy| at most p, |y| positive, and xyⁱz in the language for every nonnegative i.
latex: |w| ≥ p ⇒ w = xyz and xyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0
short: Long words in a regular language contain a loop that can be repeated arbitrarily.
long: Long words in a regular language contain a loop that can be repeated arbitrarily. It is a standard tool for proving that a language is not regular, though satisfying the lemma does not prove regularity.
proof: A DFA with p states repeats a state while reading the first p+1 symbols; the loop between repeats can be pumped.
consequence: It gives elementary separations such as the nonregularity of equal numbers of a's and b's.

title: Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: For every context-free language there is a pumping length p such that any long enough word splits as uvxyz with |vxy| at most p, |vy| positive, and uvⁱxyⁱz in the language for every nonnegative i.
latex: w = uvxyz, uvⁱxyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0
short: Repeated nonterminals in a parse tree create two synchronized pumpable substrings.
long: Repeated nonterminals in a parse tree create two synchronized pumpable substrings. The two pumped pieces are what distinguish it from the regular pumping lemma, and the length bound on vxy constrains their positions.
proof: In a parse tree of sufficient height, a path repeats a nonterminal; replace the smaller subtree by the larger one repeatedly.
consequence: It proves, for example, that the language of strings with three equal blocks is not context-free.

title: Myhill–Nerode Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A language is regular if and only if the number of equivalence classes of the relation of having the same set of acceptable continuations is finite.
latex: L regular iff the residual equivalence has finite index
short: Regular languages are exactly those with only finitely many distinguishable states.
long: Regular languages are exactly those with only finitely many distinguishable states. The equivalence classes become the states of the minimal DFA.
proof: Define x ~ y if for all z, xz in L iff yz in L; finite index gives a DFA whose states are classes, and a DFA gives finitely many classes.
consequence: It both characterizes regularity and gives an algorithm for minimal automata.

title: Undecidability of Context-Free Language Equivalence
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: No algorithm decides whether two context-free grammars generate the same language.
short: Even restricted grammars hide the halting problem.
long: Even restricted grammars hide the halting problem. Emptiness and finiteness of context-free languages are decidable, but equivalence and disjointness are not.
proof: Reduce the Post correspondence problem by building a grammar whose universality holds exactly when a PCP solution exists.
consequence: It marks the decidability boundary just above regular languages.

title: Undecidable Emptiness for Context-Sensitive Grammars
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Deciding whether a context-sensitive grammar generates at least one terminal string is undecidable.
short: A grammar with length-bounded rewriting can still encode halting.
long: A grammar with length-bounded rewriting can still encode halting. Context-sensitive languages correspond to nondeterministic linear bounded automata, whose acceptance problem is undecidable despite bounded space.
proof: Encode a Turing machine computation as a derivation of an accepting history, which exists only if the machine halts.
consequence: It shows that undecidability can occur even when every derivation is length-bounded.

title: Recursively Enumerable Languages Are Not Closed Under Complement
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The complement of a recursively enumerable language need not be recursively enumerable; the complement of the halting set is the standard counterexample.
latex: RE is not closed under complement
short: A recognizer for yes instances does not yield a recognizer for no instances.
long: A recognizer for yes instances does not yield a recognizer for no instances. Closure under union and intersection holds; complement is exactly the operation that turns semi-decidability into decidability when both sides are available.
proof: If both a set and its complement were enumerable, dovetailing their recognizers would decide the set, contradicting halting undecidability.
consequence: The asymmetry explains why positive and negative evidence differ in computation.

title: Decidable Syntactic Properties Do Not Violate Rice's Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Rice's theorem concerns semantic properties of the accepted language; purely syntactic properties such as containing a given instruction are decidable by scanning the program text.
short: The scope of Rice's theorem is language-level properties, not source-code features.
long: The scope of Rice's theorem is language-level properties, not source-code features. Program equivalence and totality are semantic and hence undecidable, while counting characters in the source is trivially decidable.
proof: A finite scan of a finite program decides any fixed syntactic question, so the property is not language-invariant and Rice's theorem does not apply.
consequence: It clarifies which static analyses can be complete and which must be conservative.

title: The Universal Turing Machine
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: There exists a single Turing machine that, given an encoding of any machine M and input w, simulates M on w.
short: One machine can run every machine when handed its description.
long: One machine can run every machine when handed its description. The encoding includes transition tables and tape contents; the universal machine loops by decoding and executing one simulated step at a time.
proof: Encode configurations as strings and implement the transition function of the simulated machine by string manipulation.
consequence: It is the theoretical foundation of stored-program computers and interpreters.

title: Partial Recursive Functions Equal Turing Computable Functions
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The partial functions computable by Turing machines are exactly the μ-recursive functions generated by constants, successor, projections, composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded minimization.
short: Several seemingly different definitions of effective computation coincide.
long: Several seemingly different definitions of effective computation coincide. This equivalence is one formulation of the Church–Turing thesis in its provable part.
proof: Implement recursion and minimization with Turing machine loops, and conversely code configurations numerically to simulate machines by μ-recursion.
consequence: It justifies choosing whichever formal model is most convenient.

title: The Ackermann Function Is Not Primitive Recursive
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The Ackermann function is total and computable but grows faster than every primitive recursive function.
latex: A(m,n) eventually dominates every primitive recursive f
short: Unbounded recursion produces growth beyond the primitive recursive fragment.
long: Unbounded recursion produces growth beyond the primitive recursive fragment. Fixed slices A(m,·) form a hierarchy: each is primitive recursive, but the diagonal function escapes the whole hierarchy.
proof: Show by induction on m that A(m,·) dominates increasingly high levels, and every primitive recursive function is eventually dominated by some level.
consequence: It separates primitive recursion from general recursion.

title: Decidable Equivalence of Regular Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Emptiness, containment, and equivalence of regular languages are all decidable.
short: Finite automata support complete algorithms for their basic decision problems.
long: Finite automata support complete algorithms for their basic decision problems. Build an automaton for the symmetric difference and check whether any accepting state is reachable from the start state.
proof: Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so the symmetric difference is regular; reachability in a finite graph is decidable.
consequence: It contrasts with the undecidability of the same questions for context-free languages.

title: Quines and the Recursion Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Self-reproducing programs exist because the recursion theorem lets a program compute its own source description.
short: Self-reference is a theorem, not a programming accident.
long: Self-reference is a theorem, not a programming accident. A quine prints its own code using two copies of a template, one as data and one as instructions; the recursion theorem explains why this is always possible.
proof: Apply the recursion theorem to the computable function that, given an index, produces a program printing that index.
consequence: It connects computability theory with real self-referential software.

title: Oracle Separations for P versus NP
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: There is an oracle A with Pᴬ = NPᴬ and an oracle B with Pᴮ ≠ NPᴮ.
short: Relative to different oracles, the P versus NP question has different answers.
long: Relative to different oracles, the P versus NP question has different answers. Baker, Gill, and Solovay constructed oracles both making the classes collapse and making them separate.
proof: A collapsing oracle is built closed under efficient self-reduction; a separating oracle diagonalizes against all polynomial-time machines.
consequence: Any proof of P versus NP must use non-relativizing techniques.

title: Turing Degrees and the Halting Degree
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Turing degrees are equivalence classes of sets mutually computable from one another, ordered by reducibility, with computable sets forming the least degree zero and the halting set forming 0′.
short: Degrees measure how much noncomputability a set contains.
long: Degrees measure how much noncomputability a set contains. The structure of degrees is rich: there are incomparable degrees and infinitely many degrees between zero and zero prime.
proof: Mutual reducibility is an equivalence relation; the jump of any set is strictly above it, giving 0 <ₜ 0′.
consequence: It provides the standard taxonomy of unsolvability.

title: Undecidability of Finiteness for Turing Machine Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: No algorithm decides whether a Turing machine accepts only finitely many strings.
short: Even the question of whether a recognizer accepts finitely much is undecidable.
long: Even the question of whether a recognizer accepts finitely much is undecidable. Finiteness is a nontrivial semantic index set, so Rice's theorem applies directly.
proof: If finiteness were decidable, one could decide halting by constructing a machine that accepts all strings unless a simulated machine halts, in which case it accepts only finitely many.
consequence: It illustrates the reach of Rice's theorem beyond emptiness.

title: Undecidable Emptiness for Turing Machines
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Deciding whether a Turing machine accepts no input at all is undecidable.
short: We cannot decide in general whether a program accepts anything.
long: We cannot decide in general whether a program accepts anything. This is the semantic property of emptiness, one of the simplest nontrivial properties covered by Rice's theorem.
proof: Emptiness depends only on the accepted language and is true for some machines and false for others, so Rice's theorem gives undecidability.
consequence: It is a common reduction source for other undecidability results.

title: Bounded Halting Is Decidable
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Given a machine, input, and explicit time bound t, deciding whether the machine halts within t steps is decidable by direct simulation.
short: Undecidability comes from unbounded time, not from simulating finite runs.
long: Undecidability comes from unbounded time, not from simulating finite runs. The simulation costs at most t steps and can be implemented on a universal machine.
proof: Simulate the machine for at most t steps and answer yes exactly when a halting configuration is reached.
consequence: It explains why bounded model checking is feasible while general verification is not.

title: From Halting Undecidability to Incompleteness
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The undecidability of the halting problem implies that no sound, effectively axiomatized theory can prove all true statements of arithmetic.
latex: True arithmetic is not recursively enumerable
short: Incompleteness is the logical shadow of the halting problem.
long: Incompleteness is the logical shadow of the halting problem. If a complete sound effective theory of arithmetic existed, one could decide halting by searching for proofs of the corresponding arithmetic statements.
proof: Encode halting as an arithmetic sentence; a decision procedure for theoremhood would decide halting, contradicting undecidability.
consequence: Computability and proof theory express the same fundamental limitation.

title: Trakhtenbrot's Theorem on Finite Satisfiability
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The set of first-order sentences that have a finite model is undecidable.
short: Restricting attention to finite structures destroys the decidability of satisfiability.
long: Restricting attention to finite structures destroys the decidability of satisfiability. By contrast, validity over all structures is semi-decidable by completeness, and validity over finite structures is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable.
proof: Trakhtenbrot reduced the halting problem to the existence of a finite model whose relations encode a halting computation.
consequence: It separates finite model theory from classical model theory.

title: The Complexity Class P
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: P is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time bounded by a polynomial in the input length.
short: Polynomial time is the standard formalization of efficient computation.
long: Polynomial time is the standard formalization of efficient computation. The class is robust across reasonable machine models because simulations cost only polynomial overhead.
proof: Definition; closure under composition of polynomial bounds shows model independence.
consequence: P anchors the main classification of tractable problems.

title: The Complexity Class NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NP is the class of decision problems whose yes instances have polynomial-size certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently problems solved by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine.
short: A solution is easy to check even when finding it may be hard.
long: A solution is easy to check even when finding it may be hard. The verifier definition avoids reliance on nondeterministic hardware and is the one used in practice.
proof: Guess a certificate nondeterministically and run the deterministic verifier; conversely, record the nondeterministic choices as the certificate.
consequence: It captures a huge family of natural search and optimization problems.

title: co-NP and Its Relation to NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: co-NP is the class of complements of NP languages; it contains problems whose no instances have short certificates.
latex: coNP = { complement of L : L ∈ NP }
short: NP certifies yes answers; co-NP certifies no answers.
long: NP certifies yes answers; co-NP certifies no answers. TAUTOLOGY is in co-NP because a falsifying assignment is a short certificate for a no instance.
proof: Complement the accepting and rejecting states of a nondeterministic polynomial-time verifier.
consequence: NP = co-NP is widely disbelieved and would imply surprising collapses.

title: P Equals NP Implies NP Equals co-NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If P equals NP then NP equals co-NP, since deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement.
short: Deterministic algorithms give yes and no answers symmetrically.
long: Deterministic algorithms give yes and no answers symmetrically. The contrapositive says NP differing from co-NP would settle P versus NP.
proof: A deterministic polynomial-time machine can flip its accept and reject states, so P = coP; substituting P = NP gives NP = coNP.
consequence: It is the simplest consequence of a collapse of P and NP.

title: NP-Complete Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: A language is NP-complete if it belongs to NP and every language in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.
latex: L ∈ NPC iff L ∈ NP and ∀ A ∈ NP : A ≤ₚ L
short: One efficient algorithm for an NP-complete problem would solve all of NP.
long: One efficient algorithm for an NP-complete problem would solve all of NP. Completeness is defined relative to a reduction notion; the standard one is polynomial-time many-one reducibility.
proof: SAT is NP-complete by Cook–Levin, and transitivity of polynomial reductions transfers completeness to any NP problem SAT reduces to.
consequence: It provides a rigorous notion of the hardest problems in NP.

title: co-NP-Complete Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: A problem is co-NP-complete if it lies in co-NP and every co-NP problem polynomial-time reduces to it; TAUTOLOGY and UNSAT are standard examples.
short: The hardest no-certificate problems mirror NP-complete ones.
long: The hardest no-certificate problems mirror NP-complete ones. A problem is co-NP-complete exactly when its complement is NP-complete.
proof: Complement a polynomial reduction to SAT to obtain a reduction to UNSAT or TAUTOLOGY.
consequence: It clarifies which problems would collapse NP and co-NP if shown NP-complete.

title: Karp's Twenty-One NP-Complete Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Karp's 1972 paper showed that twenty-one natural combinatorial problems, including clique, vertex cover, and Hamiltonian cycle, are NP-complete.
short: A single reduction from SAT launched the study of NP-completeness.
long: A single reduction from SAT launched the study of NP-completeness. Karp's list demonstrated that NP-completeness is ubiquitous rather than an artifact of logic.
proof: Each listed problem is in NP and admits a polynomial reduction from a previously established NP-complete problem.
consequence: It established the modern practice of proving hardness by chains of reductions.

title: The Polynomial Hierarchy
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The polynomial hierarchy consists of levels Σᵖₖ, Πᵖₖ, and Δᵖₖ obtained by alternating existential and universal polynomial-time quantifiers, with NP as its first existential level.
short: Alternation of guesses builds a ladder above NP and co-NP.
long: Alternation of guesses builds a ladder above NP and co-NP. The hierarchy is contained in PSPACE, and whether it is strict is a major open question.
proof: Define levels inductively with oracle machines: Σᵖ_{k+1} = NP^{Σᵖₖ} and Πᵖ_{k+1} = coNP^{Σᵖₖ}.
consequence: It organizes a wide range of problems by their quantifier structure.

title: PH Collapses If NP Equals co-NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If NP equals co-NP then the polynomial hierarchy collapses to NP.
short: One collapse at the bottom level topples the entire hierarchy.
long: One collapse at the bottom level topples the entire hierarchy. More generally, if two consecutive levels coincide the hierarchy collapses to that level.
proof: Inductively alternate quantifiers: because NP predicates are closed under universal quantification when NP equals co-NP, all higher levels collapse.
consequence: It explains why NP versus co-NP is a central question.

title: The Class PSPACE
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: PSPACE is the class of decision problems solvable by a Turing machine using an amount of memory bounded by a polynomial in the input length, with no restriction on running time.
short: Space is the scarce resource, and time may be enormous.
long: Space is the scarce resource, and time may be enormous. A polynomial-space machine can run for exponential time, so PSPACE is much larger than P.
proof: Definition; the model requires a read-only input tape so that measured space excludes the input.
consequence: PSPACE contains NP and the polynomial hierarchy.

title: Quantified Boolean Formulas Are PSPACE-Complete
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Deciding the truth of a fully quantified Boolean formula is complete for PSPACE.
short: Quantifier alternation over Boolean variables captures polynomial space.
long: Quantifier alternation over Boolean variables captures polynomial space. The problem generalizes SAT by allowing universal quantifiers interleaved with existential ones.
proof: Evaluate the quantifier tree recursively in polynomial space; conversely, simulate a polynomial-space machine's accepting computation by a quantified formula.
consequence: QBF is the canonical complete problem for PSPACE.

title: Savitch's Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Every language accepted by a nondeterministic machine in space s(n) is accepted by a deterministic machine in space s(n) squared.
short: Nondeterminism saves at most a quadratic factor of space.
long: Nondeterminism saves at most a quadratic factor of space. In particular nondeterministic polynomial space equals deterministic polynomial space.
proof: Use a recursive reachability algorithm that tests whether an accepting configuration is reachable within a bounded number of steps via a midpoint configuration.
consequence: It is a rare case where nondeterminism can be eliminated with only polynomial overhead.

title: The Class L of Logarithmic Space
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: L is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine using O(log n) workspace besides a read-only input tape.
short: Logarithmic space means only enough memory to store a few pointers.
long: Logarithmic space means only enough memory to store a few pointers. Containing the input on a separate read-only tape is essential; otherwise reading the input would already require linear space.
proof: Definition with the standard multi-tape machine model.
consequence: L is a small but surprisingly expressive class, containing undirected reachability.

title: The Class NL
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NL is the class of problems solvable by a nondeterministic Turing machine using logarithmic workspace.
short: Guessing a path needs only a logarithmic-length counter.
long: Guessing a path needs only a logarithmic-length counter. Directed reachability is the canonical NL problem because a path can be guessed one vertex at a time.
proof: A nondeterministic logspace machine guesses a path vertex by vertex, storing only the current vertex and a counter.
consequence: NL sits between L and P and equals its own complement.

title: Directed Reachability Is NL-Complete
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The problem of deciding whether a vertex t is reachable from a vertex s in a directed graph is complete for NL under logarithmic-space reductions.
short: Any logarithmic-space computation can be viewed as a reachability question.
long: Any logarithmic-space computation can be viewed as a reachability question. The computation graph of a logspace machine has polynomially many configurations, each describable in logspace.
proof: Reachability is in NL by guessing the path; any NL computation reduces to reachability on its configuration graph.
consequence: It gives a concrete focus for studying the power of nondeterministic logspace.

title: Immerman–Szelepcsényi Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NL is closed under complement, so NL equals co-NL.
short: Nondeterministic logspace can count its way to a no answer.
long: Nondeterministic logspace can count its way to a no answer. This contrasts with deterministic logspace, where L versus co-L was unknown for a long time and is now known to be equal as well.
proof: Inductively guess and verify the number of vertices reachable within k steps, using certificates for non-reachability at each stage.
consequence: It is a landmark result showing that nondeterminism and complementation can coexist in small space.

title: Undirected Connectivity Lies in Logspace
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Undirected s-t connectivity can be solved deterministically using only logarithmic space.
short: Reingold derandomized the walk-based algorithm using expander graphs.
long: Reingold derandomized the walk-based algorithm using expander graphs. The result settled a long-standing question and completed the equality L = SL, where SL is the symmetric logspace class.
proof: Replace the random walk by a deterministic traversal of a power graph built from constant-degree expanders.
consequence: It is a rare example of a complete derandomization result.

title: The Time Hierarchy Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: For every time-constructible function t, the class DTIME(t(n)) is strictly contained in DTIME(t(n)² log t(n)).
short: More time lets a machine solve strictly more problems.
long: More time lets a machine solve strictly more problems. A convenient corollary is that DTIME(nᵏ) is strictly contained in DTIME(nᵏ⁺¹).
proof: Diagonalize: a machine in the larger class simulates all machines in the smaller class on their own descriptions and flips each answer.
consequence: It guarantees that complexity classes defined by time do not all coincide.

title: The Space Hierarchy Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If s is little-o of S and S is space-constructible, then DSPACE(s(n)) is strictly contained in DSPACE(S(n)).
short: Extra memory gives strictly more computational power.
long: Extra memory gives strictly more computational power. The theorem applies to all standard space bounds and implies, for example, that L is strictly smaller than PSPACE.
proof: Diagonalization with a simulator that uses a delimiter to mark how much space a simulated machine is allowed.
consequence: It prevents the space hierarchy from collapsing.

title: Ladner's Theorem and NP-Intermediate Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If P differs from NP, then there exist languages in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete.
short: The NP landscape has intermediate rungs if P and NP differ.
long: The NP landscape has intermediate rungs if P and NP differ. The construction uses delayed diagonalization against both all polynomial-time machines and all NP-completeness reductions.
proof: Build a language that interpolates between a simple set and SAT by deciding membership based on a slowly growing time threshold.
consequence: It shows NP-completeness is not the only alternative to tractability.

title: The Class BPP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: BPP is the class of problems decidable in polynomial time by a randomized algorithm with error probability at most one third on every input.
short: Probability of a wrong answer can be made tiny by repetition.
long: Probability of a wrong answer can be made tiny by repetition. The error bound is arbitrary: majority voting reduces a constant gap to exponentially small failure.
proof: Run the algorithm independently O(k) times and output the majority answer; apply the Chernoff bound.
consequence: BPP models efficient randomized computation in practice.

title: BPP Lies in the Polynomial Hierarchy
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Every language in BPP belongs to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, indeed to the intersection of Σᵖ₂ and Πᵖ₂.
short: Randomness can be simulated by small circuits with quantifiers.
long: Randomness can be simulated by small circuits with quantifiers. This gives evidence that randomized polynomial time is not much more powerful than deterministic polynomial time.
proof: Cover most random strings by a small family of translates using a counting argument, then express acceptance with two quantifier blocks.
consequence: It links derandomization with circuit lower bounds.

title: RP and co-RP One-Sided Error
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: RP is the class where yes instances are accepted with probability at least one half and no instances are never accepted; co-RP reverses the roles.
short: One-sided error means a positive answer can be trusted.
long: One-sided error means a positive answer can be trusted. Primality's Miller–Rabin test puts compositeness in RP (under a deterministic variant).
proof: Amplify each class by repetition; a machine that detects a certificate for either answer gives zero-error expected polynomial time.
consequence: One-sided algorithms are especially useful when false positives are harmless.

title: ZPP and Zero-Error Randomized Time
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: ZPP is the class of problems solvable by a randomized algorithm that never outputs a wrong answer and runs in expected polynomial time.
short: Las Vegas algorithms are always right but have variable running time.
long: Las Vegas algorithms are always right but have variable running time. They contrast with Monte Carlo algorithms in BPP, which have fixed time but a small error probability.
proof: Run an RP algorithm and a co-RP algorithm in parallel until one produces a certified answer.
consequence: It identifies the sweet spot where randomness never compromises correctness.

title: The Class PP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: PP is the class of languages accepted by a polynomial-time randomized machine with probability greater than one half exactly on yes instances.
short: Majority vote defines a surprisingly powerful class.
long: Majority vote defines a surprisingly powerful class. Unlike BPP, the gap from one half may be exponentially small, so error cannot be amplified efficiently.
proof: Definition; note that PP contains NP, because an NP witness can be guessed with probability exponential in the witness length.
consequence: PP is much larger than BPP and contains the entire polynomial hierarchy in relatable forms.

title: The Counting Class #P
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: #P is the class of functions counting the accepting paths of a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine; counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is #P-complete.
short: Counting solutions is harder than deciding whether one exists.
long: Counting solutions is harder than deciding whether one exists. A parsimonious reduction preserves the exact number of solutions, so NP-hardness does not automatically give #P-hardness.
proof: The number of accepting computations of an NP machine is a #P function; SAT's counting version is complete under parsimonious reductions.
consequence: It underpins the complexity of approximate counting and statistical inference.

title: The Schwartz–Zippel Lemma
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If p is a nonzero polynomial of total degree d over a field and r is chosen uniformly from a finite set S, then the probability that p(r) equals zero is at most d divided by the size of S.
short: Random evaluation detects a nonzero polynomial with high probability.
long: Random evaluation detects a nonzero polynomial with high probability. It works for multivariate polynomials and requires only that the evaluation points be distinct field elements.
proof: Induct on the number of variables and degree, factoring p by a linear factor when it vanishes on a slice.
consequence: It is the workhorse of randomized polynomial identity testing.

title: Interactive Proofs Equal PSPACE
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The class IP of languages with polynomial-time probabilistic verifiers interacting with an all-powerful prover equals PSPACE.
short: Dialogue with a prover captures all polynomial-space computation.
long: Dialogue with a prover captures all polynomial-space computation. The verifier uses private randomness and the prover tries to convince it of membership; soundness must hold against dishonest provers.
proof: Arithmetize a quantified Boolean formula into a low-degree polynomial and use the sum-check protocol to verify its value recursively.
consequence: It is one of the most striking characterizations in complexity theory.

title: Two-Prover Interactive Proofs and NEXP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The class MIP of languages with polynomial-time verifiers interacting with two noncommunicating provers equals NEXP.
short: Forbidding provers from talking makes interactive proofs much stronger.
long: Forbidding provers from talking makes interactive proofs much stronger. The verifier can cross-check answers from the two provers, enforcing global consistency that a single prover cannot be forced to satisfy.
proof: Babai, Fortnow, and Lund used low-degree tests and self-correction to encode exponential-time computations into pairs of oracles.
consequence: It explains the power of multiprover protocols and underlies probabilistically checkable proofs.

title: Arthur–Merlin Protocols and Public Coins
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: AM is the class of languages with constant-round interactive proofs in which the verifier's random choices are public; AM is contained in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy.
short: Public randomness can be traded for nondeterminism plus bounded error.
long: Public randomness can be traded for nondeterminism plus bounded error. A constant-round public-coin protocol can be viewed as a Merlin message checked by a probabilistic Arthur.
proof: Guess a likely transcript and use a covering argument to verify that many verifier random strings accept it.
consequence: It connects interactive proofs with classical complexity classes.

title: The Parallel Class NC
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NC is the class of problems solvable in polylogarithmic time using polynomially many processors on a parallel random-access machine.
latex: NCᵏ: time O(logᵏ n), polynomial processors
short: NC captures problems that are efficiently parallelizable.
long: NC captures problems that are efficiently parallelizable. The levels NCᵏ correspond to different polylogarithmic time bounds; NC is the union over all k.
proof: Definition with the PRAM model allowing concurrent reads and exclusive or concurrent writes.
consequence: It provides a theoretical target for parallel algorithm design.

title: NC Is Contained in P
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Every problem in NC can be solved by a deterministic sequential algorithm in polynomial time.
short: Parallelism does not change which problems are decidable in polynomial time.
long: Parallelism does not change which problems are decidable in polynomial time. The simulation loses an amount of time proportional to the polynomial number of processors.
proof: Execute the PRAM steps one at a time, simulating all processor actions in each step sequentially.
consequence: NC is a refined subclass of P measuring parallel feasibility.

title: P-Completeness and the Circuit Value Problem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: A problem is P-complete if it is in P and every problem in P reduces to it in logarithmic space; evaluating a given Boolean circuit on a given input is P-complete.
latex: CVP is P-complete under logspace reductions
short: Some polynomial-time problems are inherently sequential.
long: Some polynomial-time problems are inherently sequential. P-complete problems are not expected to be in NC, so they are candidates for tasks that resist parallelization.
proof: Evaluate a circuit level by level in logspace; conversely encode a poly-time computation as a circuit whose evaluation yields its answer.
consequence: It identifies limits of parallel speedup within P.

title: Parity Is Not in AC Zero
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The parity function on n bits cannot be computed by polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded fan-in AND, OR, and NOT gates.
short: Shallow circuits cannot count bits modulo two.
long: Shallow circuits cannot count bits modulo two. The result is due to Fss and Ajtai and is a flagship lower bound in circuit complexity.
proof: Restrict random input bits so that any constant-depth circuit simplifies to a low-degree polynomial, which cannot equal parity.
consequence: It gives an unconditional separation between circuit classes.

title: The Threshold Circuit Class TC Zero
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: TC⁰ is the class of constant-depth polynomial-size circuit families with majority or threshold gates; it can perform integer multiplication and sorting.
short: Adding majority gates lets shallow circuits do arithmetic.
long: Adding majority gates lets shallow circuits do arithmetic. TC⁰ strictly contains AC⁰ because parity is computable by a single majority-style threshold gate.
proof: Construct constant-depth threshold circuits for addition using carry-save techniques and for multiplication by summing partial products.
consequence: It models the computational power of neural-style threshold units.

title: Fagin's Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NP is exactly the class of graph properties expressible by existential second-order sentences over finite structures.
short: Existentially guessing relations is the same as nondeterministic polynomial time.
long: Existentially guessing relations is the same as nondeterministic polynomial time. This is the founding result of descriptive complexity, linking logical expressiveness to resource bounds.
proof: A second-order existential quantifier guesses the witness relations, and the first-order part checks them in polynomial time; conversely, encode a machine computation into relations.
consequence: It gives logic-free characterizations of major complexity classes.

title: Descriptive Complexity of the Polynomial Hierarchy
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The polynomial hierarchy corresponds to second-order formulas with alternating blocks of existential and universal second-order quantifiers.
short: Quantifier alternation in logic matches alternation in computation.
long: Quantifier alternation in logic matches alternation in computation. Each level of the hierarchy corresponds to a fixed number of second-order quantifier alternations.
proof: Generalize Fagin's theorem by allowing alternation, mirroring oracle calls between ND levels.
consequence: It yields machine-independent definitions of complexity classes.

title: First-Order Logic Equals Uniform AC Zero
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The properties expressible in first-order logic over finite structures correspond exactly to languages recognized by logtime-uniform AC⁰ circuit families.
short: A first-order formula is a shallow circuit and vice versa.
long: A first-order formula is a shallow circuit and vice versa. Uniformity is needed so that the circuit for each input length can be constructed efficiently.
proof: Translate quantifiers into layers of AND and OR gates with fan-out, and build the circuits uniformly from the formula.
consequence: It is another cornerstone of descriptive complexity.

title: P/poly and Nonuniform Polynomial Time
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: P/poly is the class of languages decidable in polynomial time with polynomial-size advice that depends only on the input length.
short: Advice strings act like a different short program for each input length.
long: Advice strings act like a different short program for each input length. Equivalently P/poly is the class of languages decided by polynomial-size Boolean circuit families.
proof: Encode the advice into the circuit family, and conversely hard-wire the advice for each length into a circuit.
consequence: It is the right class for discussing circuit lower bounds.

title: Karp–Lipton Collapse Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If NP is contained in P/poly then the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its second level.
short: Small circuits for NP would make the hierarchy collapse.
long: Small circuits for NP would make the hierarchy collapse. The theorem is used as evidence that NP does not have polynomial-size circuits.
proof: Guess a good advice string existentially, then use universal quantification to check that the advised machine works on all relevant inputs.
consequence: It connects circuit lower bounds with structural complexity.

title: P Is Strictly Contained in EXPTIME
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The class P is a proper subset of EXPTIME by the time hierarchy theorem.
short: There are problems solvable in exponential time that no polynomial-time algorithm solves.
long: There are problems solvable in exponential time that no polynomial-time algorithm solves. Unlike P versus NP, this separation is unconditional.
proof: Apply the time hierarchy theorem with a superpolynomial but exponential time-constructible bound.
consequence: It shows that not all natural complexity questions are open.

title: Generalized Chess Is EXPTIME-Complete
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Deciding the winner in chess played on an arbitrarily large board with arbitrarily many pieces is EXPTIME-complete.
short: A finite game on a variable board can require exponential search.
long: A finite game on a variable board can require exponential search. The result applies to checkers and many other classic games as well.
proof: Membership follows by minimax search over a game tree of exponential depth; hardness encodes an exponential-time computation as a game position.
consequence: It explains why scaled-up versions of familiar games become intractable.

title: The Open Complexity of Graph Isomorphism
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Open. Graph isomorphism is solvable in quasipolynomial time, but it is not known to be in P nor to be NP-complete.
latex: GI ∈ QP; GI ∈ P is open
short: A problem that looks easy has resisted both efficient algorithms and hardness proofs.
long: A problem that looks easy has resisted both efficient algorithms and hardness proofs. Babai's quasipolynomial algorithm is a major recent advance, and the problem is a leading candidate for NP-intermediate status.
proof: Open.
consequence: Its status guides research on both algorithms and lower bounds.

title: The Open Classical Complexity of Factoring
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Open. Integer factorization lies in NP and co-NP and has quasipolynomial classical algorithms, but no polynomial-time classical algorithm is known.
short: Factoring seems easier than NP-complete problems yet still hard classically.
long: Factoring seems easier than NP-complete problems yet still hard classically. Shor's algorithm solves factoring in polynomial time on a quantum computer, so the open question is specifically classical.
proof: Open.
consequence: Its apparent hardness is the foundation of RSA-based cryptography.

title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Open. The exponential time hypothesis asserts that 3-SAT cannot be solved in time two to the power of a vanishing fraction of the number of variables.
short: ETH strengthens P not equal NP to a quantitative lower bound.
long: ETH strengthens P not equal NP to a quantitative lower bound. ETH implies stronger inapproximability results and fine-grained lower bounds for many problems.
proof: Open.
consequence: It has become a standard assumption in fine-grained complexity.

title: The Unique Games Conjecture
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Open. The unique games conjecture asserts that distinguishing almost satisfiable from far-from-satisfiable unique constraint systems is NP-hard.
short: A conjecture about constraint satisfaction with far-reaching approximation consequences.
long: A conjecture about constraint satisfaction with far-reaching approximation consequences. If true, it would settle the optimal approximation ratios of many optimization problems.
proof: Open.
consequence: It has reshaped the study of approximation algorithms and hardness.

title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability in Complexity Theory
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: A parameterized problem is fixed-parameter tractable if it can be solved in f(k) times n to a fixed power, where k is a parameter and f is any computable function.
short: Exponential dependence is confined to a small parameter.
long: Exponential dependence is confined to a small parameter. This gives a meaningful algorithm for problems that are NP-hard in general but easy when a structural parameter is small.
proof: Definition; vertex cover illustrates it with a bounded-depth branching algorithm of size two to the k.
consequence: It provides a positive complexity theory for NP-hard problems.

title: Clique Is W[1]-Complete
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Deciding whether a graph contains a clique of size k is complete for the parameterized class W[1], making fixed-parameter tractability unlikely.
short: Unlike vertex cover, clique seems to resist parameterization by solution size.
long: Unlike vertex cover, clique seems to resist parameterization by solution size. W[1] is the parameterized analogue of NP, and W[1]-hardness plays the role of NP-hardness in this setting.
proof: Reduce the k-step halting problem to k-clique and show k-clique belongs to W[1] via a nondeterministic guess of k vertices.
consequence: It explains why some parameterized problems are tractable and others are not.

title: Vertex Cover Is Fixed-Parameter Tractable
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Deciding whether a graph has a vertex cover of size k takes time at most two to the k times a polynomial in the graph size.
short: Branch on an edge and include one of its endpoints in the cover.
long: Branch on an edge and include one of its endpoints in the cover. If an edge remains uncovered, any cover must contain at least one of its two endpoints, giving a binary branching tree of depth k.
proof: Pick an uncovered edge (u,v), recursively try adding u and adding v, and stop after k choices; include a polynomial-time reduction rule for isolated vertices.
consequence: It is a canonical example of an FPT algorithm and underpins practical solvers.

title: Kernelization and Polynomial Kernels
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Kernelization is preprocessing that maps a parameterized instance to an equivalent instance whose size is bounded by a function of the parameter; a fixed-parameter tractable problem has such a kernel exactly when it is FPT.
short: A kernel is a provably small equivalent instance.
long: A kernel is a provably small equivalent instance. For vertex cover, the bounded-degree rule yields a kernel with at most k squared edges.
proof: If a kernel of size g(k) exists, solve the kernel by brute force; conversely, an FPT algorithm gives a kernel by running for f(k) steps.
consequence: Kernelization supplies the theoretical basis of preprocessing in solvers.

title: The PCP Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Every NP language has probabilistically checkable proofs in which a verifier uses logarithmic randomness and reads only constantly many bits of the proof.
short: A short proof can be checked by reading just a few randomly chosen positions.
long: A short proof can be checked by reading just a few randomly chosen positions. Equivalently, distinguishing satisfiable formulas from formulas far from satisfiable is NP-hard.
proof: Combine gap amplification with proof composition and low-degree tests to reduce the number of queried bits to a constant.
consequence: It is the foundation of modern hardness-of-approximation results.

title: Hardness of Approximating MAX-3SAT
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: For every positive epsilon it is NP-hard to approximate MAX-3SAT within a factor of seven eighths plus epsilon unless P equals NP.
short: Even getting close to the best possible fraction of satisfied clauses is hard.
long: Even getting close to the best possible fraction of satisfied clauses is hard. A random assignment already satisfies seven eighths of the clauses in expectation, and the PCP theorem makes any improvement hard.
proof: Use the PCP theorem with an efficient constraint system whose satisfiable instances leave a constant fraction of clauses unsatisfiable.
consequence: It is a flagship application of PCP technology to optimization.

title: Approximation Thresholds for Set Cover
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The greedy algorithm approximates minimum set cover within a factor of the logarithm of the number of elements, and achieving a factor of one minus a vanishing fraction times that logarithm is NP-hard unless NP has quasipolynomial deterministic algorithms.
latex: greedy ratio Hₙ, hardness (1 − o(1)) ln n
short: Set cover is essentially as hard to approximate as its simple greedy bound suggests.
long: Set cover is essentially as hard to approximate as its simple greedy bound suggests. For special families of sets, such as those of bounded frequency, much better ratios are possible.
proof: Charge each set's cost to newly covered elements using a harmonic-series bound; hardness comes from PCP-based reductions.
consequence: It is a central benchmark in the theory of approximation.

title: The Quantum Class BQP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: BQP is the class of decision problems solvable by a polynomial-time uniform quantum circuit family with bounded error probability.
short: Efficient quantum computation with bounded error defines a complexity class.
long: Efficient quantum computation with bounded error defines a complexity class. BQP contains BPP and is contained in PP, but its relation to NP is not known.
proof: Amplitudes can be represented as sums of exponentially many paths, giving the containment in PP.
consequence: It formalizes which problems quantum computers can efficiently solve.

title: Valiant–Vazirani Theorem and Unique SAT
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: There is a randomized polynomial-time reduction from SAT to the problem of deciding whether a formula has exactly one satisfying assignment.
short: With random hashing, hard satisfaction instances become instances with a unique witness.
long: With random hashing, hard satisfaction instances become instances with a unique witness. The reduction uses pairwise-independent hash functions to isolate a single solution with constant probability.
proof: Hash assignments into a small range and look for a unique satisfying assignment in a bucket whose hash value is zero.
consequence: It shows that uniqueness can be as hard as general satisfiability under randomized reductions.

title: One-Way Functions
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A one-way function is a function computable in polynomial time for which every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter succeeds with at most negligible probability on a randomly chosen input.
latex: f easy, f⁻¹ hard on random y
short: Easy to compute, hard to reverse.
long: Easy to compute, hard to reverse. Candidate constructions include multiplication of large primes and certain hash functions, but no function has been proved one-way.
proof: Definition; existence would imply that P differs from NP.
consequence: One-way functions are the minimal primitive for much of modern cryptography.

title: One-Way Functions and Pseudorandom Generators
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Pseudorandom generators with polynomial stretch exist if and only if one-way functions exist.
short: The ability to stretch a short random seed is equivalent to one-wayness.
long: The ability to stretch a short random seed is equivalent to one-wayness. The HILL theorem shows that a one-way function can be transformed into a generator whose output is indistinguishable from uniform.
proof: Construct a generator from a one-way function by iterated hashing; conversely, a generator that is invertible would distinguish its output from random.
consequence: It identifies a single minimal assumption for stream ciphers and many protocols.

title: The RSA Cryptosystem
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem whose public key is a product of two large primes and whose private key is derived from the prime factorization.
latex: c = mᵉ mod n, m = cᵈ mod n
short: Encryption uses a public exponent; decryption uses a secret exponent tied to the factorization.
long: Encryption uses a public exponent; decryption uses a secret exponent tied to the factorization. Security rests on the difficulty of recovering the private exponent or factoring the modulus. Practical implementations use padding schemes such as OAEP.
proof: Choose primes p and q, set n = pq and pick e coprime to Euler's totient; compute d with ed congruent to one modulo the totient.
consequence: It enables encryption and digital signatures without a shared secret.

title: RSA Correctness via Euler's Theorem
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: RSA decryption recovers the plaintext because raising to the e-th power and then to the d-th power is the identity modulo n when ed is congruent to one modulo the totient of n.
short: Euler's theorem turns the exponent arithmetic into an identity.
long: Euler's theorem turns the exponent arithmetic into an identity. Using Carmichael's function instead of Euler's totient gives a slightly sharper condition on the exponents.
proof: If m is coprime to n, Euler's theorem gives m to the totient equal to one modulo n, and ed = 1 + k times the totient; non-coprime messages follow by the Chinese remainder theorem.
consequence: It is the number-theoretic guarantee behind RSA's correctness.

title: The Open Relation Between RSA Inversion and Factoring
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Open. Inverting RSA is polynomial-time reducible to factoring the modulus, but factoring is not known to reduce to RSA inversion.
short: Breaking RSA may be easier than factoring.
long: Breaking RSA may be easier than factoring. Some oracle attacks recover the factorization given an RSA inversion oracle, but in the standard model equivalence remains unproved.
proof: Open.
consequence: RSA security is based on a potentially weaker assumption than hardness of factoring.

title: Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Two parties can agree on a shared secret over a public channel by exchanging powers of a generator in a finite cyclic group.
short: Each side contributes a secret exponent and combines it with the other's public value.
long: Each side contributes a secret exponent and combines it with the other's public value. The protocol provides no authentication by itself and is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle without certified public keys.
proof: Exponent arithmetic in the group ensures both parties compute the same element; an eavesdropper faces the computational Diffie–Hellman problem.
consequence: It is the basis of key agreement in many protocols.

title: The Discrete Logarithm Problem in Cryptography
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Given a finite cyclic group, a generator g, and an element h, the discrete logarithm problem asks for an exponent x with g to the x equal to h.
short: Reversing exponentiation in a group is hard for suitable groups.
long: Reversing exponentiation in a group is hard for suitable groups. Generic algorithms such as baby-step giant-step take about the square root of the group order, while index calculus is faster in finite fields.
proof: Definition; hardness depends strongly on the choice of group.
consequence: Its presumed hardness underlies Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography.

title: Computational Diffie–Hellman Assumption
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The computational Diffie–Hellman assumption says that given g, g to the a, and g to the b in a suitable group, computing g to the ab is infeasible.
short: Combining public shares into the shared secret should be hard.
long: Combining public shares into the shared secret should be hard. Solving discrete logarithm in the group would break computational Diffie–Hellman, but the converse implication is not known.
proof: Definition; solving discrete logarithm for either exponent would solve CDH, but the reverse reduction is unknown.
consequence: It is a standard assumption for key-agreement security.

title: Decisional Diffie–Hellman Assumption
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption says that g to the ab is computationally indistinguishable from a uniformly random group element given g to the a and g to the b.
short: The shared secret should look random to an observer.
long: The shared secret should look random to an observer. DDH is stronger than CDH and fails in groups with efficiently computable pairings.
proof: Definition; a distinguisher would leak information about the shared key.
consequence: Many encryption and commitment schemes rely on this stronger assumption.

title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Elliptic curve cryptography uses the group of points on an elliptic curve over a finite field in place of a multiplicative group to implement public-key primitives.
short: A richer group structure gives the same security with shorter keys.
long: A richer group structure gives the same security with shorter keys. Curves with smooth order are avoided, and safe curves are chosen to resist known attacks such as the MOV attack.
proof: The points of a nonsingular elliptic curve form an abelian group with efficient scalar multiplication, enabling Diffie–Hellman and signature schemes.
consequence: It is the dominant public-key technology in constrained environments.

title: Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem asks for the integer k given points P and kP on an elliptic curve over a finite field.
latex: find k from P and kP
short: Scalar multiplication is easy; reversing it is believed hard.
long: Scalar multiplication is easy; reversing it is believed hard. Unlike finite fields, elliptic curves have no known subexponential index-calculus attack for well-chosen curves, so generic square-root attacks dominate.
proof: Definition; generic group algorithms require about the square root of the largest prime subgroup order.
consequence: It explains the small key sizes of elliptic-curve systems.

title: The Advanced Encryption Standard
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: AES is a symmetric block cipher with a 128-bit block and key sizes of 128, 192, or 256 bits, built as a substitution-permutation network.
short: Repeated rounds of substitution, permutation, and key mixing scramble each block.
long: Repeated rounds of substitution, permutation, and key mixing scramble each block. The Rijndael design was selected by NIST in 2001; no practical key-recovery attack on the full cipher is known.
proof: Each round applies SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey; decryption inverts these bijective layers.
consequence: It is the worldwide standard for symmetric encryption.

title: Feistel Networks and the Data Encryption Standard
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A Feistel network builds an invertible permutation from a non-invertible round function; DES is a 16-round Feistel cipher with a 64-bit block and an effective 56-bit key.
short: Swapping halves makes each round easy to undo during decryption.
long: Swapping halves makes each round easy to undo during decryption. DES's short key makes exhaustive search feasible, which motivated triple DES and then AES.
proof: Given the next round's halves, the previous left half is recovered as the next right half xor f of the next left half and the round key.
consequence: Feistel networks remain a central design pattern in block ciphers.

title: Cryptographic Hash Function Properties
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A cryptographic hash function maps arbitrary-length inputs to fixed-length outputs and should resist preimage, second-preimage, and collision attacks.
short: A good hash hides its input and cannot be forced to collide.
long: A good hash hides its input and cannot be forced to collide. Collision resistance implies second-preimage resistance, which in turn implies one-wayness under suitable length conditions.
proof: Definition; the implications follow by using a collision finder or second-preimage finder to attack the weaker property.
