statement: For any binary prefix code with codeword lengths lᵢ, the sum of two to the minus lᵢ is at most one; conversely any sequence of lengths satisfying this bound can be realized by a prefix code.
short: Codeword lengths must fit inside the unit interval of binary strings.
long: Codeword lengths must fit inside the unit interval of binary strings. The inequality is a key tool in proving optimality properties of Huffman coding.
proof: Each codeword of length l corresponds to a cylinder set of measure two to the minus l; prefix-free sets have disjoint cylinders inside a space of measure one.
consequence: It characterizes feasible code lengths for instantaneous codes.

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Incompressibility
subject: Information Theory
statement: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program that outputs it, and most strings of length n have complexity close to n.
short: Most strings cannot be shortened because there are too few short programs.
long: Most strings cannot be shortened because there are too few short programs. Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable, and its incomputability mirrors the halting problem.
proof: There are fewer than 2 to the n programs of length below n minus c, so at most a fraction two to the minus c of strings are compressible by c bits.
consequence: It gives an individual, nonprobabilistic notion of randomness and information.

title: The TCP/IP Reference Model
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The TCP/IP model organizes networking into application, transport, internet, and link layers, with each layer providing services to the one above it.
short: Four layers from user data down to physical signalling.
long: Four layers from user data down to physical signalling. The model is defined by its protocols rather than a strict specification; the Internet Protocol and Transmission Control Protocol are its core.
proof: Describe encapsulation: each layer adds a header and passes the result downward, and decapsulation reverses the process at the receiver.
consequence: It is the architecture underlying the practical Internet.

title: The OSI Seven-Layer Model
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The OSI model divides networking into physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, and application layers.
latex: physical, link, network, transport, session, presentation, application
short: A conceptual seven-layer reference for describing network functions.
long: A conceptual seven-layer reference for describing network functions. It is primarily a teaching and standards-reference model; real stacks such as TCP/IP do not map onto it exactly.
proof: List the layers and the service each provides, noting encapsulation between adjacent layers.
consequence: It provides common vocabulary for discussing protocols and interfaces.

title: The TCP Three-Way Handshake
subject: Computer Networks
statement: TCP establishes a connection by exchanging a SYN, a SYN-ACK, and an ACK, which synchronises initial sequence numbers on both sides.
short: Three messages let both sides agree to start a reliable connection.
long: Three messages let both sides agree to start a reliable connection. Because old duplicate packets may linger, both endpoints need a fresh starting sequence number verified by the handshake.
proof: Each side sends its initial sequence number and acknowledges the other's, so after three messages both know the connection is live and synchronised.
consequence: It prevents stale connections from being accepted and initializes reliable delivery.

title: TCP Congestion Control
subject: Computer Networks
statement: TCP congestion control adjusts a congestion window using acknowledgements and loss signals to probe available bandwidth without overwhelming the network.
latex: cwnd grows on ACKs, shrinks on loss
short: Send faster until loss, then back off and probe again.
long: Send faster until loss, then back off and probe again. Classic variants include Tahoe, Reno, and NewReno; modern variants such as BBR use delay and bandwidth estimates.
proof: AIMD dynamics give convergence to a fair share of bottleneck capacity; loss is treated as a signal of queue overflow.
consequence: It is the main mechanism keeping the Internet stable under load.

title: Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease
subject: Computer Networks
statement: AIMD increases the sending rate linearly on success and halves it on congestion, which converges to a fair and efficient allocation among competing flows.
latex: w ← w + 1 per RTT; w ← w/2 on loss
short: Probe gently, retreat sharply.
long: Probe gently, retreat sharply. The sawtooth behaviour of AIMD is the classic TCP congestion-control signature.
proof: The additive increase and multiplicative decrease rule satisfies the conditions for convergence to max-min fairness in a single bottleneck.
consequence: It explains why TCP flows tend to share bandwidth fairly.

title: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance
subject: Computer Networks
statement: TCP slow start doubles the congestion window each round-trip time until a threshold, after which congestion avoidance increases it by one segment per round-trip time.
latex: cwnd doubles before ssthresh, then grows linearly
short: Exponential probing first, then careful linear growth.
long: Exponential probing first, then careful linear growth. A retransmission timeout resets the window to one segment and sets the threshold to half the previous window.
proof: On each acknowledgement the window grows by one maximum segment size; during slow start each segment generates an acknowledgement, giving exponential growth.
consequence: It allows rapid startup while limiting the risk of congestion collapse.

title: Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Three duplicate acknowledgements trigger TCP fast retransmission of the missing segment without waiting for a timeout, followed by fast recovery instead of a full slow start.
short: Duplicate ACKs are a strong hint that one segment was lost.
long: Duplicate ACKs are a strong hint that one segment was lost. Reno's fast recovery inflates the window with each additional duplicate ACK so the pipe stays full while recovering.
proof: A duplicate ACK implies a later segment arrived out of order, so the missing segment can be retransmitted immediately.
consequence: It greatly improves throughput under isolated packet losses.

title: Sliding Window Flow Control
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Sliding-window protocols let a sender transmit up to a window of unacknowledged data, advancing the window as acknowledgements arrive.
short: Keep several packets in flight instead of waiting for each one.
long: Keep several packets in flight instead of waiting for each one. TCP combines the receiver's flow-control window with the sender's congestion window, using the smaller of the two.
proof: The receiver advertises free buffer space; the sender never has more than that many unacknowledged bytes outstanding.
consequence: It improves throughput while preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.

title: Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Go-Back-N retransmits the lost packet and all subsequent packets, while selective repeat retransmits only the packets that were not acknowledged.
latex: GBN: retransmit from lost packet; SR: retransmit missing packets
short: Simple retransmission versus efficient but more complex retransmission.
long: Simple retransmission versus efficient but more complex retransmission. Selective repeat requires out-of-order buffering at the receiver and larger sequence-number space.
proof: In Go-Back-N the receiver accepts only the next expected packet and discards later ones; selective repeat buffers later packets and requests only gaps.
consequence: They illustrate the tradeoff between implementation simplicity and bandwidth efficiency.

title: IP and Best-Effort Delivery
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Internet Protocol provides connectionless, best-effort delivery of datagrams, with no guarantees of delivery, order, or duplicate suppression.
short: Packets may be lost, reordered, or duplicated.
long: Packets may be lost, reordered, or duplicated. Reliability, ordering, and flow control are provided by higher-layer protocols such as TCP.
proof: Routers forward each datagram independently using a time-to-live field to prevent infinite loops, without maintaining per-flow state.
consequence: The simple service model allows a wide variety of transport protocols.

title: IPv4 and IPv6 Address Spaces
subject: Computer Networks
statement: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, vastly expanding the number of available identifiers.
short: IPv6 solves address exhaustion with a much larger space.
long: IPv6 solves address exhaustion with a much larger space. IPv6 also simplifies header processing and removes the checksum, but is not backwards compatible with IPv4.
proof: Compare the address field lengths of the two header formats.
consequence: IPv6 deployment is driven mainly by address exhaustion.

title: Network Address Translation
subject: Computer Networks
statement: NAT maps private IP addresses inside a local network to a smaller number of public addresses by rewriting packet headers and tracking active connections.
short: Many internal hosts share one public address.
long: Many internal hosts share one public address. Port-aware NAT lets multiple hosts share a single address but complicates inbound connections and peer-to-peer protocols.
proof: Maintain a translation table keyed by internal address and port, and rewrite source fields on outbound packets and destination fields on inbound ones.
consequence: It delayed IPv4 exhaustion and is ubiquitous in home and enterprise routers.

title: CIDR and Subnetting
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Classless Inter-Domain Routing represents an address block by a prefix and length, allowing flexible aggregation of routes and subdivision of address spaces.
short: A prefix length replaces rigid address classes.
long: A prefix length replaces rigid address classes. CIDR enables route aggregation, which keeps routing tables manageable.
proof: Interpret the address as a bit string and use the prefix length as the number of significant bits in a longest-prefix match.
consequence: It is essential to scalable routing and efficient address allocation.

title: DNS Hierarchical Name Resolution
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Domain Name System maps human-readable hostnames to IP addresses using a distributed hierarchy of root, top-level, authoritative, and recursive resolvers with caching.
short: A global distributed directory translates names into addresses.
long: A global distributed directory translates names into addresses. Records have time-to-live values that control caching, and DNSSEC can authenticate responses.
proof: A resolver queries servers from the root down the hierarchy until an authoritative answer is found, caching intermediate results.
consequence: It is a critical piece of Internet infrastructure.

title: BGP and Path-Vector Routing
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Border Gateway Protocol is the Internet's inter-domain routing protocol; each autonomous system advertises reachable prefixes with the path of autonomous systems it would traverse.
short: Routers choose paths based on policies and advertised AS sequences.
long: Routers choose paths based on policies and advertised AS sequences. BGP emphasises policy and scalability over shortest paths and can take time to converge after failures.
proof: Each update carries an AS path; an AS ignores routes containing itself, preventing loops, and local policies select the preferred route.
consequence: It holds the global routing system together.

title: OSPF and Link-State Routing
subject: Computer Networks
statement: OSPF is an interior link-state protocol in which routers flood information about their neighbours and compute shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm.
short: Every router builds a full map and computes its own routes.
long: Every router builds a full map and computes its own routes. Areas limit the size of the link-state database; Hello packets detect neighbour failures.
proof: Flooding gives every router in an area the same graph, and Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest paths from that router to all others.
consequence: It converges quickly and supports scalable intra-domain routing.

title: Distance-Vector Routing and Count to Infinity
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Distance-vector protocols can take many iterations to recover from a link failure, with routing metrics increasing toward infinity; split horizon and poison reverse mitigate this.
short: Neighbours can reinforce each other's stale bad news.
long: Neighbours can reinforce each other's stale bad news. Routing Information Protocol uses a hop-count limit of fifteen to bound the problem.
proof: After a route disappears, two routers may each believe the other has a path, incrementing the metric in turn until the maximum is reached.
consequence: It motivates the use of link-state or path-vector protocols in larger networks.

title: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Classic shared-medium Ethernet uses carrier sense multiple access with collision detection: a station listens before sending and detects collisions while transmitting.
short: Listen before talking, stop and retry if two talk at once.
long: Listen before talking, stop and retry if two talk at once. A random backoff after a collision reduces repeated collisions; switched full-duplex Ethernet no longer needs CSMA/CD.
proof: Stations sense the medium and transmit; if simultaneous transmissions corrupt a frame, all detect the collision and jam before backing off randomly.
consequence: It explains the design of early LANs and minimum frame-size requirements.
wiki: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection

title: The Spanning Tree Protocol
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops in bridged Ethernet networks by blocking ports so that the active topology is a tree.
short: Keep redundant links but disable some until needed.
long: Keep redundant links but disable some until needed. If an active link fails, the protocol unblocks a previously disabled port to restore connectivity.
proof: Switches elect a root bridge and compute shortest paths to it; ports not on those paths are blocked, eliminating cycles.
consequence: It allows physical redundancy without broadcast storms.

title: MAC Address Learning in Switches
subject: Computer Networks
statement: An Ethernet switch learns which port leads to each MAC address by inspecting source addresses of incoming frames and uses that table to forward future frames selectively.
short: Switches learn where devices live by watching their traffic.
long: Switches learn where devices live by watching their traffic. Unknown destination addresses are flooded; table entries expire after a timeout to handle moved devices.
proof: Record source address and incoming port; on forwarding, look up the destination and send only to the matching port.
consequence: It makes switched Ethernet far more efficient than shared hubs.

title: ARP and Neighbor Discovery
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Address Resolution Protocol maps IPv4 addresses to link-layer MAC addresses on a local network; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead.
short: Find the hardware address of the next hop on this link.
long: Find the hardware address of the next hop on this link. ARP operates by broadcasting a request and caching the reply, which makes it vulnerable to spoofing without defenses.
proof: A host broadcasts who owns a given IP address and the owner replies with its MAC address, which is then cached.
consequence: It bridges the network and link layers.

title: The End-to-End Principle
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The end-to-end principle says that application-level functions should be implemented at the communicating endpoints rather than inside the network whenever possible.
short: Keep the network simple and let hosts do the clever work.
long: Keep the network simple and let hosts do the clever work. It explains why TCP ensures reliability even though the IP layer is unreliable; middleboxes such as NAT are practical exceptions.
proof: Only endpoints have complete knowledge of the application's needs, and duplicating functions inside the network cannot make them fully correct.
consequence: It has shaped Internet architecture and debates about network neutrality.

title: Hidden Node Problem and RTS/CTS
subject: Computer Networks
statement: In a wireless network two stations out of range of each other may transmit to the same access point simultaneously and collide, since neither senses the other.
latex: hidden terminals cause collisions at receiver
short: Not hearing a neighbour does not mean not interfering with it.
long: Not hearing a neighbour does not mean not interfering with it. The RTS/CTS exchange reserves the medium around the receiver and reduces collisions for large frames.
proof: Station A cannot sense B but both reach the access point; simultaneous transmissions overlap there, so a collision occurs despite clear carrier sense at each sender.
consequence: It motivated the design of wireless medium-access protocols.

title: Software-Defined Networking
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Software-defined networking separates the control plane that decides routes from the data plane that forwards packets, centralising routing decisions in a controller.
latex: control plane separated from data plane
short: One logical controller tells switches how to forward traffic.
long: One logical controller tells switches how to forward traffic. OpenFlow is a standard interface between controller and switches; benefits include programmability and easier management.
proof: Switches forward according to flow tables installed by the controller, so changing policy does not require changing each device's distributed routing algorithm.
consequence: It enables flexible, centrally managed networks.

title: The Von Neumann Architecture
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The von Neumann architecture stores both program instructions and data in the same addressable memory, with a processor that fetches and executes instructions sequentially.
latex: CPU ↔ unified memory for code and data
short: Instructions are data, so a program can be stored and modified like any other information.
long: Instructions are data, so a program can be stored and modified like any other information. This stored-program idea enables general-purpose computers but also creates the instruction-fetch bottleneck.
proof: Describe the cycle: fetch an instruction from the address in the program counter, decode it, execute it, and update the counter.
consequence: It is the blueprint of almost every general-purpose computer today.

title: The Harvard Architecture
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The Harvard architecture keeps instruction memory and data memory physically separate, allowing simultaneous access to both.
short: Two memories mean instructions and data can be fetched in parallel.
long: Two memories mean instructions and data can be fetched in parallel. Modern processors often use a modified Harvard design: separate level-one caches but a shared main memory.
proof: Because the two memories have distinct address spaces and buses, instruction fetch and data access do not conflict.
consequence: It is common in embedded processors and digital signal processors.

title: RISC and CISC Instruction Sets
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: RISC architectures use a small set of simple instructions with load-store memory access, while CISC architectures provide richer instructions that may perform multi-step operations.
latex: RISC: simple, regular; CISC: complex, dense
short: Keep instructions simple and fast, or expressive and compact.
long: Keep instructions simple and fast, or expressive and compact. The distinction has blurred as CISC processors translate complex instructions into internal micro-operations and RISC processors add specialised instructions.
proof: Compare instruction formats, addressing modes, and memory access rules of representative designs.
consequence: The tradeoff shapes compiler design and pipeline implementation.

title: The Fetch–Decode–Execute Cycle
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A processor repeatedly fetches the instruction addressed by the program counter, decodes its opcode and operands, executes it, and updates the program counter.
short: The CPU's heartbeat is one instruction at a time.
long: The CPU's heartbeat is one instruction at a time. Pipelining overlaps these stages for different instructions, raising throughput without reducing single-instruction latency.
proof: Describe how control signals drive the datapath through each stage and how branches modify the program counter.
consequence: It is the foundation for understanding instruction-level parallelism.

title: Instruction Pipelining
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Pipelining overlaps the execution of several instructions by dividing processing into stages, so ideally one instruction completes per cycle after the pipeline fills.
short: Like an assembly line, different instructions occupy different stages at once.
long: Like an assembly line, different instructions occupy different stages at once. Actual speedup is limited by hazards, pipeline-register overhead, and imperfect branch prediction.
proof: With k balanced stages and a steady stream of instructions, one stage completes per clock after an initial latency of k cycles.
consequence: It is the primary technique for increasing processor throughput.

title: Pipeline Hazards
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Pipeline hazards are situations preventing the next instruction from executing in its designated cycle: structural resource conflicts, data dependencies, and control dependencies from branches.
short: An assembly line stalls when the next task needs an unavailable result or a different route.
long: An assembly line stalls when the next task needs an unavailable result or a different route. Data hazards are mitigated by forwarding and scheduling; control hazards by prediction; structural hazards by duplicating resources.
proof: Classify dependencies between instructions and show that without intervention the required value or resource is not ready at the needed stage.
consequence: Hazards determine the real speedup of a pipeline.

title: Branch Prediction
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Branch prediction guesses the outcome of a conditional branch so the pipeline can keep fetching without waiting for the branch to resolve.
short: Guess where the program will go and recover if wrong.
long: Guess where the program will go and recover if wrong. Dynamic predictors use branch-history tables and two-bit saturating counters; a wrong guess flushes wrongly fetched instructions.
proof: Maintain history indexed by branch address and update it with actual outcomes; accuracy above the misprediction threshold yields a speedup.
consequence: Accurate prediction is essential for deep pipelines.

title: Superscalar Execution
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A superscalar processor issues multiple independent instructions per clock cycle to duplicated functional units.
short: More than one instruction can start on every tick.
long: More than one instruction can start on every tick. Finding enough independent instructions requires wide issue logic, register renaming, and aggressive prediction.
proof: Provide multiple execution units and issue logic that checks dependencies before issuing instructions in the same cycle.
consequence: It raises throughput beyond what a single pipeline can deliver.

title: Out-of-Order Execution and Tomasulo's Algorithm
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Tomasulo's algorithm allows instructions to execute as soon as their operands are ready, using reservation stations and register renaming to avoid false dependencies.
short: Execute ready instructions first and rename registers to remove spurious waits.
long: Execute ready instructions first and rename registers to remove spurious waits. Results are broadcast on a common data bus to all waiting reservation stations, and retirement logic preserves precise exceptions.
proof: Rename destination registers to tags, issue instructions to reservation stations, and broadcast results so dependent instructions wake up.
consequence: It is a foundational technique for exploiting instruction-level parallelism.

title: The Memory Hierarchy
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The memory hierarchy arranges storage from fast small registers and caches through main memory to slow large secondary storage, exploiting locality to close the speed gap.
short: Keep frequently used data close to the processor.
long: Keep frequently used data close to the processor. Each level trades capacity and cost for latency; effective performance depends on hit rates at each level.
proof: Locality implies that recent or nearby data is likely to be reused, so keeping a small fast copy gives most of the benefit of a large slow store.
consequence: It is central to computer performance.

title: Locality of Reference
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Programs tend to access the same locations repeatedly (temporal locality) and nearby locations soon after (spatial locality).
short: Recent and neighbouring data are likely to be needed again.
long: Recent and neighbouring data are likely to be needed again. Caches, virtual memory, and prefetching all rely on this empirical property.
proof: Observed program behaviour shows loops and sequential traversal; these yield repeated and clustered access patterns.
consequence: It justifies caches and many performance optimizations.

title: Cache Lines and Spatial Locality
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Caches transfer data in blocks called cache lines, so fetching one word also brings in neighbouring words that may be used soon.
short: Fetch a block, not a single word.
long: Fetch a block, not a single word. Larger lines exploit spatial locality but increase miss penalties and can cause false sharing between cores.
proof: Memory is addressed by line; a miss loads the whole line containing the requested word.
consequence: Line size is a key cache design parameter.

title: Direct-Mapped and Set-Associative Caches
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A direct-mapped cache places each memory block in exactly one cache line, while a k-way set-associative cache allows a block in any of k lines within one set.
short: Simplicity versus fewer conflict misses.
long: Simplicity versus fewer conflict misses. Fully associative caches allow any block anywhere but require more comparison hardware.
proof: Partition the address into tag, set index, and offset; direct mapping uses one line per set, associativity uses k.
consequence: Associativity trades hardware cost against hit rate.

title: The Three Cs of Cache Misses
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Cache misses are classified as compulsory misses on first access, capacity misses because the cache is too small, and conflict misses because of mapping collisions.
short: Three distinct reasons a lookup can fail.
long: Three distinct reasons a lookup can fail. The classification guides optimizations such as prefetching, larger caches, and higher associativity.
proof: Partition misses by whether the block was everaccessed, whether it was evicted because of total size, or because of set contention.
consequence: It provides a vocabulary for cache-performance analysis.

title: Cache Coherence and the MESI Protocol
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: MESI is a cache-coherence protocol giving each cached line one of four states: modified, exclusive, shared, or invalid, so multiple cores see a consistent view of memory.
short: Track who owns and may modify each cached line.
long: Track who owns and may modify each cached line. Write-invalidate protocols broadcast invalidations on writes; directory-based schemes scale this to many cores.
proof: Transitions on reads, writes, and snoops ensure at most one modified copy and that any shared copies agree with memory.
consequence: It underpins correct shared-memory multiprocessing.

title: Write-Back versus Write-Through Caches
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Write-through caches update main memory on every write, while write-back caches mark a line dirty and write it to memory only on eviction.
short: Update memory immediately or postpone until eviction.
long: Update memory immediately or postpone until eviction. Write-back reduces memory traffic but requires dirty bits and more complex coherence handling.
proof: With write-back, the cache line holds the only valid copy of modified data until it is written back, so a dirty bit records the need.
consequence: The choice affects bandwidth, latency, and coherence complexity.

title: Virtual Memory and Paging
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Virtual memory gives each process a large private address space divided into fixed-size pages, which are mapped to physical frames by a page table and loaded on demand.
short: Programs see a big private memory; the OS maps it to real pages.
long: Programs see a big private memory; the OS maps it to real pages. A page fault occurs when a referenced page is not resident, causing the operating system to fetch it from disk.
proof: The memory management unit translates virtual addresses via the page table; demand paging loads pages only when first accessed.
consequence: It enables isolation, memory overcommitment, and simpler programming.

title: Translation Lookaside Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A translation lookaside buffer is a small cache of recent virtual-to-physical address translations that avoids walking the page table on every memory access.
short: Cache address translations just as caches data.
long: Cache address translations just as caches data. A TLB miss requires a page-table walk, which is costly; large pages reduce TLB pressure.
proof: Check the TLB first; on a hit, combine the cached frame number with the page offset to form the physical address.
consequence: TLB performance can dominate memory-access time.

title: Amdahl's Law
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The maximum speedup from parallelizing a fraction p of a computation by a factor s is one divided by the sum of the unparallelized fraction and p over s.
short: The serial part of a program limits the gains from parallelism.
long: The serial part of a program limits the gains from parallelism. As s grows the speedup approaches 1/(1−p), so even a small serial fraction caps performance.
proof: Let total work be one unit; after acceleration the time is (1−p) plus p/s, and speedup is the reciprocal.
consequence: It explains why adding processors has diminishing returns.

title: Gustafson's Law
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Gustafson's law argues that with a fixed time budget, scaling the problem size with the number of processors gives speedup of the form (1−p) plus p times the number of processors.
short: Bigger machines can tackle bigger problems in the same time.
long: Bigger machines can tackle bigger problems in the same time. It offers a more optimistic view than Amdahl's law by allowing the parallel portion to grow with available hardware.
proof: Normalize the serial fraction in the scaled workload and observe that the parallel part grows linearly with the number of processors.
consequence: It motivates weak scaling in parallel performance evaluation.

title: Flynn's Taxonomy
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Flynn's taxonomy classifies architectures by the number of instruction and data streams: SISD, SIMD, MISD, and MIMD.
short: Count instruction streams and data streams.
long: Count instruction streams and data streams. Most modern systems are MIMD, often with SIMD units inside each core.
proof: Define the four combinations of single or multiple instruction and data streams.
consequence: It provides a simple vocabulary for parallel machines.

title: SIMD and Vector Processing
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: SIMD execution applies one instruction to many data elements in parallel using wide vector registers or lanes.
latex: one operation on a vector of elements
short: Do the same thing to many pieces of data at once.
long: Do the same thing to many pieces of data at once. It is highly effective for multimedia, scientific kernels, and machine learning, but requires regular data parallelism.
proof: Broadcast a single instruction to multiple functional lanes operating on different register elements.
consequence: It delivers energy-efficient throughput for data-parallel code.

title: The PRAM Parallel Model
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The parallel random-access machine model consists of many processors sharing a global memory, distinguished by whether concurrent reads and writes are allowed.
short: An idealized shared-memory parallel computer.
long: An idealized shared-memory parallel computer. Algorithms are analysed by parallel time and processor count, with work as their product.
proof: Define processors with local registers and shared memory, and specify conflict rules for concurrent accesses.
consequence: It is a standard theoretical model for parallel algorithms.

title: The Bulk Synchronous Parallel Model
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The bulk synchronous parallel model organizes computation into supersteps in which processors perform local work, communicate, and then synchronise at a barrier.
short: Compute locally, exchange messages, then meet at a barrier.
long: Compute locally, exchange messages, then meet at a barrier. Its cost model accounts for computation time, communication volume, and synchronisation overhead, making it more realistic than PRAM.
proof: Analyse each superstep as a sequence of local computation, routing of messages, and a global barrier before the next step.
consequence: It underpins practical parallel frameworks such as Pregel.

title: The Von Neumann Bottleneck
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The von Neumann bottleneck is the limited rate at which data can be transferred between processor and memory, which can leave fast processors idle waiting for instructions or operands.
short: Compute is fast but feeding it is slow.
long: Compute is fast but feeding it is slow. Caches, prefetching, and wider buses mitigate but do not remove the limitation.
proof: Compare processor cycle time with memory latency and bandwidth; when memory cannot keep up, the pipeline stalls.
consequence: It motivates most of modern memory-hierarchy design.

title: The Roofline Model
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The roofline model bounds achievable performance by the smaller of peak arithmetic throughput and memory bandwidth multiplied by arithmetic intensity.
short: A kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound depending on its arithmetic intensity.
long: A kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound depending on its arithmetic intensity. Arithmetic intensity is operations per byte of memory traffic; the model gives a visual ceiling for optimizing kernels.
proof: A kernel needing I operations per byte cannot exceed bandwidth times I, and cannot exceed the processor's peak operation rate.
consequence: It guides performance tuning on modern processors and accelerators.

title: Relational Algebra Operations and Codd's Completeness
subject: Database Systems
statement: Relational algebra is a procedural query language built from selection, projection, join, union, difference, and renaming over relations. Codd's original operator set is relationally complete: it expresses every domain-independent first-order query over relations.
short: A small set of relation operators is expressive enough for every first-order database query.
long: A small set of relation operators is expressive enough for every first-order database query. Selection filters rows, projection drops columns, and natural join combines relations on shared attribute names; set operations require union-compatible relations. Relational completeness is the standard benchmark for judging a query language's expressive power.
proof: Selection and projection implement conjunction and existential quantification of first-order formulas, while union, difference, and join implement disjunction, negation, and combination across relations; the standard translation between algebra and safe relational calculus gives completeness.
consequence: The core of SQL is relationally complete, while aggregation and recursion go beyond first-order expressiveness.

title: Tuple Relational Calculus and Domain Independence
subject: Database Systems
statement: Tuple relational calculus describes a query result as the set of tuples t for which a first-order formula F(t) holds. A query is domain independent when its answer does not change if the underlying domain is enlarged with fresh values.
short: Declarative queries are formulas over tuple variables, but only domain-independent formulas behave like real database queries.
long: Declarative queries are formulas over tuple variables, but only domain-independent formulas behave like real database queries. Syntactic safety is a decidable sufficient condition for domain independence: every quantified variable must draw values from the active domain or query constants. Full domain independence is undecidable, so practical query languages enforce syntactic restrictions.
proof: If a variable is unconstrained, enlarging the domain admits tuples with new values that were not previously answers; binding every variable to database values or constants prevents such spurious answers.
consequence: Safety rules explain why SQL cannot express certain first-order formulas and guide the translation from calculus to algebra.

title: Armstrong's Axioms for Functional Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: Functional dependencies satisfy reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity: if Y is a subset of X then X determines Y; if X determines Y then XZ determines YZ; and if X determines Y and Y determines Z then X determines Z.
latex: Y\subseteq X \Rightarrow X\to Y;\quad X\to Y \Rightarrow XZ\to YZ;\quad X\to Y,\ Y\to Z \Rightarrow X\to Z
short: Three simple inference rules capture everything that follows from a set of functional dependencies.
long: Three simple inference rules capture everything that follows from a set of functional dependencies. The extra rules of pseudotransitivity and decomposition are derivable from the three axioms. A set of dependencies closed under the axioms is a canonical description of the schema's constraints.
proof: Soundness follows directly from the definition of functional dependence; completeness follows by constructing, for any dependency not derivable from F, a relation instance satisfying F but violating that dependency.
consequence: Normal-form definitions and decomposition algorithms rest on this complete inference system.

title: Attribute Closure Algorithm for Functional Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: The closure X+ of an attribute set X under dependencies F is the largest set of attributes determined by X. Repeatedly add Y whenever a dependency X' to Y has its left side X' contained in the current closure; X determines Y exactly when Y belongs to X+.
short: Repeatedly applying dependencies whose left side is already known computes every attribute determined by X.
long: Repeatedly applying dependencies whose left side is already known computes every attribute determined by X. The algorithm terminates after at most as many iterations as there are attributes, since each step adds at least one attribute. It also tests whether X is a superkey by checking whether the closure includes every attribute.
proof: Every addition is justified by a dependency in F, so the result is contained in the true closure; the process reaches a fixed point, so no further dependency can add an attribute, making the result the full closure.
consequence: Closure computation underlies key discovery, lossless-join testing, and normal-form checking.

title: Lossless-Join Decomposition Test
subject: Database Systems
statement: A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless with respect to dependencies F exactly when F implies that the intersection of R1 and R2 functionally determines R1 or determines R2.
latex: R_1\bowtie R_2=R \iff (R_1\cap R_2)\to R_1 \in F^{+}\ \text{or}\ (R_1\cap R_2)\to R_2 \in F^{+}
short: A two-way decomposition loses no information precisely when the shared attributes determine one of the two pieces.
long: A two-way decomposition loses no information precisely when the shared attributes determine one of the two pieces. The chase algorithm tests the criterion by building a canonical tuple set and checking whether joining the projections can create spurious tuples. Losslessness guarantees that every tuple obtainable by rejoining was present in the original relation.
proof: If the intersection determines one side, equal shared values force equal full tuples, so the join produces no spurious rows; conversely the chase produces a counterexample relation when neither dependency holds.
consequence: Normalisation algorithms use this test to ensure schema refinement preserves all original information.

title: Dependency Preservation in Schema Decomposition
subject: Database Systems
statement: A decomposition preserves dependencies when the union of the projections of F onto each subrelation logically implies F. Without this property, enforcing a constraint requires joining the subrelations, which can be expensive.
short: Preserving dependencies lets the database check constraints locally instead of reassembling whole tuples.
long: Preserving dependencies lets the database check constraints locally instead of reassembling whole tuples. Third normal form always admits a dependency-preserving lossless decomposition, whereas Boyce–Codd normal form does not always do so. Designers therefore sometimes accept the weaker normal form for practical constraint enforcement.
proof: Project each dependency onto the attributes of a subrelation by computing closures within that subrelation; if the combined projected set entails the original dependencies by Armstrong's axioms, all checks can be performed locally.
consequence: The trade-off between BCNF purity and efficient constraint checking shapes real relational schemas.

title: Third Normal Form Eliminates Transitive Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: A schema is in third normal form when for every nontrivial dependency X to A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute belonging to some candidate key. This excludes transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on other non-key attributes.
latex: X\to A,\ A\notin X \Rightarrow X\ \text{superkey}\ \lor\ A\ \text{prime}
short: 3NF forbids non-key facts that depend on other non-key facts rather than on the whole key.
long: 3NF forbids non-key facts that depend on other non-key facts rather than on the whole key. A classic violation is a relation with attributes for employee, department, and department budget: budget depends on department, which depends on employee. Splitting department information into its own relation removes the redundancy.
proof: If the condition fails, a non-key attribute is determined by a set that is not a key, giving exactly the transitive redundancy the normal form forbids; the definition is the absence of such dependencies.
consequence: 3NF reduces update anomalies while always permitting a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition.

title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form Defined
subject: Database Systems
statement: A schema is in Boyce–Codd normal form when every nontrivial functional dependency has a superkey as its determinant. It is strictly stronger than third normal form because it removes the exception for prime right-hand sides.
latex: X\to A,\ A\notin X \Rightarrow X\ \text{is a superkey}
short: BCNF requires every determinant to be a key, eliminating all redundancy due to functional dependencies.
long: BCNF requires every determinant to be a key, eliminating all redundancy due to functional dependencies. Overlapping candidate keys can leave a schema in 3NF but not BCNF, since a determinant may consist of part of a key. Decomposing to BCNF can, in rare cases, prevent dependency preservation.
proof: Replacing the 'A is prime' escape clause of 3NF with the requirement that X be a superkey yields BCNF, and schemas satisfying BCNF automatically satisfy 3NF.
consequence: BCNF gives the cleanest relational designs, at the possible cost of more joins or costlier constraint checks.

title: Multivalued Dependencies and Fourth Normal Form
subject: Database Systems
statement: A multivalued dependency X determines Y independently when the set of Y values associated with an X value does not depend on the remaining attributes. A schema is in fourth normal form when every nontrivial multivalued dependency has a superkey on its left side.
short: 4NF removes redundancy caused by two independent repeating groups in the same relation.
long: 4NF removes redundancy caused by two independent repeating groups in the same relation. If a person has several skills and several languages, storing every skill-language pair repeats both facts. Fourth normal form splits the relation into one relation for skills and one for languages.
proof: A multivalued dependency permits a lossless decomposition into projections on XY and on the complement; requiring the determinant to be a key ensures such independence only arises from key structure.
consequence: 4NF handles redundancy that functional dependencies alone cannot detect.

title: Join Dependencies and Fifth Normal Form
subject: Database Systems
statement: A join dependency asserts that a relation equals the natural join of projections onto several attribute subsets. Fifth normal form requires every nontrivial join dependency to be implied by the candidate keys.
short: 5NF eliminates redundancy that only appears when three or more projections are rejoined.
long: 5NF eliminates redundancy that only appears when three or more projections are rejoined. The classic supplier-part-project example cannot be decomposed into two relations without loss but can be decomposed into three; 5NF rules out such cases unless the decomposition follows from keys.
proof: If a join dependency is not implied by keys, the relation contains combinations that are reconstructible from smaller projections, so projection and rejoin removes redundancy; 5NF forbids exactly those dependencies.
consequence: 5NF is the end point of normalisation based on join dependencies and is rarely deliberately violated.

title: ACID Properties of Transactions
subject: Database Systems
statement: ACID transactions guarantee atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability: a transaction either takes effect entirely or not at all, preserves database invariants, executes as if alone, and its committed effects survive failures.
short: ACID is the standard contract that makes database updates reliable under concurrency and crashes.
long: ACID is the standard contract that makes database updates reliable under concurrency and crashes. Logging and recovery provide atomicity and durability, concurrency control provides isolation, and integrity constraints provide consistency. Real systems relax individual properties for performance in specific workloads.
proof: The four properties are enforced by distinct mechanisms: transaction logs for all-or-nothing commit and crash survival, locks or multiversion schemes for isolation, and constraint checks at commit for consistency.
consequence: ACID semantics let application developers reason about updates as single indivisible events.

title: Write-Ahead Logging Guarantees Atomicity
subject: Database Systems
statement: Write-ahead logging requires that the log record describing a change reach stable storage before the corresponding data page is written to disk. Recovery then replays or undoes logged actions after a crash.
short: Persisting the log first ensures recovery always knows about changes that reached disk.
long: Persisting the log first ensures recovery always knows about changes that reached disk. Log-sequence numbers order log records and page writes so recovery can determine which actions must be redone. Without the write-ahead rule, a modified page could exist on disk with no way to undo it.
proof: If a data page were written before its log record, a crash in between would leave an irrecoverable change; forcing the log record to stable storage first makes the log a complete record of every disk change.
consequence: The write-ahead rule is the foundation of almost all commercial crash-recovery schemes.

title: ARIES Recovery and Repeating History
subject: Database Systems
statement: ARIES recovery repeats history in the redo pass, replaying all logged actions including those of transactions that later abort, and then undoes only transactions active at the crash. Compensation log records make undo progress restartable.
short: ARIES first reconstructs the exact state at the crash, then rolls back only the losers.
long: ARIES first reconstructs the exact state at the crash, then rolls back only the losers. The analysis pass identifies dirty pages and active transactions from the log, redo restores the state to the crash point, and undo follows the log chain backwards for loser transactions.
proof: Redo of every action restores the database to its crash-time state; undo then writes a compensation record for each reversed action, and because those records are never undone, repeated crashes cannot repeat undo work.
consequence: Repeating history simplifies recovery and supports fine-grained locking and partial rollbacks.

title: Isolation Levels and Read Anomalies
subject: Database Systems
statement: SQL isolation levels trade concurrency against anomalies: read uncommitted allows dirty reads, read committed prevents them, repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads, and serializable prevents the standard anomalies.
short: Stronger isolation levels forbid more read anomalies but reduce potential concurrency.
long: Stronger isolation levels forbid more read anomalies but reduce potential concurrency. A dirty read sees uncommitted data, a non-repeatable read sees changed values on re-reading a row, and a phantom sees new rows matching a repeated predicate. Each level is defined by which of these phenomena are forbidden.
proof: The levels form a hierarchy because each additional forbidden phenomenon is a specific dependency pattern; preventing a strictly larger set of patterns can only reduce the set of admissible schedules.
consequence: Choosing an isolation level is an explicit performance-versus-correctness decision in application design.

title: Conflict Serializability and Precedence Graphs
subject: Database Systems
statement: A schedule is conflict serializable when non-conflicting operations can be commuted to produce a serial schedule. Its precedence graph, with an edge from Ti to Tj whenever Ti reads or writes an item before Tj writes it, is acyclic exactly in that case.
latex: T_i\to T_j \iff op_i(x)\prec op_j(x),\ \text{one operation writes}
short: Acyclic precedence graphs characterise schedules equivalent to some serial execution.
long: Acyclic precedence graphs characterise schedules equivalent to some serial execution. Conflicting operations are those on the same item where at least one is a write. Topologically sorting an acyclic precedence graph gives a serial order equivalent to the original schedule.
proof: Edges record orderings of operations that cannot be swapped; a cycle means the conflicting orderings cannot all be honoured in a serial order, while a topological order of an acyclic graph yields an equivalent serial schedule.
consequence: Conflict serializability is the tractable correctness criterion used by most locking-based systems.

title: Two-Phase Locking Implies Serializability
subject: Database Systems
statement: Two-phase locking requires every transaction to acquire all its locks before releasing any. Every complete schedule produced under two-phase locking is conflict serializable.
latex: growing\ phase \to lock\ point \to shrinking\ phase
short: Forbidding new locks after the first unlock guarantees serialisable execution.
long: Forbidding new locks after the first unlock guarantees serialisable execution. The moment a transaction releases its last lock is its lock point. Ordering transactions by lock point gives a serial order consistent with the precedence graph, so no cycle can exist.
proof: If Ti has a precedence edge to Tj, Ti must have accessed a shared item before Tj, so Ti reaches its lock point no later than Tj; this makes lock points a topological order of the precedence graph.
consequence: Two-phase locking is the workhorse correctness protocol of transactional databases.

title: Strict Two-Phase Locking Prevents Cascading Aborts
subject: Database Systems
statement: Strict two-phase locking holds all exclusive locks until the transaction commits or aborts. It yields conflict-serializable schedules and prevents cascading aborts because no transaction can read data later rolled back.
short: Keeping exclusive locks to commit time avoids reads of uncommitted data that would need undoing.
long: Keeping exclusive locks to commit time avoids reads of uncommitted data that would need undoing. Rigorous two-phase locking holds both shared and exclusive locks until commit, giving an even simpler serialisation order. Strictness simplifies recovery but lowers concurrency.
proof: An exclusive lock remains held until the holder ends, so no other transaction can read or write the item in the interim; an abort therefore cannot invalidate any other transaction's reads.
consequence: Most commercial databases use a strict or rigorous locking variant for recoverability.

title: Phantom Reads and Predicate Locking
subject: Database Systems
statement: A phantom read occurs when a transaction repeats a predicate query and sees rows inserted by another transaction. Row-level locks do not cover nonexistent rows, so predicate locks or next-key locks are required to prevent phantoms.
short: New rows matching a predicate can appear even when every existing row is locked.
long: New rows matching a predicate can appear even when every existing row is locked. Next-key locking combines a record lock with a gap lock on the index interval preceding the record, preventing insertions into the queried range.
proof: Locking existing rows leaves gaps between them where another transaction may insert a matching row; a lock on the predicate or the index gap closes those gaps.
consequence: Phantom handling is a major difference between repeatable-read and serializable isolation levels.

title: Snapshot Isolation and Write Skew Anomaly
subject: Database Systems
statement: Snapshot isolation lets each transaction read from a consistent snapshot but permits write skew: two concurrent transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint items, yielding a state no serial execution could produce.
short: Both transactions can commit under snapshot isolation even though together they break an invariant.
long: Both transactions can commit under snapshot isolation even though together they break an invariant. In the classic example two doctors read that at least one is on call and each takes themselves off call; each writes a different row, so the first-committer-wins rule does not stop either.
proof: Each transaction sees the other's write as absent from its snapshot, and because they write disjoint items neither is aborted by the write-conflict rule; the resulting state violates the read invariant.
consequence: Snapshot isolation is not serializable, a subtlety that matters for invariant-preserving application code.

title: Optimistic Concurrency Control Validation Phase
subject: Database Systems
statement: Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions work on private copies and validates them at commit. A transaction aborts if another transaction committed a write to an item in its read set since its snapshot.
short: Assume conflicts are rare, then check at commit that the snapshot is still current.
long: Assume conflicts are rare, then check at commit that the snapshot is still current. The typical phases are read, validation, and write. Backward validation checks against transactions that committed earlier; forward validation checks against currently active ones.
proof: If no committed transaction changed any item read by T after T's snapshot, T's effects can be placed immediately after that snapshot in a serial order, so cycles among committed transactions are impossible.
consequence: Optimistic control excels in read-heavy workloads where aborting the rare conflicting transaction is cheaper than locking.

title: B+ Tree Structure and Fanout
subject: Database Systems
statement: A B+ tree stores keys only in linked leaves, while internal pages hold separator keys and child pointers. Large fanout keeps a database index shallow, typically three or four disk pages deep even for millions of keys.
short: High branching keeps index traversal to a handful of disk page reads.
long: High branching keeps index traversal to a handful of disk page reads. Every leaf is at the same depth, and sibling links make range scans sequential. Internal nodes are packed with as many separators as fit in a page.
proof: Each internal page with f children multiplies the number of reachable leaves by f, so leaf count grows exponentially in height and height is logarithmic in key count.
consequence: B+ trees are the default index structure for relational databases and many file systems.

title: Clustered versus Unclustered Indexes
subject: Database Systems
statement: A clustered index determines the physical order of table rows, whereas an unclustered index stores key values together with pointers to rows. A table can have at most one clustered index but many unclustered ones.
short: Only one ordering of the rows can be physical; other orderings must be separate lookup structures.
long: Only one ordering of the rows can be physical; other orderings must be separate lookup structures. Clustered indexes make range scans of the key efficient because matching rows lie near one another. Unclustered indexes add an extra random read per matched row unless they cover the query.
proof: Rows occupy one physical sequence, so only one index can define that sequence; any other index must store a mapping from key to physical row location.
consequence: Choosing the clustered key is a high-impact physical design decision.

title: Hash Indexes for Equality Predicates
subject: Database Systems
statement: A hash index maps a key through a hash function to a bucket of row pointers. It answers equality predicates in expected constant time but cannot support ordered range scans.
short: Hashing gives fast exact-match lookups but loses key order.
long: Hashing gives fast exact-match lookups but loses key order. Overflow buckets handle collisions, and dynamic hashing schemes grow the bucket array while relocating only part of the entries. Ordered indexes are required for inequalities and prefix searches.
proof: The hash function distributes equal keys to the same bucket, so lookup examines one bucket; hashing destroys ordering information, so a range query has no way to restrict the search to a contiguous part of the index.
consequence: Workloads dominated by point lookups benefit from hash indexes; range-heavy workloads need ordered indexes.

title: Covering Index Avoids Base Table Lookups
subject: Database Systems
statement: A covering index contains every column a query needs, allowing the engine to answer the query from the index alone without fetching base table rows.
short: If the index already holds the answer, the table never has to be touched.
long: If the index already holds the answer, the table never has to be touched. Adding trailing columns to an index can make a query covering, but increases index size, memory use, and update cost.
proof: Index entries store values for their key columns and included columns, so when all referenced columns are present there is no need to follow a row pointer.
consequence: Covering indexes can turn a random-I/O-heavy query into a sequential index scan.

title: Selectivity Estimate Drives Index Usage
subject: Database Systems
statement: Selectivity is the fraction of rows returned by a predicate. An index is attractive when the predicate is selective enough that index probes plus row fetches cost less than a sequential scan of the whole table.
short: Few matching rows favour an index; many matching rows favour a full scan.
long: Few matching rows favour an index; many matching rows favour a full scan. A low-selectivity predicate, such as one matching one percent of rows, usually merits an index. A predicate matching most rows is cheaper to serve by scanning once.
proof: A full scan costs proportional to the table's page count, whereas an indexed access costs roughly the index descent plus one fetch per matching row; comparing the two gives a selectivity crossover point.
consequence: Statistics and histograms are critical because a bad selectivity estimate can produce a disastrous plan choice.

title: Database Cost-Based Query Optimizer
subject: Database Systems
statement: A cost-based query optimizer enumerates alternative logical and physical plans, estimates each plan's cost using catalog statistics, and chooses the plan with the lowest estimated cost.
short: The optimizer searches the space of equivalent plans and picks the cheapest estimated one.
long: The optimizer searches the space of equivalent plans and picks the cheapest estimated one. Transformations such as selection pushdown and join reordering generate candidates; costs combine CPU, I/O, and memory estimates from statistics such as row counts and histograms.
proof: The optimizer applies sound equivalence rules to produce plans that all compute Q, then evaluates a cost formula on each and selects the minimum, so the choice is optimal with respect to its model.
consequence: Plan quality depends on both the search space and the accuracy of the underlying statistics.

title: Selection Pushdown in Query Plans
subject: Database Systems
statement: Selection pushdown moves filters as close to the base relations as possible so that fewer rows participate in later joins and aggregations.
short: Filter early so downstream operators process fewer tuples.
long: Filter early so downstream operators process fewer tuples. A filter can be pushed below a join if all attributes it references come from one side; otherwise it stays above or is split into separate filters.
proof: When p only mentions attributes of R, any joined tuple satisfying p has an R component satisfying p, and conversely every join built from filtered R tuples satisfies p, so the two plans are equivalent.
consequence: Pushdown is one of the most effective and cheapest query rewrites available to an optimizer.

title: Join Algorithms for Relational Queries
subject: Database Systems
statement: Nested-loop join compares pairs of rows, hash join builds a hash table on one input and probes with the other, and sort-merge join sorts both inputs and merges on the join key. Hash join is usually preferred for large equi-joins, sort-merge when inputs are already ordered.
short: Three classic strategies trade memory, sorting cost, and comparison count.
long: Three classic strategies trade memory, sorting cost, and comparison count. Block nested loops reduce I/O by buffering pages of the outer relation. Grace hash join partitions overflow to disk when the build side exceeds memory.
proof: Nested loops examines every pair, hash join restricts comparisons to rows sharing a hash bucket, and sort-merge advances two cursors in sorted order, visiting each input once after sorting.
consequence: The choice of join algorithm dominates the cost of analytical queries over large tables.

title: Dynamic Programming for Join Order Selection
subject: Database Systems
statement: Dynamic-programming join enumeration computes the cheapest plan for each subset of relations by combining optimal subplans of smaller subsets. It is optimal for a cost model satisfying the principle of optimality but exponential in the number of relations.
short: Solve every subset once and reuse those optimal subplans to build larger ones.
long: Solve every subset once and reuse those optimal subplans to build larger ones. Systems switch to greedy or randomized search beyond roughly ten relations because the subset count grows as two to the number of relations.
proof: An optimal plan for S splits into two subplans whose own replacements by cheaper equivalents cannot increase total cost, so combining optimal subplans over all splits finds the minimum.
consequence: This algorithm explains why optimizer quality matters most for queries joining many tables.

title: Materialized Views and Query Rewriting
subject: Database Systems
statement: A materialized view stores a query result physically, replacing repeated expensive computation with reads. Optimizers can rewrite matching queries to use the stored result, provided freshness requirements are met.
short: Cache a derived table and let the optimizer redirect compatible queries to it.
long: Cache a derived table and let the optimizer redirect compatible queries to it. Refresh strategies range from immediate maintenance on every base update to periodic rebuilding. Query rewriting must account for nulls, duplicates, and aggregate semantics.
proof: If the view definition is algebraically equivalent to a subexpression of the query, substituting the stored result preserves the answer under the same relational semantics.
consequence: Materialized views are a key performance tool in data warehouses with repetitive aggregate queries.

title: Consistent Hashing for Data Sharding
subject: Database Systems
statement: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a circular identifier space and assigns each key to the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only keys in the affected arc.
short: Only a small fraction of keys change owners when the cluster size changes.
long: Only a small fraction of keys change owners when the cluster size changes. Virtual nodes, multiple points per physical node, smooth the load distribution and reduce hotspots. The expected fraction of remapped keys when adding one node among n is about one over n.
proof: Keys between a newly inserted node and its predecessor are the only ones whose clockwise successor changes, so the shared arc length determines the remapped fraction.
consequence: Consistent hashing keeps rebalancing cost low in distributed key-value stores and sharded databases.

title: Multiversion Concurrency Control Snapshot Reads
subject: Database Systems
statement: Multiversion concurrency control retains old versions of rows tagged with transaction timestamps. A transaction reads the version visible at its snapshot, so readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.
short: Keeping old versions lets each reader see a stable past state without locking.
long: Keeping old versions lets each reader see a stable past state without locking. Version chains are garbage-collected once no active snapshot needs them. MVCC combines well with optimistic or first-committer-wins conflict rules.
proof: Visibility rules choose the newest version whose creator committed before the reader's snapshot and whose deleter committed after it, giving every reader a consistent point-in-time view.
consequence: MVCC underlies high-concurrency systems such as PostgreSQL and snapshot-isolation engines.

title: Bitmap Indexes for Low-Cardinality Columns
subject: Database Systems
statement: A bitmap index stores one bit per row for each distinct value of a low-cardinality column. Bitwise AND and OR implement conjunctions and disjunctions of predicates with great speed, but updates are costly.
short: Bit vectors turn set operations on rows into cheap bit-parallel operations.
long: Bit vectors turn set operations on rows into cheap bit-parallel operations. Compressed bitmaps such as Roaring bitmaps reduce storage for sparse or clustered values. Columns with very high cardinality produce too many bitmaps to be practical.
proof: Each bit vector marks exactly the rows having a value, and a bitwise AND or OR computes the intersection or union of those row sets in one pass over machine words.
consequence: Bitmap indexes are especially effective in read-mostly data warehouses with many low-cardinality dimensions.

title: Candidate Key Discovery from Functional Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: A candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose closure includes every attribute. Enumerating subsets in order of increasing size and testing each closure finds all candidate keys.
short: Find the smallest attribute sets that determine the entire relation.
long: Find the smallest attribute sets that determine the entire relation. Attributes that appear only on right-hand sides of dependencies cannot belong to any key, which prunes the search. Attributes that appear on neither side must belong to every key.
proof: Any superset of a key is a superkey by augmentation, so the first subsets whose closure covers all attributes are exactly the minimal ones, i.e. the candidate keys.
consequence: Key discovery is the first step in normal-form analysis and decomposition design.

title: Process Control Block and Context Switch
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A process control block is the kernel structure holding a process's state, program counter, registers, memory map, open files, and scheduling data. A context switch saves the outgoing process's state there and loads the incoming process's state.
short: The kernel stores each process's execution context so it can be paused and resumed.
long: The kernel stores each process's execution context so it can be paused and resumed. Context switches are triggered by timer interrupts, system calls, or blocking operations. Their cost motivates schedulers to avoid switching too frequently.
proof: Before selecting another process, the kernel saves registers and status into the outgoing PCB; restoring the incoming PCB's registers makes that process continue exactly where it stopped.
consequence: PCBs make multiprogramming possible and underpin process isolation and scheduling.

title: CPU Scheduling Metrics and Trade-offs
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Turnaround time is completion minus arrival, waiting time is total time in the ready queue, response time is first response minus arrival, and throughput is completed jobs per unit time. Scheduling policies trade these metrics against one another.
short: Different scheduling goals favour different definitions of speed and fairness.
long: Different scheduling goals favour different definitions of speed and fairness. Interactive systems prioritise low response time and jitter, while batch systems may prioritise throughput or mean turnaround. No single policy optimises all metrics simultaneously.
proof: These quantities are derived by decomposing a job's residency into arrival-to-start, start-to-finish, and I/O intervals, giving the stated equalities.
consequence: Explicit metric choices are necessary before comparing scheduling algorithms.

title: Convoy Effect in First-Come First-Served Scheduling
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Under first-come first-served scheduling, many short jobs queue behind one long CPU-bound job, forming a convoy of processes waiting for a single long burst. Mean waiting time can become very large.
short: One long nonpreemptive job can delay an entire queue of short jobs.
long: One long nonpreemptive job can delay an entire queue of short jobs. The effect is particularly harmful when short jobs would have finished quickly and released resources. Preemptive policies such as round robin mitigate it.
proof: Each short job arriving behind the long job waits for the entire remaining burst, and the waiting times accumulate linearly with the number of queued jobs.
consequence: FIFO fairness does not imply good average performance, motivating more sophisticated schedulers.

title: Shortest Job First Minimises Mean Waiting Time
subject: Operating Systems
statement: For a batch of jobs available simultaneously, shortest-job-first scheduling minimises the mean waiting time and is optimal among nonpreemptive policies for that metric.
short: Running the shortest job next removes the largest possible contribution to total waiting.
long: Running the shortest job next removes the largest possible contribution to total waiting. The preemptive variant, shortest remaining time first, is optimal when jobs arrive over time and preemption is free. Both require estimates or knowledge of burst lengths.
proof: Swapping an adjacent pair with the longer job first reduces total waiting by the difference of their bursts, so repeatedly sorting by increasing burst length eliminates all such improvements and achieves the minimum.
consequence: This optimality result is the theoretical benchmark against which practical schedulers are compared.

title: Round-Robin Scheduling and Time Quantum
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Round-robin scheduling gives each ready process a fixed time quantum and cycles through the ready queue. A process that does not finish within its quantum is placed at the back of the queue.
short: A fixed quantum bounds how long any ready process waits for its next turn.
long: A fixed quantum bounds how long any ready process waits for its next turn. A very large quantum degenerates toward first-come first-served, while a very small one causes excessive context-switch overhead.
proof: With n ready processes and quantum q, at most n-1 other processes run before the same process is scheduled again, giving the stated bound on response delay.
consequence: Round robin provides good interactive response and is the basis of many time-sharing schedulers.

title: Starvation under Priority Scheduling
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes when higher-priority work arrives continuously. Aging gradually raises the effective priority of waiting processes to bound their delay.
short: Without aging, a busy high-priority queue can postpone low-priority work indefinitely.
long: Without aging, a busy high-priority queue can postpone low-priority work indefinitely. Starvation differs from deadlock: the system keeps making progress, but some processes never progress. Aging converts starvation into bounded waiting.
proof: If the highest-priority queue never becomes empty, a low-priority process is never selected; increasing its priority with waiting time eventually makes it the highest-priority runnable process.
consequence: Starvation avoidance is a required property of any fair scheduler.

title: Multilevel Feedback Queue Scheduling
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A multilevel feedback queue uses several priority queues and moves jobs between them according to observed behaviour. Jobs that yield frequently remain high, while CPU-bound jobs drift to lower-priority queues with longer quanta.
short: Observed short bursts earn high priority without knowing job lengths in advance.
long: Observed short bursts earn high priority without knowing job lengths in advance. Demotion happens when a job exhausts its quantum; promotion can occur after waiting or I/O. The scheme approximates shortest remaining processing time adaptively.
proof: Jobs that finish quickly or block early never get demoted, so they stay in high-priority queues and receive prompt service; long jobs settle into lower queues where fewer context switches occur.
consequence: Multilevel feedback queues were historically used in general-purpose time-sharing systems and remain a standard design pattern.

title: Belady's Anomaly for FIFO Replacement
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Belady's anomaly is the observation that FIFO page replacement can incur more page faults with more frames. Adding memory is therefore not monotonically beneficial for every replacement policy.
short: More frames can perversely cause more faults under FIFO because the evicted pages change.
long: More frames can perversely cause more faults under FIFO because the evicted pages change. The classic counterexample uses three and four frames with a nine-access reference string. Stack algorithms such as LRU and OPT do not exhibit the anomaly.
proof: For a suitable reference string, the extra frame changes which page FIFO evicts, causing a frequently reused page to be absent at a crucial moment; a direct trace of the string establishes the inequality.
consequence: The anomaly motivated the theory of stack replacement algorithms, whose fault sets are nested in memory size.

title: Optimal Page Replacement Lower Bound
subject: Operating Systems
statement: OPT replaces the page whose next use is farthest in the future and achieves the minimum possible number of faults for a given reference string and frame count. It is an offline algorithm requiring knowledge of the future.
short: Evicting the page needed farthest in the future is provably best, if you know the future.
long: Evicting the page needed farthest in the future is provably best, if you know the future. OPT is used as a benchmark in simulation studies because no online policy can beat it. LRU approximates it using recent past accesses as a proxy for future ones.
proof: An exchange argument transforms any optimal policy into one that evicts the farthest-next-use page without increasing faults, so OPT's choices are optimal at every fault.
consequence: OPT provides the lower bound against which practical replacement policies are evaluated.

title: Clock Page Replacement Approximation
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The clock algorithm scans a circular list of resident pages and clears each page's use bit; the first page whose bit is already clear is evicted.
short: A circular scan with use bits approximates LRU at low cost.
long: A circular scan with use bits approximates LRU at low cost. Variants use additional modified bits to prefer clean victims and reduce write-back cost. The hand of the clock advances only on page faults, keeping overhead small.
proof: A set use bit indicates recent access, so clearing it gives that page one more chance; a page whose bit is clear on the current sweep has not been used since the previous sweep and is a reasonable victim.
consequence: Clock and its variants are widely used because they need only a bit per page and no per-access list updates.

title: Working Set Model of Program Locality
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The working set of a process at time t is the set of pages referenced during the preceding window of length delta. The working-set model asserts that a process needs this set resident to avoid excessive paging.
short: Recently used pages form a good predictor of the pages a process needs next.
