long: Recently used pages form a good predictor of the pages a process needs next. The model explains why multiprogramming degree should adapt to the sum of working sets. Page-fault frequency is a practical proxy for working-set size.
proof: Temporal locality means references cluster in time, so pages seen in the recent window have a high probability of being referenced again soon.
consequence: Working-set ideas guide memory allocation and thrashing prevention in real systems.

title: Demand Paging and Page Fault Service
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Demand paging loads a page only when access to an absent page triggers a fault. The handler finds the page on disk, selects a victim if memory is full, updates the page table, and restarts the faulting instruction.
short: Pages are fetched lazily and the interrupted instruction is simply retried.
long: Pages are fetched lazily and the interrupted instruction is simply retried. Hardware sets a fault when the present bit is clear; the kernel distinguishes a legitimate page-in from an access violation by checking the process's virtual address map.
proof: Restarting the faulting instruction after installing the page makes the delay invisible to the program, which observes the same architectural state as if the page had always been resident.
consequence: Demand paging enables large virtual address spaces and efficient memory sharing.

title: Thrashing and Page Fault Frequency
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Thrashing occurs when a system spends more time handling page faults than executing useful work, usually because the sum of active working sets exceeds physical memory. Lowering multiprogramming or adding memory restores progress.
short: Too many processes competing for too few frames cause a self-sustaining storm of faults.
long: Too many processes competing for too few frames cause a self-sustaining storm of faults. Page-fault frequency monitors can detect thrashing: if the rate is too high, the kernel suspends a process; if too low, it can admit another.
proof: When each process lacks frames for its working set, servicing one fault evicts a page another process will soon need, so fault rates rise and useful work stalls.
consequence: Thrashing control is a classic example of feedback-based resource management.

title: Copy-on-Write Fork Implementation
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Copy-on-write fork lets parent and child initially share physical pages marked read-only. A store to a shared page traps the kernel, which creates a private copy for the writing process and resumes execution.
short: Defer copying until a process actually modifies a shared page.
long: Defer copying until a process actually modifies a shared page. The technique makes process creation cheap for workloads that immediately execute a new program. Kernel bookkeeping tracks reference counts on shared page frames.
proof: Sharing costs nothing for pages neither process writes; the write fault identifies exactly which page must become private, preserving the illusion of separate address spaces.
consequence: Copy-on-write is essential for fast fork-based process creation and for memory-efficient snapshots.

title: Page Table Dirty and Referenced Bits
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A page table entry typically carries a present bit, protection bits, a referenced bit set on access, and a dirty bit set on modification. The operating system uses these bits for protection decisions and page replacement.
short: Hardware-maintained bits give the kernel cheap hints about recent page behaviour.
long: Hardware-maintained bits give the kernel cheap hints about recent page behaviour. Referenced bits support approximate LRU or clock replacement; dirty bits avoid writing clean pages back to disk when evicting.
proof: Hardware sets reference and dirty bits automatically on memory accesses, so the kernel obtains usage information without trapping on every access.
consequence: These bits are a small but crucial interface between memory management hardware and the operating system.

title: Deadlock Necessary Conditions
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption of resources, and a circular wait among processes. All four conditions must hold simultaneously.
short: Breaking any one of the four Coffman conditions prevents deadlock.
long: Breaking any one of the four Coffman conditions prevents deadlock. Deadlock avoidance and prevention strategies each target a different condition: spooling removes mutual exclusion, atomic acquisition removes hold-and-wait, preemption removes no-preemption, and ordering removes circular wait.
proof: If any condition fails, some process can always acquire a needed resource or be forced to release one, so the system cannot remain permanently stuck.
consequence: The four conditions organise the entire taxonomy of deadlock handling techniques.

title: Resource Allocation Graph Deadlock Detection
subject: Operating Systems
statement: In a resource allocation graph with one instance per resource type, a cycle is necessary and sufficient for deadlock. With multiple instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.
short: Cycles signal deadlock exactly when each resource type has a single instance.
long: Cycles signal deadlock exactly when each resource type has a single instance. Detection periodically searches for cycles and then aborts or rolls back a process in each cycle. The general multiple-instance case uses a matrix-based detection algorithm analogous to the safety test.
proof: A cycle of single-instance resources leaves every process in it waiting for a resource held by another member, so none can proceed; conversely a deadlock must contain such a cycle. With multiple instances, an available copy may break a cycle.
consequence: Graph-based detection is simple and efficient for systems with unique resources.

title: Banker's Algorithm for Deadlock Avoidance
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The banker's algorithm grants a request only if a safe sequence exists in which every remaining process can finish using currently available resources plus those released by finished processes.
short: Never let the system enter a state from which all processes might not finish.
long: Never let the system enter a state from which all processes might not finish. The algorithm maintains available, maximum, allocation, and need matrices. It rejects requests that would make the state unsafe even if they do not immediately deadlock.
proof: The safety test repeatedly adds the resources of a process whose remaining need fits the available pool; if all processes can be ordered this way, that order is a safe sequence.
consequence: Avoidance is safer than detection but requires advance knowledge of maximum resource needs.

title: Deadlock Prevention by Resource Ordering
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Imposing a total order on resource types and requiring processes to request resources in increasing order makes circular wait impossible.
short: A global ordering rule rules out cycles in the wait-for relation.
long: A global ordering rule rules out cycles in the wait-for relation. The scheme may force a process to hold high-order resources longer than needed, reducing concurrency. Other prevention strategies attack different Coffman conditions instead.
proof: Along any chain of hold-and-wait edges resource types strictly increase, so returning to the starting process would require a strict increase that ends where it began, which is impossible.
consequence: Ordering is a practical prevention strategy when resource types are few and stable.

title: Mutex Locks and Critical Sections
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A mutex is a lock allowing only one thread at a time inside a critical section. Acquiring and releasing it enforces mutual exclusion on shared state.
short: A mutex serialises access to shared state so updates cannot interleave.
long: A mutex serialises access to shared state so updates cannot interleave. Implementations rely on atomic hardware primitives such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap. Recursive mutexes allow reacquisition by the same thread, while error-checking mutexes detect misuse.
proof: The atomic lock operation ensures only one thread observes the unlocked state and enters; all others wait until the holder releases it.
consequence: Mutexes are the basic building block for thread-safe software.

title: Semaphores as Counting Synchronisation Primitives
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A semaphore is an integer counter with atomic wait and signal operations; wait blocks when the counter is zero. Counting semaphores manage several identical resources, and binary semaphores act as locks.
latex: P(s):\ s\leftarrow s-1,\quad V(s):\ s\leftarrow s+1
short: An atomic counter controls how many threads may proceed past a point.
long: An atomic counter controls how many threads may proceed past a point. A blocked thread is placed on a queue and awakened by a later signal. Semaphores can also express ordering constraints between threads, not just mutual exclusion.
proof: Atomicity prevents two concurrent waits from both decrementing a counter of one below zero, so at most the available count of threads is admitted.
consequence: Semaphores express both mutual exclusion and resource counting in a single primitive.

title: Monitors and Condition Variables
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A monitor encapsulates shared data and procedures, allowing at most one thread to execute inside it at a time. Condition variables inside a monitor let threads wait for a state condition and be signaled when it may hold.
short: Monitors bundle locking and waiting into one structured abstraction.
long: Monitors bundle locking and waiting into one structured abstraction. Calling wait atomically releases the monitor lock and blocks; signal wakes a waiting thread, which reacquires the lock before continuing. Mesa semantics allow spurious wakeups and require condition testing in a loop.
proof: Mutual exclusion at monitor entry protects the shared state, while the atomic release-and-block of wait avoids missing a signal between testing a condition and sleeping.
consequence: Monitors are the synchronisation model behind Java and many modern languages.

title: Bounded-Buffer Producer-Consumer Problem
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The bounded-buffer producer–consumer problem coordinates producers and consumers with three semaphores: one counting empty slots, one counting full slots, and one protecting the buffer.
short: Two counting semaphores bound occupancy while a mutex protects the queue.
long: Two counting semaphores bound occupancy while a mutex protects the queue. A producer waits for an empty slot, inserts an item under the mutex, and signals a full slot; a consumer performs the reverse operations.
proof: The empty count never exceeds the buffer capacity because producers decrement it before inserting, the full count prevents consumers from removing absent items, and the mutex serialises access to the shared buffer.
consequence: The pattern underlies pipelines, message queues, and bounded blocking queues.

title: Readers-Writers Problem and Writer Starvation
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The readers–writers problem permits concurrent readers but requires exclusive access for writers. A writer-preference policy blocks new readers once a writer is waiting so writers cannot starve.
latex: readers>0 \Rightarrow writers wait;\ writer\_waiting \Rightarrow new\ readers\ wait
short: Reader concurrency is valuable, but unbounded reader arrival can starve writers forever.
long: Reader concurrency is valuable, but unbounded reader arrival can starve writers forever. A reader count and mutex let the first reader acquire a database lock and the last reader release it. Writer preference introduces a queue to give waiting writers priority.
proof: Without preference, a continuous stream of new readers keeps the read lock held indefinitely; blocking arrivals once a writer waits guarantees the writer eventually acquires exclusive access.
consequence: The problem illustrates how fairness, not just mutual exclusion, must be designed explicitly.

title: Dining Philosophers and Resource Hierarchy
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The dining philosophers problem illustrates deadlock when each process holds one resource while waiting for another held by a neighbour. Imposing a global order on resources, or limiting the number of concurrent diners, breaks the circular wait.
short: Symmetric hold-and-wait among neighbours deadlocks unless a rule breaks the symmetry.
long: Symmetric hold-and-wait among neighbours deadlocks unless a rule breaks the symmetry. The resource hierarchy solution requires every philosopher to pick the lower-numbered fork first. A semaphore allowing at most n-1 philosophers also prevents deadlock.
proof: With a global order, the philosopher holding the highest-needed lower fork can always acquire the other, so at least one diner progresses and the cycle is broken.
consequence: The fable is a standard teaching example for deadlock conditions and prevention.

title: Futex Fast Path and Kernel Slow Path
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A futex performs uncontended lock operations entirely in user space with atomic instructions and enters the kernel only when a thread must block or wake another.
latex: CAS(word) \text{ fast path};\ futex(SYS) \text{ slow path}
short: Keep the common uncontended case free of system calls.
long: Keep the common uncontended case free of system calls. The kernel futex call registers a waiter on a user-space address and supports wake operations. Shared futexes work across processes via mapped memory.
proof: Uncontended acquisition and release reduce to a compare-and-swap on a user-space word; the kernel is involved only when the atomic operation detects contention and blocking is necessary.
consequence: Futexes are the foundation of low-overhead locking in Linux thread libraries.

title: Inodes and Directory Entries
subject: Operating Systems
statement: In Unix-like file systems, an inode holds a file's metadata and data-block pointers, while directory entries map human-readable names to inode numbers.
short: Names are separate from file identity, which is stored in the inode.
long: Names are separate from file identity, which is stored in the inode. Hard links are additional directory entries pointing to the same inode; the file's data disappears only when the last link is removed.
proof: Separating names from metadata lets several names refer to one inode, so the kernel maintains a link count in the inode to know when to free its blocks.
consequence: The inode abstraction underpins links, permissions, and file identity in Unix systems.

title: Journaling File Systems and Write Ordering
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A journaling file system writes a record of intended metadata changes before applying them, so a crash can be repaired by replaying committed transactions and discarding incomplete ones.
short: Recording intent first turns crash recovery into log replay rather than a full scan.
long: Recording intent first turns crash recovery into log replay rather than a full scan. Ordering modes differ in whether file data is written before metadata. Full journaling of data gives the strongest guarantees at the cost of extra writes.
proof: Because the log states which operations were intended and which committed, recovery can distinguish completed transactions from partial ones and restore a consistent metadata state.
consequence: Journaling dramatically reduces file system check time after unclean shutdowns.

title: Hard Links versus Symbolic Links
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A hard link is another directory entry for an existing inode, while a symbolic link is a separate file containing a pathname to a target. Deleting the original name leaves a hard link working but breaks a symbolic link.
short: Hard links share identity; symbolic links store a redirect.
long: Hard links share identity; symbolic links store a redirect. Hard links generally cannot cross file system boundaries and cannot link directories. Symbolic links can cross boundaries but become dangling if the target is moved or removed.
proof: Hard links reference the inode directly, so they remain valid as long as the inode exists; symbolic links are resolved by path lookup at access time, so moving the target breaks resolution.
consequence: The distinction affects backup, deletion, and path-resolution behaviour.

title: RAID Levels and Redundancy
subject: Operating Systems
statement: RAID combines disks for throughput, capacity, or fault tolerance: RAID 0 stripes without redundancy, RAID 1 mirrors, RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity, and RAID 6 adds a second parity stripe.
short: Striping improves performance, mirroring or parity survives disk failure.
long: Striping improves performance, mirroring or parity survives disk failure. Parity is computed with bitwise exclusive-or, allowing a failed disk to be reconstructed from surviving blocks and parity. RAID 6 tolerates two simultaneous failures.
proof: Exclusive-or parity satisfies data_1 xor ... xor data_k = parity, so any missing block is recovered by XORing all other blocks and the parity block.
consequence: RAID is the standard way to trade disk count for reliability and throughput.

title: Rate-Monotonic Scheduling and Priorities
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Rate-monotonic scheduling assigns fixed priorities by period, with shorter periods receiving higher priority. For independent periodic tasks whose deadlines equal their periods, it is optimal among fixed-priority policies.
short: Shorter periods earn higher fixed priority and give the best fixed-priority schedule.
long: Shorter periods earn higher fixed priority and give the best fixed-priority schedule. Feasibility is guaranteed when total utilisation is at most n times the nth root of two, though some sets above that bound are still schedulable. Exact response-time analysis gives a tighter test.
proof: An exchange argument shows that if some fixed-priority assignment is feasible, swapping adjacent priority assignments so the shorter period is higher preserves feasibility; hence rate-monotonic order is optimal.
consequence: Rate-monotonic analysis is a standard design tool for hard real-time systems.

title: Earliest Deadline First Scheduling Optimality
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Earliest-deadline-first scheduling always runs the ready task with the nearest absolute deadline. On a single processor it is optimal for independent preemptive tasks with deadlines equal to periods.
short: The most urgent task runs first, and no other policy can meet a deadline EDF misses.
long: The most urgent task runs first, and no other policy can meet a deadline EDF misses. EDF can achieve utilisation up to one hundred percent but is less predictable under overload than fixed-priority scheduling, where low-priority tasks simply miss deadlines.
proof: If EDF misses a deadline, a feasibility argument shows every legal schedule misses one: any schedule can be transformed into an EDF schedule without increasing any job's lateness by swapping adjacent out-of-order executions.
consequence: EDF is the theoretical optimum for uniprocessor dynamic-priority real-time scheduling.

title: Priority Inversion and Priority Inheritance
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task while a medium-priority task preempts the holder. Priority inheritance temporarily raises the holder to the highest priority of waiting tasks.
short: Temporarily boost the lock holder so it can finish and release the lock.
long: Temporarily boost the lock holder so it can finish and release the lock. The Mars Pathfinder mission famously experienced priority inversion. Priority ceilings offer an alternative by assigning each lock a fixed high priority.
proof: Raising the holder above the medium-priority task lets it complete its critical section, after which the high-priority task proceeds, hence the inversion is bounded by one critical section.
consequence: Priority inheritance is required in real-time systems that share resources across priority levels.

title: Jitter in Real-Time Systems
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Jitter is variation in the start or completion times of periodically recurring tasks relative to an ideal schedule. Real-time systems constrain jitter because variability can violate deadlines even when average latency is low.
short: Predictable timing matters as much as fast average timing.
long: Predictable timing matters as much as fast average timing. Interrupt handling, cache misses, and garbage collection are common sources of jitter. Hard real-time systems use dedicated scheduling and minimal interrupt masking to bound it.
proof: Each invocation's actual start time differs from its ideal periodic instant by accumulated interference, so the maximum deviation quantifies timing variability.
consequence: Jitter bounds are central to audio, control loops, and networked media applications.

title: Container Namespaces and Control Groups
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Linux namespaces give a group of processes private views of resources such as process identifiers, mount points, and network interfaces. Control groups limit and account for their CPU, memory, and I/O usage.
short: Namespaces virtualise what a process sees; control groups cap what it can consume.
long: Namespaces virtualise what a process sees; control groups cap what it can consume. Containers combine namespaces, cgroups, and a private filesystem image without running a separate kernel. They are lighter than virtual machines but share the host kernel.
proof: The kernel tags processes with namespace memberships so lookups resolve within their private view, while cgroup membership routes resource accounting and enforcement to the group's limits.
consequence: Namespaces and cgroups are the technical foundation of modern container runtimes.

title: DMA and Interrupt-Driven I/O
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Direct memory access lets a device transfer blocks of data between itself and main memory without the CPU copying each word. The CPU programs the controller and receives an interrupt when the transfer completes.
short: The CPU sets up the transfer and is interrupted only when it finishes.
long: The CPU sets up the transfer and is interrupted only when it finishes. DMA reduces CPU overhead for disks, network cards, and graphics devices. The memory controller must arbitrate bus access between the CPU and the DMA engine.
proof: The controller takes over bus transactions for the duration of the transfer, so the CPU is free to run other work until the completion interrupt signals that the buffer is ready.
consequence: DMA is essential for high-throughput I/O without saturating the processor.

title: Lexical Analysis with Finite Automata
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A lexer scans characters and groups them into tokens using patterns described by regular expressions. A scanner generator compiles token patterns into a finite automaton that recognises token classes.
short: Token patterns become automata that consume input in linear time.
long: Token patterns become automata that consume input in linear time. Longest-match rules and token priorities resolve cases where several patterns match a prefix. The resulting token stream is the parser's input.
proof: Regular expressions and finite automata recognise the same language class, so converting each token pattern to an automaton and taking their union recognises exactly the token set.
consequence: Clean separation of lexing and parsing simplifies both phases of a compiler front end.

title: DFA Minimisation in Lexer Generation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Every regular language has a unique minimal DFA up to renaming of states. Partition refinement splits blocks of states that behave differently on some input symbol until no further split is possible.
short: Merge indistinguishable automaton states to obtain the smallest scanner.
long: Merge indistinguishable automaton states to obtain the smallest scanner. The algorithm starts with accepting and non-accepting states and refines by transition behaviour. It runs in polynomial time in the number of states.
proof: States in one block are equivalent for all strings observed so far; refining on each symbol separates exactly states distinguishable by some suffix, and the final quotient is minimal and unique.
consequence: Minimisation keeps generated scanners small and fast.

title: Recursive-Descent Parsing and Backtracking
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A recursive-descent parser implements grammar productions as mutually recursive procedures that consume tokens. Predictive recursive descent requires disjoint first sets for alternatives to avoid backtracking.
short: Each grammar production becomes a procedure that recognises its right-hand side.
long: Each grammar production becomes a procedure that recognises its right-hand side. Backtracking parsers try alternatives and restore the input position on failure. Left recursion must be eliminated before using recursive descent.
proof: Each procedure consumes the terminals of its production and calls procedures for nonterminals, so the resulting call tree mirrors a valid derivation of the input string.
consequence: LL grammars support simple, efficient, hand-written parsers.

title: LR(0) Item Sets and Shift-Reduce Parsing
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: An LR(0) item is a production with a marker showing how much of its right-hand side has been consumed. Canonical collections of item sets form the states of a shift-reduce parser operating with a stack and input lookahead.
short: Item sets track all possible production positions consistent with the prefix already parsed.
long: Item sets track all possible production positions consistent with the prefix already parsed. Shift moves a terminal onto the stack; reduce replaces a production's right-hand side by its left-hand side. Conflicts signal that the grammar is not LR(0).
proof: Each item set records valid positions in productions for the parsed prefix, so shifting or reducing according to the automaton maintains a stack encoding a viable prefix.
consequence: LR parsing recognises a broad class of grammars deterministically in linear time.

title: LALR Parser Construction
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: LALR parser generation merges LR(1) item sets with identical cores while retaining lookahead information. The resulting tables are much smaller than canonical LR(1) tables and may introduce reduce-reduce conflicts.
short: Merging lookahead states trades a little power for much smaller tables.
long: Merging lookahead states trades a little power for much smaller tables. Yacc and Bison generate LALR parsers by default. Grammars that are LALR-compatible avoid the conflicts that merging can create.
proof: Merging states with the same LR(0) core unions their lookahead sets; the automaton still recognises the same viable prefixes, but extra lookaheads can create spurious conflicts.
consequence: LALR is the practical standard for parser generators.

title: Ambiguous Grammars and Operator Precedence
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: An ambiguous grammar admits more than one parse tree for a string. Parser generators usually resolve common ambiguities by declaring operator precedence and associativity instead of rewriting the grammar.
short: Precedence declarations choose one of several possible parse trees.
long: Precedence declarations choose one of several possible parse trees. A shift-reduce conflict on an expression grammar is resolved by comparing the precedence of the pending operator with the next token.
proof: The expression 1+2*3 has two derivations under the ambiguous grammar; precedence rules resolve the shift-reduce conflict so that multiplication binds tighter.
consequence: Ambiguity resolution directly determines the semantics of expressions.

title: Syntax Error Recovery in Parsers
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Error recovery techniques such as panic mode discard tokens until a synchronising token is found, allowing a parser to continue and report several errors in one run.
short: Skip forward to a token that can legitimately follow the faulty construct.
long: Skip forward to a token that can legitimately follow the faulty construct. Other strategies include phrase-level recovery and error productions. Poor recovery can cascade, producing many spurious messages after the first error.
proof: Discarding input until a token in the follow set of the current nonterminal restores a consistent parsing state, so subsequent input can be analysed.
consequence: Effective recovery greatly improves the developer experience of a compiler.

title: Concrete versus Abstract Syntax Trees
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A concrete syntax tree records every grammar symbol in a derivation, while an abstract syntax tree retains only semantically meaningful nodes. Compilers normally discard punctuation and syntactic sugar after parsing.
short: The AST is the grammar-free skeleton the rest of the compiler works with.
long: The AST is the grammar-free skeleton the rest of the compiler works with. Unary productions introduced for precedence are collapsed, and tokens such as semicolons are dropped, leaving operator and operand nodes.
proof: Removing punctuation and chain nodes preserves the semantic content of a derivation while shrinking the tree, so subsequent passes can operate on a cleaner representation.
consequence: The AST is the interface between the parser and semantic analysis.

title: Three-Address Code as an Intermediate Representation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Three-address code is an intermediate representation in which each instruction has at most three operands and one operator, such as t1 = t2 + t3. It makes evaluation order explicit while remaining largely machine independent.
short: Flatten expressions into simple instructions with temporaries.
long: Flatten expressions into simple instructions with temporaries. Quadruples and triples are common implementations. Three-address code is close enough to machine code for optimisation yet far enough to stay portable.
proof: Introducing a fresh temporary for each subexpression flattens an arbitrary syntax tree into instructions each having at most three operands.
consequence: It is a widely used bridge between syntax trees and target machine code.

title: Control-Flow Graphs and Basic Blocks
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence with a single entry and a single exit. A control-flow graph uses basic blocks as nodes and possible control transfers as edges.
short: Partition code into straight-line chunks and connect them by branches.
long: Partition code into straight-line chunks and connect them by branches. Leaders are the first instruction, branch targets, and instructions following branches. Loops and dominators are defined on the resulting graph.
proof: Splitting at leaders gives maximal straight-line regions, and adding an edge for every possible transfer between them yields a graph representing all execution paths.
consequence: Nearly all dataflow analyses and optimisations operate on control-flow graphs.

title: Phi Nodes in SSA Merging
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: In static single assignment form a phi node selects a value according to the control-flow edge used to reach a join point. Phi nodes give each variable exactly one definition even where paths merge.
short: A phi node chooses among reaching definitions at a merge point.
long: A phi node chooses among reaching definitions at a merge point. Phi nodes are later lowered into moves in predecessor blocks during register allocation. Correct placement is computed from dominance frontiers.
proof: Inserting a phi whose arguments are the definitions reaching each incoming edge preserves value semantics while ensuring every variable has a single defining instruction.
consequence: SSA simplifies constant propagation, dead-code elimination, and many other passes.

title: Dominator Trees and Immediate Dominators
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Node d dominates node n in a control-flow graph if every path from the entry to n passes through d. The immediate dominator of n is its closest strict dominator, and these relations form the dominator tree.
short: Dominators identify nodes that must execute before a given point.
long: Dominators identify nodes that must execute before a given point. Dominance frontiers, built from the dominator tree, determine where phi nodes are required in SSA conversion.
proof: Dominance is reflexive and transitive and each node except the entry has a unique immediate dominator, so the relation forms a tree rooted at the entry.
consequence: Dominators underpin loop detection, SSA construction, and code motion.

title: Liveness Analysis by Backward Dataflow
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A variable is live at a point if its current value may be used before being redefined. Liveness analysis propagates use and definition sets backwards over the control-flow graph to a fixed point.
short: Work backwards from uses to find variables whose values still matter.
long: Work backwards from uses to find variables whose values still matter. The analysis is a must-free may-analysis: a variable is live if some path from the point reaches a use before a definition.
proof: Uses make variables live at block entry unless defined first, and live variables at a successor's entry are live at the block's exit; iterating to a fixed point handles cycles in loops.
consequence: Liveness drives register allocation, dead-code elimination, and spill decisions.

title: Reaching Definitions Analysis
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Reaching definitions analysis determines which assignments may have produced the current value of a variable at each program point. It is a forward may-analysis over the control-flow graph.
short: Track which definitions can still flow to each point without being overwritten.
long: Track which definitions can still flow to each point without being overwritten. A definition kills previous definitions of the same variable and generates itself. Join points union the incoming definition sets.
proof: A definition reaches a point exactly when a path exists from its assignment to that point with no intervening redefinition; union at joins and propagation through blocks compute those paths.
consequence: Reaching definitions support constant propagation and use-def chains.

title: Constant Folding and Propagation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Constant folding evaluates compile-time constant expressions, and constant propagation replaces variables known to hold constants with those values. The passes are usually iterated until no further change occurs.
short: Compute what is known at compile time and reuse it everywhere.
long: Compute what is known at compile time and reuse it everywhere. Sparse conditional constant propagation combines propagation with branch reachability to avoid incorrect substitutions on infeasible paths.
proof: Replacing a variable by a provably equal constant and evaluating pure operators preserves semantics under the language's evaluation rules.
consequence: These are among the simplest and most widely applied compiler optimisations.

title: Dead Code Elimination
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Dead code elimination removes instructions whose results are never used and that have no side effects. Liveness information identifies such instructions safely.
short: Unused pure computations can be deleted without changing behaviour.
long: Unused pure computations can be deleted without changing behaviour. Aggressive elimination also removes unreachable basic blocks and branches with constant conditions.
proof: If the defined value is not live at the instruction's exit and the instruction has no side effects, executing it cannot influence any later observable action.
consequence: Dead-code removal shrinks binaries and reduces wasted runtime work.

title: Common Subexpression Elimination
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Common subexpression elimination replaces repeated computations of the same expression with a single previously computed value, provided no operand changed in between.
short: Reuse a result when the same computation is still available.
long: Reuse a result when the same computation is still available. Available-expression analysis determines which expressions are still valid at each point, killing expressions whose operands are redefined.
proof: If available-expression analysis proves the operands retained their values since the earlier computation, reusing the stored result yields the same value.
consequence: The optimisation is especially effective across repeated address calculations.

title: Loop-Invariant Code Motion
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Loop-invariant code motion moves computations that depend only on loop-invariant values outside the loop, provided the move introduces no new exceptions or side effects.
short: Compute once outside the loop what would otherwise be recomputed each iteration.
long: Compute once outside the loop what would otherwise be recomputed each iteration. Safety checks ensure the hoisted instruction executes at least as often as in the original and does not change exception behaviour.
proof: An expression whose operands never change inside the loop has the same value on every iteration, so computing it once before entry yields the same results.
consequence: Hoisting is a major source of speedups in numeric and array code.

title: Register Allocation via Graph Colouring
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Register allocation can be modelled as graph colouring: vertices are live ranges and edges connect interfering ranges that cannot share a register. Colouring with k colours assigns k machine registers.
short: Interfering live ranges need different registers, like adjacent vertices need different colours.
long: Interfering live ranges need different registers, like adjacent vertices need different colours. Chaitin-style allocators simplify the interference graph by removing low-degree vertices and then colour greedily during spill-recovery.
proof: Two variables simultaneously live cannot share a register without destroying a value, so a proper colouring of the interference graph is a valid allocation.
consequence: Colouring gives a principled framework for one of the backend's most important tasks.

title: Spilling and Rematerialisation in Register Allocation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: When a live range cannot be coloured with the available registers, the allocator spills it to memory. Rematerialisation recomputes a cheap value on demand instead of storing and reloading it.
short: Either save a value to memory or recreate it cheaply when needed.
long: Either save a value to memory or recreate it cheaply when needed. Spill code inserts loads and stores at defined points; rematerialisation is preferred for constants and simple address computations.
proof: Removing a spilled vertex lowers interference degree until colouring succeeds; if a value is cheap to recompute from live operands, recomputation is a correct alternative to storage.
consequence: Good spill choices often matter more than the colouring heuristic itself.

title: Instruction Scheduling for Pipeline Latency
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Instruction scheduling reorders independent instructions to fill delay slots created by long-latency operations while preserving data dependences and observable ordering.
latex: load\ r1;\ use\ r1\Rightarrow\text{insert independent work}
short: Do useful work while waiting for a slow operation to finish.
long: Do useful work while waiting for a slow operation to finish. List scheduling builds a dependence graph and repeatedly picks a ready instruction with highest priority. Speculative scheduling must respect exception semantics.
proof: Reordering instructions with no dependence between them leaves data flow unchanged while allowing the processor to overlap latency with other work.
consequence: Scheduling is essential to exploit superscalar and pipelined processors.

title: Static Linking and Relocation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A static linker resolves symbolic references among object files, combines their sections, and applies relocations so that addresses refer to the final program layout.
short: The linker patches placeholder addresses once the final layout is known.
long: The linker patches placeholder addresses once the final layout is known. Object files contain symbol tables and relocation entries describing where patches are needed. Static linking produces a self-contained executable.
proof: Each object file lists placeholder locations and symbolic targets; after assigning section addresses the linker resolves symbols and rewrites each placeholder with the final value.
consequence: Relocation is the mechanism that makes separately compiled modules combinable.

title: Just-in-Time Compilation and Warm-Up
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A just-in-time compiler translates bytecode to native machine code at run time, typically for frequently executed methods. Warm-up is the early period when interpretation dominates before hot code is compiled.
short: Compile at run time only the code that proves worth compiling.
long: Compile at run time only the code that proves worth compiling. JIT compilers use execution profiles to guide optimisation, which can produce better code than ahead-of-time compilation for dynamic languages.
proof: Monitoring identifies hot methods; compiling them with profile information produces native code whose speed justifies the compilation cost.
consequence: JIT compilation combines portability with strong steady-state performance.

title: Tiered Compilation in HotSpot JVM
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Tiered compilation runs code first in an interpreter, then in a lightly optimising compiler, and finally in an aggressively optimising compiler as invocation counts grow.
short: Spend compilation effort only on code that proves hot.
long: Spend compilation effort only on code that proves hot. Lower tiers produce code quickly and gather profiles; higher tiers use those profiles for expensive optimisations such as inlining and speculative type specialisation.
proof: The lower tiers have low compilation cost and supply profile data, so delaying expensive optimisation until a method is hot avoids wasting effort on cold code.
consequence: Tiered execution improves both startup time and peak throughput.

title: Deoptimisation and Bailout in JIT
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A JIT compiler can deoptimise specialised native code back to bytecode when an assumed condition fails, such as an unexpected object type. Bailout preserves language semantics despite speculative optimisation.
short: Guard the optimistic assumptions and fall back when they break.
long: Guard the optimistic assumptions and fall back when they break. Deoptimisation reconstructs interpreter frames from the compiled state, including inlined frames, which requires precise metadata.
proof: Guards detect violated assumptions and transfer control to an unoptimised representation whose execution reproduces the specified behaviour.
consequence: Speculative optimisation can be aggressive without sacrificing correctness.

title: Escape Analysis and Scalar Replacement
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Escape analysis determines whether an allocated object can be referenced outside its creating method or thread. Non-escaping objects may be scalar-replaced, keeping their fields in registers rather than on the heap.
short: Avoid allocating objects that never leave the local scope.
long: Avoid allocating objects that never leave the local scope. Escape information also enables lock elision because thread-local objects need no synchronisation.
proof: If no reference to the object survives the analysis scope, substituting its component values is observationally equivalent and removes allocation and collection work.
consequence: Escape analysis reduces garbage-collector pressure and synchronisation cost.

title: Inline Expansion in Compilers
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Inlining replaces a function call with the callee's body, removing call overhead and exposing optimisations across the former boundary. Excessive inlining can increase code size and hurt instruction-cache locality.
short: Substitute a call by its body to expose more optimisation opportunities.
long: Substitute a call by its body to expose more optimisation opportunities. Inlining decisions use call frequency, callee size, and profile data. Recursive functions need special handling or size cutoffs.
proof: Binding parameters to argument values and substituting the callee's body implements the same computation, so the transformed program is semantically equivalent.
consequence: Inlining is often the optimisation that enables many others.

title: GC Roots and Reachability
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A tracing garbage collector treats stack variables, registers, globals, and runtime internals as roots and reclaims objects unreachable from them. Garbage is defined by reachability, not by reference count.
short: Anything the program can no longer reach can be reclaimed.
long: Anything the program can no longer reach can be reclaimed. Precise collectors need accurate stack maps identifying which slots hold references; missing a root would incorrectly reclaim a live object.
proof: An object unreachable from any root can never be accessed by the program again, so reclaiming its storage is safe.
consequence: Root accuracy is a correctness requirement for automatic memory management.

title: Tri-Colour Marking Invariant
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Incremental tracing collectors colour objects white, grey, and black. The tri-colour invariant forbids a black object from pointing directly to a white object, ensuring all reachable objects are eventually discovered.
short: Maintain a grey frontier so tracing cannot lose a reachable object.
long: Maintain a grey frontier so tracing cannot lose a reachable object. Write barriers re-grey a source or shade a target when a black-to-white reference is created. The invariant is broken only momentarily inside barrier code.
proof: Any white object reachable from a root must be reached through a grey frontier; if a black-to-white edge appears, a barrier restores the invariant by greying one endpoint.
consequence: The invariant is the correctness foundation of concurrent and incremental collectors.

title: Stop-the-World versus Incremental Collection
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Stop-the-world collectors pause application threads while tracing, which is simple but can cause long pauses. Incremental and concurrent collectors interleave tracing with execution and use barriers to stay correct.
short: Shorter pauses are bought with more sophisticated coordination.
long: Shorter pauses are bought with more sophisticated coordination. Concurrent collectors must handle the heap graph changing during marking and usually stop briefly for final root rescanning.
proof: Pausing prevents mutation during tracing; allowing mutation requires barriers that record changes so the collector does not overlook newly reachable objects.
consequence: Pause-time goals drive the choice of collector design.

title: Write Barriers and Remembered Sets
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A generational collector records cross-generation references in a remembered set using write barriers on pointer updates. Minor collections then scan roots plus the remembered set instead of the whole heap.
short: Remember the old-to-young pointers so young collections stay cheap.
long: Remember the old-to-young pointers so young collections stay cheap. Card marking divides the old generation into cards and flags a card when a pointer inside it is updated. Remembered sets must be maintained even during concurrent phases.
proof: Old-to-young pointers are the only non-root way a young object can be reachable after a minor collection, so recording them at write time suffices to find all live young objects.
consequence: Write barriers are a small per-write cost that makes generational collection practical.

title: Conservative Garbage Collection
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A conservative collector scans memory without precise type information and treats any bit pattern that could be a pointer as a possible reference. It is safe without accurate pointer maps but may retain unreachable objects.
short: Better to keep a dead object than to reclaim a live one.
long: Better to keep a dead object than to reclaim a live one. Conservative collection works with languages such as C where pointer locations cannot always be identified. Interior pointers can force an entire object to be retained.
proof: Treating every plausible pointer as genuine can only retain extra objects, never reclaim a reachable one, so the collector is safe though imprecise.
consequence: Conservative collectors trade memory efficiency for language compatibility.

title: Bytecode Verification in the JVM
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: The JVM verifier checks that untrusted bytecode respects type and stack discipline before execution, preventing forged pointers and stack corruption. Verification is a static dataflow analysis over the instruction graph.
short: Prove type safety of bytecode before allowing it to run.
long: Prove type safety of bytecode before allowing it to run. Verification tracks operand-stack and local-variable types at every instruction and checks that all control-flow paths agree at merge points.
proof: Abstract interpretation of types along every control-flow path shows each instruction receives values of expected types, so malformed code is rejected before execution.
consequence: Verification is a key part of the JVM sandboxing model.

title: Garbage Collection Safepoints
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A safepoint is a program location where the runtime can stop all threads to inspect their roots safely. Precise collectors require threads to reach safepoints before tracing begins.
short: Stop threads only where their reference locations are known.
long: Stop threads only where their reference locations are known. The compiler emits safepoint polls at loop backedges and call sites. Stack maps describe which registers and stack slots contain references at each safepoint.
proof: At a safepoint the runtime knows exactly which locations hold references, giving a consistent root set; arbitrary stopping points would make root discovery unreliable.
consequence: Safepoint placement balances pause latency against poll overhead.

title: Unit Tests and Coverage Criteria
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Unit tests exercise individual program units in isolation. Coverage criteria such as statement, branch, and path coverage measure which parts of the code a test suite actually executes.
short: Coverage measures how much of the code a test suite has touched.
long: Coverage measures how much of the code a test suite has touched. Branch coverage is stronger than statement coverage, and path coverage is stronger still but rarely exhaustive. High coverage does not guarantee the absence of bugs.
proof: Instrumenting code records which statements or branches execute, and the ratio of executed items to total items defines the corresponding coverage metric.
consequence: Coverage gives an objective, if incomplete, measure of test-suite breadth.

title: Mutation Testing Measures Test Suite Strength
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Mutation testing creates small syntactic variants of a program and checks whether a test suite kills them by failing. A high mutation score indicates a suite sensitive to fault-like changes.
short: A test suite is strong if it notices deliberate small faults.
long: A test suite is strong if it notices deliberate small faults. Equivalent mutants produce the same behaviour as the original and are usually excluded. Mutation testing is computationally expensive because each mutant requires a full test run.
proof: Each mutant differs by one fault-like change; if no test distinguishes it from the original, that class of defect is undetected, so survival exposes a weakness.
consequence: Mutation scores often correlate better with defect detection than statement coverage.

title: Property-Based Testing with Generated Inputs
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Property-based testing generates many inputs and checks that a stated invariant holds for each. Shrinking reduces a failing input to a small, informative counterexample.
short: State universal properties and let the machine search for counterexamples.
long: State universal properties and let the machine search for counterexamples. Generators encode the input domain, and shrinking repeatedly simplifies a failing value while preserving the failure.
proof: Generated sampling explores many inputs beyond handwritten cases; stepwise shrinking removes parts of a failing input while the property still fails, yielding a minimal witness.
consequence: Property-based testing finds edge cases that example-based tests often miss.

title: Coverage-Guided Fuzzing
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Coverage-guided fuzzing mutates seed inputs, keeps mutants that reach new code coverage, and repeats, using coverage as a search heuristic.
short: Grow a corpus of inputs that explores more of the program.
long: Grow a corpus of inputs that explores more of the program. Instrumentation records edge coverage, and sanitizers detect memory-safety violations during execution.
proof: Retaining inputs that expand coverage focuses search on unexplored regions, and mutation explores variations of promising seeds.
consequence: Fuzzing has discovered large numbers of real security vulnerabilities.

title: Regression Testing and Test Oracles
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Regression testing reruns existing tests after changes to detect newly introduced defects. A test oracle determines whether an execution's outcome is correct.
short: Reuse past expectations to catch behavioural changes.
long: Reuse past expectations to catch behavioural changes. Oracles may be explicit expected values, reference implementations, or invariants. The oracle problem refers to cases where correctness is hard to specify.
proof: Storing expected outcomes from a trusted baseline allows later executions to be compared, so a behavioural change is detected as a regression.
consequence: Regression suites are the main defence against breaking working software.

title: Integration Testing versus System Testing
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Integration testing checks that modules interact correctly, while system testing checks the complete product against its specification. Integration tests target interfaces; system tests target end-to-end behaviour.
short: First check that pieces fit, then check the assembled product.
long: First check that pieces fit, then check the assembled product. Common integration strategies include bottom-up, top-down, and sandwich approaches using stubs and drivers.
proof: Combining modules exposes interface mismatches invisible to unit tests, while exercising the assembled system validates requirements that emerge only from the whole.
consequence: The two levels catch disjoint classes of defects.

title: Continuous Integration and Automated Builds
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Continuous integration merges changes frequently into a shared branch and automatically builds and tests each integration, detecting conflicts and regressions early.
short: Integrate often and let automation check every merge.
long: Integrate often and let automation check every merge. Fast feedback encourages small changes and makes failures easy to localise to a recent commit.
proof: Building and testing on every merge shortens the interval between introducing and detecting a defect, which reduces the cost of diagnosing it.
consequence: Continuous integration is a foundation of modern collaborative development.

title: Static versus Dynamic Type Checking
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Static type checking rejects ill-typed programs before execution, while dynamic checking detects type errors during execution. Static checking catches errors earlier but can reject safe programs that a dynamic language accepts.
short: Prove safety ahead of time or check it while running.
long: Prove safety ahead of time or check it while running. Gradual typing combines both by allowing typed and untyped code to interoperate with casts at boundaries.
proof: A static type system proves a property for all executions by construction, while dynamic checks inspect operations at run time and only report errors on paths actually taken.
consequence: The choice affects error detection timing, flexibility, and runtime overhead.

title: Hindley-Milner Type Inference
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Hindley–Milner type inference assigns principal types to expressions in a typed lambda calculus with let-polymorphism without annotations. Algorithm W computes the most general type scheme by unification.
short: Unification discovers the most general type automatically.
long: Unification discovers the most general type automatically. The principal type property means every other valid typing is an instance of the inferred one.
proof: Generating fresh type variables and unifying constraints from applications yields the most general unifier, which is the principal type scheme.
consequence: ML and Haskell families combine strong static typing with little annotation burden.

title: Exhaustiveness Checking for Algebraic Data Types
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Exhaustiveness checking verifies that a pattern match covers every constructor of an algebraic data type. A non-exhaustive match can fail at run time, so compilers warn or reject such code.
short: Ensure every possible value is handled by some pattern.
long: Ensure every possible value is handled by some pattern. Nested patterns and guards complicate coverage checking; some compilers use binary decision diagrams to decide exhaustiveness.
proof: Each pattern covers a subset of constructor combinations, and comparing their union with the full constructor set detects missing cases.
consequence: Exhaustiveness makes refactoring data types safer because missing cases are reported at compile time.

title: Weakest Precondition Calculus
subject: Software Engineering
statement: The weakest precondition of a program and a postcondition is the weakest assertion guaranteeing that postcondition after execution. It is computed backwards through assignments, sequences, and conditionals.
short: Work backwards from the desired postcondition to what must hold before.
long: Work backwards from the desired postcondition to what must hold before. For conditionals the weakest precondition is a conjunction guarded by the branch conditions; loops require loop invariants or least fixed points.
proof: Substituting e for x in Q is exactly the condition on the pre-state making Q true after the assignment; composition follows by backward propagation.
consequence: Weakest preconditions are the basis of deductive program verification tools.

title: Design by Contract
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Design by contract specifies preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants that cooperating components must satisfy. Violations identify which side of a module boundary broke the agreement.
short: Document the obligations and guarantees of every component.
long: Document the obligations and guarantees of every component. Eiffel integrates contracts into the language; other systems use annotations or assertion libraries.
proof: Checking preconditions at entry and postconditions and invariants at exit localises responsibility to caller or callee.
consequence: Contracts make module interfaces more precise and debugging more direct.

title: Software Refactoring Preserves Behaviour
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Refactoring restructures code without changing externally observable behaviour. Tests serve as a safety net verifying behaviour preservation across the transformation.
short: Change the structure, not the behaviour.
long: Change the structure, not the behaviour. Typical refactorings include extract method, rename variable, and replace conditional with polymorphism.
proof: Each refactoring is a behaviour-preserving transformation, and the test suite checks that observable outputs remain unchanged after applying it.
consequence: Refactoring keeps designs clean without introducing new functionality.

title: Coupling and Cohesion in Module Design
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities inside a module are, while coupling measures the strength of dependencies between modules. Good designs favour high cohesion and low coupling.
short: Keep related code together and dependencies few.
long: Keep related code together and dependencies few. Highly cohesive modules change for one reason; loosely coupled modules limit the propagation of changes across the system.
proof: A module with a single focused responsibility has fewer reasons to change, and weak dependencies reduce the number of other modules affected by a change.
consequence: These principles guide decomposition into maintainable components.

title: Semantic Versioning Rules
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Semantic versioning uses major.minor.patch numbers: a major increment signals incompatible API changes, a minor increment adds backward-compatible functionality, and a patch increment makes backward-compatible fixes.
short: Version numbers encode the compatibility impact of a release.
long: Version numbers encode the compatibility impact of a release. Pre-release identifiers and build metadata extend the basic format. Consumers can express dependency constraints using these rules.
proof: The specification defines each component's meaning, so comparing two versions determines whether an upgrade should preserve existing clients.
consequence: Semantic versioning makes dependency management predictable.

title: Technical Debt Metaphor
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Technical debt describes the future maintenance cost of choosing a quick, limited solution over a more robust one. Like financial debt it accumulates interest when deferred work makes later changes harder.
short: A quick fix today can make every future change more expensive.
long: A quick fix today can make every future change more expensive. Debt may be deliberate and beneficial when a short-term goal justifies it, but it becomes harmful when it is invisible or never repaid.
proof: A shortcut leaves code harder to understand or extend, so subsequent changes require more effort than they would in a clean design.
consequence: Making debt visible helps teams schedule remediation.

title: Cyclomatic Complexity of Control Flow
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Cyclomatic complexity of a control-flow graph is E minus N plus twice the number of connected components. It bounds the number of linearly independent execution paths and is used as a code complexity metric.
short: Count independent paths as a measure of testing difficulty.
long: Count independent paths as a measure of testing difficulty. For a single connected component the formula reduces to E minus N plus two. High cyclomatic complexity correlates with harder-to-test code.
proof: The cyclomatic number of a graph counts independent cycles, which for a single-entry single-exit flow graph equals the maximum number of independent execution paths.
consequence: The metric is widely used to flag functions that need more testing or refactoring.

title: Needham-Schroeder Protocol and Replay
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The original Needham–Schroeder symmetric-key protocol is vulnerable to replay: if an old session key is recovered, an attacker can replay a recorded message and convince a principal to accept that key.
short: A valid old message can be reused when freshness is not tied to a new nonce.
long: A valid old message can be reused when freshness is not tied to a new nonce. The Lowe attack on the public-key variant similarly exploits a missing identity check in the response message.
proof: The replayed message carries no nonce freshly generated by the receiving principal in the current run, so it is accepted as evidence of a new session key.
consequence: The attack established that freshness mechanisms are indispensable in authentication protocols.

title: Kerberos Ticket-Based Authentication
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Kerberos authenticates clients to services using tickets issued by a trusted key distribution centre. A ticket contains a session key and client identity encrypted for the service, so the client never sends its password.
short: A trusted third party issues encrypted tickets that prove identity.
long: A trusted third party issues encrypted tickets that prove identity. The ticket-granting ticket lets a client obtain service tickets without re-entering its password; authenticators with timestamps prevent replay.
proof: Only the intended service can decrypt its ticket, and the client proves knowledge of the enclosed session key with a fresh authenticator, giving mutual authentication.
consequence: Kerberos underpins single sign-on in many enterprise environments.

title: TLS Handshake and Certificate Chain
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The TLS handshake negotiates cryptographic parameters, authenticates the server through a certificate chain to a trusted root, and derives a shared session key. Subsequent records use authenticated encryption.
short: Negotiate, authenticate, derive keys, then protect traffic.
long: Negotiate, authenticate, derive keys, then protect traffic. Certificate revocation checking and hostname verification are essential parts of authentication in practice.
proof: Signatures chain from a trusted root through intermediates to the server's certificate, and an ephemeral key exchange produces a session key known only to the endpoints.
consequence: TLS is the foundation of confidentiality and integrity on the web.

title: Man-in-the-Middle Attack on Unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Unauthenticated Diffie–Hellman is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack: an attacker creates one shared secret with each party and relays traffic, which neither party can detect.
short: Secret sharing without authentication gives no assurance about who the peer is.
long: Secret sharing without authentication gives no assurance about who the peer is. Digital signatures or certificates on the exchanged public values authenticate the parties and prevent the attack.
proof: Each endpoint accepts the attacker's public value as coming from the other party, so the attacker shares a key with each and can decrypt and re-encrypt relayed messages.
consequence: Authentication is a necessary companion to key agreement.

title: Perfect Forward Secrecy with Ephemeral Keys
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Perfect forward secrecy ensures that compromising a long-term private key does not reveal past session keys. It is achieved by generating fresh ephemeral keys per session and discarding them afterwards.
short: Past sessions stay secret even if today's long-term key leaks.
long: Past sessions stay secret even if today's long-term key leaks. TLS 1.3 requires ephemeral key exchange for this reason; static RSA key transport does not provide forward secrecy.
proof: Each session key depends on ephemeral exponents that are no longer stored, so later knowledge of the long-term signing key cannot reconstruct them.
consequence: Forward secrecy limits the damage of delayed key compromise.

title: Challenge-Response Authentication
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Challenge–response authentication proves knowledge of a secret by requiring a correct reply to a fresh random challenge. Freshness prevents an eavesdropper from replaying a previously recorded response.
short: A new random question makes old answers useless.
long: A new random question makes old answers useless. The function may be a keyed hash, encryption, or digital signature depending on the setting.
proof: A freshly generated challenge makes the probability that a recorded response matches negligible, so a valid reply demonstrates current knowledge of the secret.
consequence: Challenge–response is a core pattern in authentication protocols.

title: Nonces Prevent Replay Attacks
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A nonce is a value used only once, typically generated freshly at random. Including nonces in authenticated messages lets a receiver detect replayed messages from earlier runs.
short: A fresh one-time value distinguishes this run from every earlier run.
long: A fresh one-time value distinguishes this run from every earlier run. Nonces may be random numbers or counters, but they must not repeat within the relevant security context.
proof: The receiver compares the nonce with values seen in current runs; an old message carries a nonce that does not match a freshly generated one.
consequence: Nonces are a simple and widely used freshness mechanism.

title: Bell-LaPadula Confidentiality Model
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The Bell–LaPadula model enforces confidentiality using two rules: no read up, so a subject cannot read a higher classification, and no write down, so it cannot write to a lower classification.
short: Information may flow upward in sensitivity but never downward.
long: Information may flow upward in sensitivity but never downward. The simple security property and the star property are state invariants of the model, applied to subjects and objects with security levels.
proof: Forbidding reads from higher levels and writes to lower levels prevents information from reaching a subject with insufficient clearance.
consequence: The model is the classical formal basis for mandatory access control.

title: Biba Integrity Model
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The Biba integrity model is the dual of Bell–LaPadula: subjects may not read lower-integrity data and may not write to higher-integrity data, preventing contamination of trusted information.
short: Reverse the information-flow rules to protect integrity rather than secrecy.
long: Reverse the information-flow rules to protect integrity rather than secrecy. Biba uses integrity levels and can be combined with confidentiality models when both properties matter.
proof: Reversing the direction of Bell–LaPadula's flow restrictions keeps low-integrity data from influencing high-integrity objects.
consequence: Biba is the standard formal model for integrity policies.

title: Capability-Based Security
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: In capability-based security, possession of an unforgeable reference called a capability grants authority over an object. A capability combines designation and permission in one transferable token.
short: Holding the unforgeable token is the authority.
long: Holding the unforgeable token is the authority. Capabilities may be implemented with kernel-protected handles or unguessable cryptographic tokens, and they support fine-grained delegation.
proof: Because capabilities cannot be forged or guessed without being granted, only a holder can name and access the object with the encoded rights.
consequence: Capability systems avoid ambient authority and make least privilege easier to enforce.

title: Access Control Lists versus Capabilities
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Access control lists attach a list of permitted principals to each object, whereas capabilities attach permissions to the reference a principal holds. The two are dual in where authority is stored.
short: ACLs ask who may access an object; capabilities ask what the bearer may do.
long: ACLs ask who may access an object; capabilities ask what the bearer may do. Delegation is easy with capabilities but awkward with ACLs, while revocation is often easier with ACLs.
proof: An ACL is consulted at the object on each access, while a capability is presented with the request; passing a capability simply transfers the reference.
consequence: The distinction shapes the design of operating systems and distributed authorization systems.

title: Principle of Least Privilege
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The principle of least privilege grants each component only the permissions it needs for its legitimate task and no more. It limits damage from accidents and compromised components.
short: Give exactly the permissions required, nothing more.
long: Give exactly the permissions required, nothing more. It applies to users, processes, and services, and is implemented through roles, sandboxing, and scoped tokens.
proof: Restricting rights reduces the set of actions available to a faulty or compromised component, bounding the harm it can cause.
consequence: Least privilege is a baseline requirement in security engineering.

title: Defence in Depth
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Defence in depth layers independent security controls so that failure of one does not expose the system. Typical layers include firewalls, authentication, encryption, logging, and input validation.
short: Several independent barriers are safer than one perfect one.
long: Several independent barriers are safer than one perfect one. The principle acknowledges that individual controls fail and aims to slow or detect an attacker rather than rely on a single boundary.
proof: An attacker must defeat several independent controls, so overall compromise probability is lower than with a single control.
consequence: Layered defences reduce risk from both known and unknown vulnerabilities.

title: Password Salting against Rainbow Tables
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Salting stores a unique random value with each password hash so identical passwords produce different hashes. Precomputed rainbow tables become ineffective because each salt requires its own table.
short: A per-account random value defeats precomputed password tables.
long: A per-account random value defeats precomputed password tables. Salts need not be secret, but they must be unique and generated with sufficient randomness.
proof: Including a different salt per account in the hash input means a precomputed chain for one salt cannot be reused for another account.
consequence: Salting is mandatory in any password storage scheme.

title: Key Stretching with bcrypt
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Key stretching applies a deliberately expensive iterative computation to a password before storing the derived value. Schemes such as bcrypt slow offline guessing while keeping legitimate logins tolerable.
short: Make every password guess expensive.
long: Make every password guess expensive. The work factor can be increased over time as hardware gets faster. Memory-hard schemes such as Argon2 also limit GPU and ASIC advantages.
proof: An attacker must repeat the full work factor for every guess, so raising the iteration count increases attack cost linearly while each legitimate login pays it only once.
consequence: Key stretching substantially raises the cost of offline cracking.

title: Multifactor Authentication Factors
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Multifactor authentication requires credentials from at least two distinct categories: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is. Combining categories reduces the impact of a single stolen credential.
short: Two different kinds of evidence beat two of the same kind.
long: Two different kinds of evidence beat two of the same kind. A password plus a hardware token is stronger than two passwords because the attack surfaces differ.
proof: Compromising one factor leaves at least one independent barrier, so an attacker must break multiple distinct mechanisms.
consequence: Multifactor authentication is recommended for high-value accounts.

title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework in which a client obtains a limited access token from an authorization server and uses it with a resource server. It delegates access without sharing the resource owner's credentials.
short: Delegate limited access using scoped, expiring tokens.
long: Delegate limited access using scoped, expiring tokens. Authorization code with PKCE is the recommended flow for public clients; implicit flows are deprecated.
proof: The token encodes scope and expiry, so the client acts only within the granted permissions and the resource owner's password never reaches it.
consequence: OAuth 2.0 is the dominant delegation protocol for web APIs.

title: Zero Trust Architecture
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Zero trust architecture assumes no implicit trust based on network location and requires continuous verification of identity, device state, and policy for every access request.
short: Network position is not evidence of trustworthiness.
long: Network position is not evidence of trustworthiness. It replaces perimeter-based defences with per-request authentication, authorisation, and least-privilege access.
proof: Treating each request independently means a breached internal host gains no automatic access to other resources, limiting lateral movement.
consequence: Zero trust guides the design of modern enterprise and cloud networks.

title: Linear Temporal Logic Semantics
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Linear temporal logic extends propositional logic with operators over time along a single path: next, eventually, globally, and until. Formulas are evaluated at positions of an infinite execution trace.
short: Express properties of sequences, such as eventually reaching a goal.
long: Express properties of sequences, such as eventually reaching a goal. LTL is interpreted over linear traces, in contrast to branching-time logics such as CTL. Safety and liveness properties are naturally written in LTL.
proof: The semantics are recursive on traces: eventually holds if some future position satisfies p, globally if all positions do, and p until q if q holds at a future point with p holding before it.
consequence: LTL is the standard specification language for model checkers of reactive systems.

title: Computation Tree Logic and Branching Time
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Computation tree logic quantifies over branching futures using path quantifiers A and E combined with temporal operators. It expresses claims such as 'on all paths eventually p' or 'there exists a path where p holds until q'.
