short: Branching-time logic asks whether all or some futures satisfy a temporal property.
long: Branching-time logic asks whether all or some futures satisfy a temporal property. CTL differs from LTL by allowing path quantification at every temporal operator, making it suitable for state-based model checking.
proof: A formula is evaluated at a state of a transition system by considering all or some outgoing paths and applying the temporal operator along each chosen path.
consequence: CTL is the specification language of several classical model checkers.

title: Kripke Structures for Model Checking
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A Kripke structure consists of states, a transition relation between them, and a labelling of states with atomic propositions. It is the standard semantic model for temporal-logic model checking.
short: A labelled transition system gives temporal formulas a precise meaning.
long: A labelled transition system gives temporal formulas a precise meaning. Paths through the structure represent possible executions, and total transition relations ensure every finite prefix has an extension.
proof: The transition relation generates all executions and the labelling determines which atomic propositions hold at each state, giving an interpretation of temporal formulas.
consequence: Model-checking algorithms compute the set of states satisfying a formula over such a structure.

title: Safety and Liveness Properties
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Safety properties state that nothing bad ever happens, while liveness properties state that something good eventually happens. Every property of infinite traces is the intersection of a safety property and a liveness property.
short: Safety is refuted by a finite prefix; liveness needs an infinite trace.
long: Safety is refuted by a finite prefix; liveness needs an infinite trace. Mutual exclusion is safety, while eventual progress is liveness. Deadlock freedom combines aspects of both.
proof: Safety violations occur at some finite prefix, whereas liveness violations require an infinite trace with no good event; this distinction yields the decomposition theorem for trace properties.
consequence: The distinction determines what kind of counterexample a model checker must produce.

title: State Explosion Problem in Model Checking
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The global state space of a concurrent system grows roughly as the product of its components' state counts, making explicit enumeration infeasible for large systems.
short: Composing components multiplies their state spaces.
long: Composing components multiplies their state spaces. Symbolic representations, partial-order reduction, symmetry reduction, and abstraction all attack different aspects of the explosion.
proof: A global state is a tuple of component states, so the number of possible tuples is the product of component counts and is exponential in the number of components.
consequence: Coping with state explosion is the central engineering challenge of model checking.

title: Symbolic Model Checking with BDDs
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Symbolic model checking represents sets of states and transition relations with reduced ordered binary decision diagrams rather than enumerating states individually. This can compress exponentially many states into manageable graphs.
short: Represent whole state sets as Boolean functions.
long: Represent whole state sets as Boolean functions. Reachability is computed by repeated image operations on BDDs until a fixed point is reached.
proof: A reduced ordered BDD is a canonical representation of a Boolean function; applying image and preimage operators symbolically computes reachable states without visiting each state one at a time.
consequence: BDD-based checking verified many hardware designs with enormous state spaces.

title: Bounded Model Checking with SAT
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Bounded model checking encodes the existence of a counterexample of length k as a propositional formula. A satisfying assignment gives a concrete execution trace violating the property.
short: Search for a short violating trace using a SAT solver.
long: Search for a short violating trace using a SAT solver. Increasing k gives completeness up to a bound, while induction or diameter bounds can establish absence of longer counterexamples.
proof: The formula encodes the transition relation for k steps and the negation of the property at some step, so any satisfying assignment describes a valid error trace.
consequence: Advances in SAT solving have made BMC highly effective for hardware and software.

title: Bisimulation Equivalence
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A bisimulation is a relation between states of two transition systems such that related states match each other's moves and reach related successors. Bisimilar states satisfy the same branching-time temporal formulas.
latex: R\subseteq S_1\times S_2,\quad s_1\ R\ s_2
short: Two systems are equivalent if each can mimic the other's every move.
long: Two systems are equivalent if each can mimic the other's every move. Bisimulation is finer than trace equivalence because it preserves branching structure, not merely the set of observable sequences.
proof: The back-and-forth conditions let every step from one state be matched from the related state, so modal and branching-time formulas cannot distinguish them.
consequence: Bisimulation is the standard behavioural equivalence for concurrent processes.

title: Petri Nets Model Concurrent Systems
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A Petri net is a bipartite graph of places and transitions in which tokens mark places and enabled transitions consume tokens from inputs and produce tokens on outputs. It models concurrency, synchronisation, and resource sharing.
short: Token flows describe concurrent activity and resource use.
long: Token flows describe concurrent activity and resource use. Place invariants and transition invariants support static analysis of reachability and boundedness properties.
proof: A transition fires only when its input places hold enough tokens, and the marking update records the resulting distribution, so firing sequences represent concurrent executions.
consequence: Petri nets are widely used to model protocols, workflows, and manufacturing systems.

title: DPLL and CDCL SAT Solving
subject: Formal Methods
statement: DPLL decides propositional satisfiability by branching on variables with unit propagation and pure-literal elimination. CDCL extends it by deriving conflict clauses and backjumping to the decision level responsible for the conflict.
short: Learn from conflicts so the search does not repeat mistakes.
long: Learn from conflicts so the search does not repeat mistakes. Conflict clauses are derived by resolution and often include learnt literals that guide subsequent branching heuristics.
proof: A learnt clause is implied by the original formula and excludes the failing assignment, so backjumping to the asserted level preserves completeness while avoiding repeated conflicts.
consequence: CDCL solvers power verification, planning, and many combinatorial applications.

title: Satisfiability Modulo Theories
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Satisfiability modulo theories decides satisfiability of Boolean combinations of formulas over background theories such as arithmetic, arrays, or bit vectors. SMT solvers combine a SAT solver with specialised theory solvers.
short: Boolean search paired with decision procedures for richer theories.
long: Boolean search paired with decision procedures for richer theories. The Nelson–Oppen combination method merges disjoint theories by exchanging equalities between shared terms.
proof: The SAT solver treats theory atoms as Boolean variables, theory solvers check consistency of candidate assignments, and returned conflicts refine the Boolean search.
consequence: SMT is the engine behind program verification, symbolic execution, and software analysis tools.

title: Widening Operators in Abstract Interpretation
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A widening operator accelerates fixed-point computation over infinite abstract domains by extrapolating increasing chains after finitely many steps. It trades precision for guaranteed convergence.
short: Force an ascending analysis to stabilise while staying sound.
long: Force an ascending analysis to stabilise while staying sound. Narrowing can recover precision after widening by descending toward a more accurate fixed point.
proof: Widening guarantees that ascending chains stabilise; because each widened step over-approximates the concrete update, the resulting fixed point remains a sound over-approximation.
consequence: Widening makes static analysis of loops and recursive programs terminates in practice.

title: Proof-Carrying Code
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Proof-carrying code attaches a machine-checkable safety proof to a program so a consumer can validate it without trusting the producer. The proof is checked against a specified safety policy before execution.
short: Ship a proof along with the code and check it locally.
long: Ship a proof along with the code and check it locally. The trusted computing base is reduced to a small proof checker rather than a complex compiler or verifier.
proof: The checker validates the proof in a small trusted kernel, and a valid proof establishes that the code satisfies the safety policy.
consequence: Proof-carrying code enables safe execution of untrusted software from arbitrary sources.

title: Runtime Verification with Monitors
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Runtime verification checks a property against an executing system using a monitor that observes events and issues verdicts. It is lighter than model checking but covers only the executions actually observed.
short: Check a specification against the running system's event stream.
long: Check a specification against the running system's event stream. Monitors can be generated automatically from temporal logic formulas and may be online or offline.
proof: The monitor is an automaton for the property specification, so processing an observed trace determines whether a prefix violates the property or satisfies it.
consequence: Runtime verification bridges formal specification and deployed systems.

title: Temporal Logic Model Checking Algorithm
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Explicit-state temporal-logic model checking labels states with satisfied subformulas bottom-up, using set operations for Boolean connectives and fixed points for until and globally operators.
short: Compute the set of states satisfying each subformula in turn.
long: Compute the set of states satisfying each subformula in turn. The until operator is the least fixed point of a monotone function on state sets, while globally is a greatest fixed point.
proof: Atomic propositions give base sets, Boolean operators use set operations, and iterating the monotone until operator from the empty set yields exactly the states with a witnessing path.
consequence: The decision procedure runs in time polynomial in the model and formula size.

title: Fitts's Law of Pointing Time
subject: Computer Science
statement: Fitts's law models movement time to a target as a logarithmic function of the distance to the target divided by its width. Larger and closer targets are acquired more quickly.
short: The index of difficulty grows logarithmically with distance over width.
long: The index of difficulty grows logarithmically with distance over width. The law applies to mouse pointing, touch input, and many motor tasks, with device-specific constants.
proof: Controlled experiments show movement time is linear in the index of difficulty log2(1+D/W) across a wide range of target sizes and distances.
consequence: Interface designers use the law to choose target sizes and place frequently used controls close at hand.

title: Hick's Law of Choice Reaction Time
subject: Computer Science
statement: Hick's law states that decision time grows logarithmically with the number of equally likely choices. Each additional option adds less time than the previous one.
short: More choices slow decisions, but with diminishing returns.
long: More choices slow decisions, but with diminishing returns. The law is used to design menus and to justify progressive disclosure of rarely used options.
proof: Subjects behave approximately as if performing a binary search through the alternatives, so the expected number of decisions grows as log2 of the choice count.
consequence: Reducing simultaneous choices can speed user decisions, especially in time-critical interfaces.

title: Nielsen's Usability Heuristics
subject: Computer Science
statement: Nielsen's ten usability heuristics are broad design principles including visibility of system status, match with the real world, user control and freedom, consistency, error prevention, and flexibility.
short: A short checklist for finding usability problems in an interface.
long: A short checklist for finding usability problems in an interface. Heuristic evaluation asks inspectors to compare an interface against each principle and list violations with severity ratings.
proof: The heuristics distil recurring findings from usability practice into a compact checklist, which inspectors apply systematically to find problems cheaply.
consequence: Heuristic evaluation finds many issues early without user studies.

title: Affordances and Signifiers
subject: Computer Science
statement: An affordance is an action an object supports, while a signifier communicates where that action is available. Good interfaces make useful affordances visible through signifiers such as shape, labels, and icons.
short: Show users what can be done and where.
long: Show users what can be done and where. A button's raised appearance is a signifier for clickability; a flat unlabelled region may hide an equally real affordance.
proof: Users infer possible actions from perceived properties, so signifiers make supported actions discoverable without trial and error.
consequence: Clear signifiers reduce exploration and misuse in interfaces.

title: Cognitive Load Theory for Interfaces
subject: Computer Science
statement: Cognitive load theory distinguishes intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load. Interfaces should minimise extraneous load so users can devote limited working memory to the task itself.
short: Remove mental work that does not contribute to the user's goal.
long: Remove mental work that does not contribute to the user's goal. Consistent layouts, clear labels, and progressive disclosure all reduce extraneous load.
proof: Working memory capacity is limited, so reducing load unrelated to the task leaves more capacity for task-relevant processing.
consequence: The theory provides a principled basis for simplifying complex interfaces.

title: Feedback and Visibility in Interactive Systems
subject: Computer Science
statement: Visibility of system status requires every action to produce timely, appropriate feedback. Without feedback users cannot tell whether an action succeeded and often repeat it unnecessarily.
short: Tell users what happened so they know where they stand.
long: Tell users what happened so they know where they stand. Progress indicators, confirmations, and visible state changes are common forms of feedback.
proof: Feedback closes the loop between user action and system state, letting the user update their mental model and avoid duplicate actions.
consequence: Missing feedback is one of the most common sources of user frustration.

title: WCAG Accessibility Guidelines
subject: Computer Science
statement: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines define conformance levels A, AA, and AAA for making web content accessible. They cover text alternatives, keyboard access, contrast, navigation, and error identification.
short: An international checklist for accessible web content.
long: An international checklist for accessible web content. Meeting level AA is a common legal and organisational target for public websites.
proof: The guidelines enumerate testable success criteria grouped into levels, so conformance can be assessed systematically against a published standard.
consequence: WCAG provides a shared, measurable basis for inclusive design.

title: Mental Models and User Expectations
subject: Computer Science
statement: Users interact through mental models of how a system works. Interfaces matching those expectations reduce errors, while mismatches cause confusion even if the system is technically correct.
short: Design for the model users already have, or teach them a new one clearly.
long: Design for the model users already have, or teach them a new one clearly. Consistent metaphors and predictable feedback help users form accurate mental models.
proof: Users predict outcomes from their mental model; when predictions match system behaviour interactions succeed, while inconsistencies force relearning.
consequence: Mental-model mismatches explain many errors that are not simple usability flaws.

title: The Graphics Rendering Equation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The rendering equation expresses outgoing radiance at a surface point as emitted radiance plus an integral of incoming radiance weighted by the BRDF and a cosine factor over the hemisphere.
short: Light leaving a point is emission plus reflected incoming light.
long: Light leaving a point is emission plus reflected incoming light. It is an integral equation because incoming radiance may itself have been reflected elsewhere, giving global illumination effects.
proof: Radiance leaving a point equals emitted radiance plus the contribution of incoming radiance from every direction, with the BRDF giving the fraction scattered toward the viewer.
consequence: Most photorealistic rendering algorithms are numerical solvers for this equation.

title: Rasterisation Pipeline Stages
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The rasterisation pipeline transforms vertices by model, view, and projection matrices, clips primitives, maps them to screen coordinates, and fills pixels with interpolated attributes before shading.
short: Geometry flows through transformations, clipping, and pixel coverage.
long: Geometry flows through transformations, clipping, and pixel coverage. Programmable shader stages replace fixed-function stages in modern GPUs while preserving the overall pipeline structure.
proof: Each stage applies a defined transformation to geometry or fragments, and their composition maps a 3D scene description into final pixel colours.
consequence: The pipeline structure explains both GPU hardware design and graphics APIs.

title: Ray Tracing and Recursive Rays
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Ray tracing computes pixel colours by casting rays from the camera through the image plane and finding intersections with scene geometry. Recursive secondary rays model reflection, refraction, and shadows.
short: Follow light paths from the camera to estimate each pixel's radiance.
long: Follow light paths from the camera to estimate each pixel's radiance. Acceleration structures such as bounding volume hierarchies reduce the cost of intersection tests, and recursion depth is usually capped.
proof: At each intersection the contribution is emitted light plus recursively evaluated light along reflected and refracted directions, approximating the rendering equation by path sampling.
consequence: Ray tracing naturally produces shadows, reflections, and global illumination effects.

title: Z-Buffer Depth Testing
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The z-buffer algorithm stores a depth value per pixel and keeps the fragment whose depth is smallest. It resolves visibility independently for each pixel without sorting all primitives globally.
short: Keep only the nearest fragment at each pixel.
long: Keep only the nearest fragment at each pixel. Depth precision and near-plane placement affect z-fighting between close surfaces.
proof: Replacing a pixel only when the incoming fragment is closer ensures the stored colour belongs to the nearest surface along the view ray.
consequence: Depth buffering is the dominant hidden-surface method in real-time graphics.

title: Painter's Algorithm and Depth Sorting
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The painter's algorithm draws distant primitives first so nearer ones cover them. It requires a global depth order and fails for intersecting polygons or cyclic overlap.
short: Draw back to front, but overlapping cycles have no valid order.
long: Draw back to front, but overlapping cycles have no valid order. Newell's algorithm splits polygons to handle many cyclic cases at extra cost.
proof: If every primitive is drawn after all primitives behind it, the last colour written at each pixel is that of the nearest covering primitive; cyclic overlap prevents such an order.
consequence: Depth buffering has largely superseded pure painter's ordering in interactive rendering.

title: Backface Culling by Winding Order
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Backface culling discards triangles whose projected vertex winding is opposite to the chosen front-face convention, avoiding work on surfaces facing away from the camera.
short: Triangle orientation reveals which side faces the viewer.
long: Triangle orientation reveals which side faces the viewer. Double-sided objects must disable culling or render both orientations explicitly.
proof: For closed objects with consistent winding, a triangle whose normal points away from the camera cannot be visible from outside, so discarding it is safe.
consequence: Culling roughly halves geometry work for typical closed meshes.

title: Phong Shading Model
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The Phong shading model computes surface intensity from ambient, diffuse, and specular terms, interpolating normals across a polygon and evaluating lighting per pixel.
short: Ambient fill, cosine-lit diffuse, and a power-law highlight.
long: Ambient fill, cosine-lit diffuse, and a power-law highlight. The exponent controls highlight sharpness; Blinn–Phong uses a half vector for cheaper and often more plausible highlights.
proof: Lambert's cosine law gives the diffuse term, and raising the alignment of reflected and view directions to a power approximates a specular lobe.
consequence: Phong shading is a foundational local illumination model.

title: Gouraud Shading and Vertex Interpolation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Gouraud shading computes lighting at polygon vertices and interpolates the resulting colours across the surface. It is cheaper than per-pixel shading but can miss narrow specular highlights.
short: Light at vertices, then blend colours across the triangle.
long: Light at vertices, then blend colours across the triangle. Because highlights are sampled only at vertices, a highlight centred inside a large triangle may be invisible.
proof: Barycentric weights interpolate vertex colours linearly over the triangle, giving smooth appearance using only vertex lighting computations.
consequence: It was an early and inexpensive route to smooth-shaded surfaces.

title: Barycentric Coordinates for Triangle Interpolation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Barycentric coordinates write a point inside a triangle as an affine combination of its vertices with nonnegative weights summing to one. They give a natural way to interpolate attributes over a triangle.
short: Weights relative to triangle vertices drive smooth attribute interpolation.
long: Weights relative to triangle vertices drive smooth attribute interpolation. The same weights interpolate colour, texture coordinates, normals, and depth during rasterisation.
proof: Solving the affine combination for a point gives unique weights for a nondegenerate triangle, and any vertex-defined attribute interpolates with those weights.
consequence: Barycentric interpolation is a core operation of rasterisers.

title: Mipmapping and Texture Minification
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Mipmaps are precomputed lower-resolution versions of a texture. The renderer selects a level whose texel density matches the pixel footprint, reducing aliasing when a texture is minified.
short: Use a smaller prefiltered texture when pixels cover many texels.
long: Use a smaller prefiltered texture when pixels cover many texels. Trilinear filtering blends between adjacent mip levels for smoother transitions.
proof: Averaging texels into coarser levels band-limits the texture, so sampling a level near the pixel footprint avoids high-frequency aliasing.
consequence: Mipmapping greatly improves texture quality at oblique viewing angles.

title: Bilinear Texture Interpolation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Bilinear interpolation blends the four texels surrounding a sample location using fractional offsets along two axes. It smooths texture magnification at modest cost.
short: Average the four nearest texels weighted by distance.
long: Average the four nearest texels weighted by distance. Nearest-neighbour sampling is cheaper but produces blocky magnified textures.
proof: Linear interpolation along one axis followed by linear interpolation along the other yields a weighted average of the four neighbouring texels.
consequence: Bilinear filtering is a standard baseline for texture sampling.

title: Shadow Mapping Algorithm
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Shadow mapping renders the scene from the light source into a depth map, then compares each fragment's depth in light space with the stored depth to decide whether it is shadowed.
short: A fragment behind the first surface seen by the light is in shadow.
long: A fragment behind the first surface seen by the light is in shadow. A bias term avoids shadow acne caused by depth precision errors; percentage-closer filtering softens shadow edges.
proof: A fragment farther from the light than the first surface recorded in the depth map lies behind an occluder and is therefore unlit by that light.
consequence: Shadow mapping is the dominant real-time shadow technique.

title: Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Screen-space ambient occlusion estimates how exposed each pixel is to ambient light by sampling nearby depth values. Darkening occluded regions approximates global illumination cheaply.
short: Nearby geometry darkens creases and contact regions.
long: Nearby geometry darkens creases and contact regions. The effect is view dependent and misses occluders outside the sampled screen neighbourhood.
proof: Nearby occluding geometry reduces the visible hemisphere for ambient light, so counting unoccluded samples gives a multiplicative approximation to ambient illumination.
consequence: SSAO adds perceptual depth cues at low rendering cost.

title: Marching Cubes for Isosurfaces
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Marching cubes extracts an isosurface from a scalar field by subdividing space into cubes and triangulating the portions of each cube where the field crosses a threshold.
short: Turn a scalar volume into a polygonal surface.
long: Turn a scalar volume into a polygonal surface. The eight corner signs select a configuration from a lookup table; ambiguous cases require careful disambiguation to avoid cracks.
proof: The corner values determine which edges cross the isolevel, and a fixed lookup table gives triangle connectivity consistent across neighbouring cubes.
consequence: Marching cubes is a standard method for visualising volumetric data.

title: Bresenham's Line-Drawing Algorithm
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Bresenham's line algorithm rasterises a straight line using integer arithmetic by maintaining an error term that decides when to step along the secondary axis.
short: Choose the nearest pixel at each step without floating point.
long: Choose the nearest pixel at each step without floating point. The error term is updated incrementally from the line slope, making the algorithm fast enough for early graphics hardware.
proof: The error tracks the deviation between the ideal line and the selected pixel centre, so updating it incrementally selects the closest pixel in each column.
consequence: The algorithm is a classic example of efficient incremental computation.

title: Cohen-Sutherland Line Clipping
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Cohen–Sutherland line clipping assigns each endpoint a four-bit outcode describing its position relative to a rectangular viewport and uses bitwise tests to accept, reject, or clip the segment.
short: Quickly reject obviously invisible lines and clip the rest.
long: Quickly reject obviously invisible lines and clip the rest. If both endpoints share an outside region the line is discarded; if both outcodes are zero it is accepted; otherwise it is split at a boundary and retested.
proof: A shared outside bit means both endpoints lie beyond the same boundary, so the whole segment is outside; repeated bisection at boundaries converges to the visible portion.
consequence: Outcodes give a cheap early reject in 2D clipping pipelines.

title: de Casteljau's Algorithm for Bezier Curves
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: de Casteljau's algorithm evaluates a Bézier curve by repeated linear interpolation between control points. The intermediate points also split the curve into two subcurves.
short: Repeated midpoint-style interpolation evaluates and subdivides a curve.
long: Repeated midpoint-style interpolation evaluates and subdivides a curve. The construction is numerically stable and forms the basis of adaptive curve subdivision.
proof: Repeated convex combinations implement the Bernstein polynomial form, so the final point equals the curve value at t and the intermediate polygons describe two subcurves.
consequence: The algorithm underlies curve rendering and CAD subdivision.

title: B-Splines and NURBS
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: B-spline curves are linear combinations of control points weighted by local polynomial basis functions. NURBS extend them with rational weights, allowing exact representation of conic sections.
short: Local basis functions give flexible, stable curve and surface modelling.
long: Local basis functions give flexible, stable curve and surface modelling. B-spline basis functions have local support and form a partition of unity, so moving one control point affects only a limited part of the curve.
proof: The basis functions' local support and partition of unity make the curve a local blend of control points; dividing weighted basis functions by their sum gives the rational extension.
consequence: NURBS are the standard geometry representation in computer-aided design.

title: Alpha Blending and Compositing
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Alpha blending combines a foreground colour with a background using an opacity value: the result is alpha times foreground plus one minus alpha times background, with premultiplied or straight alpha used consistently.
short: Opacity weights the foreground and background contributions.
long: Opacity weights the foreground and background contributions. Order matters for non-premultiplied blending with multiple transparent layers.
proof: Alpha encodes the fraction of pixel coverage by the foreground, so a convex combination of the two colours gives the observed composite.
consequence: Alpha compositing enables transparency, antialiasing, and layered image synthesis.

title: False Sharing between Cache Lines
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: False sharing occurs when threads on different cores modify distinct variables that happen to lie on the same cache line. Coherence invalidates the whole line, causing heavy traffic despite no logical sharing.
short: Coherence granularity can create contention between unrelated variables.
long: Coherence granularity can create contention between unrelated variables. Padding or aligning per-thread counters to cache-line boundaries removes the effect.
proof: Coherence operates at cache-line granularity, so a write by one core invalidates the line in other cores even if they access different offsets within it.
consequence: False sharing can dominate the cost of otherwise embarrassingly parallel code.

title: Memory Barriers and Fences
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Memory barriers restrict reordering of memory operations by the compiler or hardware across the barrier. Acquire and release barriers establish ordering guarantees between threads.
short: Fences constrain when memory operations may become visible to others.
long: Fences constrain when memory operations may become visible to others. A full fence orders all four combinations of loads and stores, while acquire and release fences order only relevant subsets.
proof: Hardware respects the barrier's ordering constraints, so later operations cannot be observed before an acquire and earlier operations cannot be observed after a release.
consequence: Correct lock-free algorithms depend on carefully placed barriers.

title: Race Conditions and Data Races
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one writes, and no synchronisation orders the accesses. Racy programs typically behave nondeterministically.
short: Unordered concurrent writes make outcomes timing dependent.
long: Unordered concurrent writes make outcomes timing dependent. Some languages declare data-race-free programs as the only ones with defined semantics.
proof: Without an ordering constraint either access may occur first, so the resulting values and subsequent control flow can depend on timing.
consequence: Eliminating data races is the first step to reliable parallel programming.

title: DRF-SC Guarantee for Data-Race-Free Programs
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A data-race-free program on relaxed hardware behaves as if its memory operations were executed in a sequentially consistent order consistent with program order.
short: Race-free code can be reasoned about as if memory were sequential.
long: Race-free code can be reasoned about as if memory were sequential. The guarantee depends on hardware or language memory models satisfying the DRF-SC condition and on correct use of synchronisation.
proof: Synchronisation operations order conflicting accesses, reducing all observable interleavings to a sequentially consistent order of the remaining operations.
consequence: Programmers can use simple sequential reasoning when synchronisation is correct.

title: Branch Target Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A branch target buffer caches destination addresses and prediction bits for recent branches so the front end can fetch along the predicted path before the branch resolves.
short: Remember where branches went last time to fetch ahead.
long: Remember where branches went last time to fetch ahead. Mispredictions squash wrongly fetched instructions and refill the buffer with the correct target.
proof: Branch behaviour shows locality, so recording previous targets lets the fetch unit continue without waiting; incorrect guesses are discarded at resolution.
consequence: Target prediction is essential for keeping deep pipelines busy.

title: Speculative Execution and Reorder Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Speculative execution lets instructions past unresolved branches run, with results held in a reorder buffer until proven correct. Misspeculated results are discarded rather than committed.
short: Execute ahead but keep results private until they are certain.
long: Execute ahead but keep results private until they are certain. Reorder buffers also support precise exceptions by committing results in program order.
proof: The reorder buffer keeps speculative values out of architectural state, so a misprediction can be handled by discarding them and restarting on the correct path.
consequence: Speculation extracts parallelism beyond basic blocks.

title: NUMA and Memory Locality
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: In non-uniform memory access systems a processor reaches its local memory faster than memory attached to other sockets. Placing threads near the data they use improves performance.
short: Memory access time depends on where the data lives.
long: Memory access time depends on where the data lives. NUMA-aware allocators and schedulers try to first-touch pages on the socket that will use them.
proof: Remote accesses traverse an interconnect adding latency and consuming bandwidth, so keeping computation near its data reduces access cost.
consequence: Ignoring NUMA placement can halve the performance of memory-bound servers.

title: TLB Shootdown on Context Switch
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: When page tables change, stale translation lookaside buffer entries in other cores must be invalidated. A shootdown interrupts those cores, which flush affected translations and acknowledge completion.
short: Broadcast invalidations so no core keeps an old mapping.
long: Broadcast invalidations so no core keeps an old mapping. Frequent shootdowns are a significant cost in systems with many cores and frequent memory-map changes.
proof: Without invalidation a core could translate using an obsolete mapping; waiting for acknowledgements ensures no stale entry remains when the operation completes.
consequence: Shootdown cost grows with core count, influencing page-table design and kernel scalability.

title: IOMMU and Device Address Translation
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: An input-output memory management unit translates device-visible addresses into physical addresses and enforces access permissions. It lets devices use virtual addresses and protects memory from faulty or malicious devices.
short: An MMU for DMA-capable devices.
long: An MMU for DMA-capable devices. IOMMUs also support device assignment to virtual machines by isolating each device's address space.
proof: The IOMMU applies a translation table to each DMA request and checks permissions, so devices reach only pages the operating system mapped for them.
consequence: IOMMUs enable safe direct device access and efficient virtualisation.

title: Metastability in Clock Domain Crossing
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A signal crossing between unrelated clock domains can violate setup or hold time and become metastable before settling. Synchronisers with two or more flip-flops reduce the probability of failure.
short: Give a changing signal enough time to settle before it is used.
long: Give a changing signal enough time to settle before it is used. Handshake synchronisers and FIFOs handle multi-bit crossings where simple two-flop synchronisers are insufficient.
proof: Metastability resolution is probabilistic with exponential decay in settling time, so adding a synchronisation stage multiplies the mean time between failures.
consequence: Clock-domain-crossing discipline is essential for reliable digital design.

title: Brent's Theorem on Parallel Time
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: A computation with work W and critical-path length S can be scheduled on p processors in time at most W/p plus S.
short: Time is bounded by ideal work splitting plus the critical path.
long: Time is bounded by ideal work splitting plus the critical path. The bound is tight up to constants for greedy schedulers and underlies work-span analysis.
proof: A greedy scheduler keeps all but one processor busy while the critical path advances, giving the additive bound on execution time.
consequence: Span, not only total work, determines achievable speedup.

title: Message Passing Interface Collectives
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: MPI collectives such as broadcast, reduce, scatter, and allreduce coordinate communication among a group of processes. Allreduce combines values from all ranks and delivers the result to every rank.
short: Group communication operations hide the details of multi-party exchange.
long: Group communication operations hide the details of multi-party exchange. Tree and butterfly algorithms implement collectives with logarithmic communication steps.
proof: Combining partial reductions in a communication tree gives every rank the same associative reduction result after logarithmically many rounds.
consequence: Collectives are heavily used in scientific computing and distributed training.

title: Work-Stealing Schedulers
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: In work stealing, each processor owns a deque of ready tasks and steals from another processor's deque only when it runs out of work. The scheme balances load with mostly local operations.
short: Work locally, steal only when idle.
long: Work locally, steal only when idle. Stealing from the opposite end of the deque reduces contention with the owner and tends to take larger subtrees.
proof: Local operations need little synchronisation, while stealing transfers work from busy to idle processors, improving balance without a central queue.
consequence: Work stealing is the standard scheduler in fork-join runtimes.

title: GPU Warp Divergence
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: A GPU executes threads of a warp in lockstep, so when they take different control-flow paths the hardware serialises the paths. Divergence can greatly reduce effective throughput.
short: Threads that disagree on a branch run in separate passes.
long: Threads that disagree on a branch run in separate passes. Predication can replace short divergent branches with masked instructions to avoid serialisation.
proof: All lanes share one instruction stream, so distinct outcomes are executed in separate passes with inactive lanes masked, summing their costs.
consequence: Branch-free or branch-uniform code is important for GPU performance.

title: Coalesced GPU Memory Access
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: GPU memory is most efficient when consecutive threads access consecutive addresses, allowing requests to merge into a few wide transactions. Strided access wastes bandwidth.
short: Contiguous accesses by a warp minimise memory transactions.
long: Contiguous accesses by a warp minimise memory transactions. Array-of-structures layouts can fragment accesses, whereas structure-of-arrays layouts often coalesce them.
proof: The memory subsystem groups neighbouring addresses into one transaction, so contiguous access by a warp serves all lanes with minimal requests.
consequence: Data layout is as important as arithmetic optimisation on GPUs.

title: Load Balancing Algorithms
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Load balancing distributes work across servers or processors so no single one is overloaded. Static schemes assign work in advance, while dynamic schemes react to observed load.
short: Spread requests so that no server becomes a bottleneck.
long: Spread requests so that no server becomes a bottleneck. Round-robin, least-connections, and consistent hashing are common choices with different assumptions about request costs.
proof: Sending new work to the least loaded server reduces the maximum imbalance; round robin balances only when requests have similar cost.
consequence: Good balancing improves latency and resource utilisation at scale.

title: Content Delivery Networks and Edge Caching
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A content delivery network caches content at geographically distributed edge nodes so users fetch it from a nearby server. This reduces latency and origin bandwidth.
short: Move content close to users to shorten network paths.
long: Move content close to users to shorten network paths. Cache invalidation and request routing determine how much traffic the origin still sees.
proof: Serving from a nearby cache shortens the network path and avoids repeated long-haul transfers when the cached copy is fresh.
consequence: CDNs are essential to the performance and reliability of large web services.

title: Serverless Cold Starts
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Serverless platforms start function instances on demand. A cold start is the extra latency of provisioning and initialising a new instance before handling the first request.
short: On-demand execution pays startup cost on the first call.
long: On-demand execution pays startup cost on the first call. Keeping instances warm, shrinking packages, and pre-initialising runtimes reduce cold-start latency.
proof: With no warm instance available the platform must load code and initialise the runtime, adding startup time to that request.
consequence: Cold starts matter for latency-sensitive serverless applications.

title: Microservices and Service Decomposition
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Microservices architecture splits an application into small independently deployable services with well-defined interfaces and separate data ownership. It increases autonomy but adds network and operational complexity.
short: Independent services trade local simplicity for distributed complexity.
long: Independent services trade local simplicity for distributed complexity. Each service can be scaled and released independently, but failures and latency become distributed concerns.
proof: Independent deployment follows from separate code and data ownership, while interactions become remote calls that need versioning, discovery, and failure handling.
consequence: The architecture suits large organisations more than small applications.

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A circuit breaker monitors calls to a remote service and stops sending requests when failures pass a threshold, later probing for recovery. It prevents cascading failures and wasted retries.
short: Stop calling a failing dependency until it recovers.
long: Stop calling a failing dependency until it recovers. Fallback responses and timeouts complement the breaker to keep the caller responsive.
proof: Blocking calls while a dependency is failing lets the caller degrade gracefully and gives the dependency time to recover before traffic resumes.
consequence: Circuit breakers improve resilience of microservice architectures.

title: Idempotency in Distributed APIs
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether applied once or several times. Idempotency keys let clients retry requests safely after ambiguous failures.
short: Retries must not duplicate the side effects of a request.
long: Retries must not duplicate the side effects of a request. Recording processed keys with their responses gives the same result on replay of a request.
proof: A unique key plus a record of processed requests maps repeated calls to the original result, so a timeout can be retried without double processing.
consequence: Idempotency is essential for reliable APIs over unreliable networks.

title: Container Orchestration with Kubernetes
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Kubernetes schedules containerised workloads on a cluster, maintains a desired number of replicas, and provides service discovery, rolling updates, and self-healing.
short: Controllers continuously drive observed state toward desired state.
long: Controllers continuously drive observed state toward desired state. Declarative configuration lets operators specify intent rather than imperative steps.
proof: Controllers compare desired and observed state and take actions to close the gap, so failed containers are replaced automatically.
consequence: Orchestration makes large container deployments manageable.

title: Elastic Auto-Scaling
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Elastic auto-scaling adjusts allocated resources to observed demand, adding capacity during spikes and removing it afterwards to control cost.
short: Match resource supply to demand dynamically.
long: Match resource supply to demand dynamically. Scaling policies use metrics such as CPU use, request rate, or queue depth and must account for startup delay.
proof: Monitoring drives replica-count changes that move capacity toward the level needed for the observed load target.
consequence: Elasticity is a defining economic advantage of cloud computing.

title: Distributed Tracing and Observability
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Distributed tracing records a request's path across services as spans carrying timing and causal relationships. It helps diagnose latency and failures in microservice systems.
short: Follow one request across every service it touches.
long: Follow one request across every service it touches. Trace context propagation, sampling, and aggregation are needed to keep overhead manageable.
proof: Propagating a trace identifier through service calls lets spans be assembled into a causal tree, revealing where time was spent across boundaries.
consequence: Tracing is a core observability tool for production distributed systems.

title: The Mars Pathfinder Priority Inversion Incident
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The 1997 Mars Pathfinder mission suffered repeated system resets caused by priority inversion between a high-priority communications task and a low-priority task holding a mutex.
short: A textbook synchronisation pitfall once threatened a planetary landing.
long: A textbook synchronisation pitfall once threatened a planetary landing. A medium-priority task preempted the mutex holder while the high-priority task waited, so the reset watchdog fired. Enabling priority inheritance eliminated the resets.
proof: Flight software traces showed the high-priority task blocked on a lock held by a preempted low-priority task; once the holder inherited the higher priority it finished quickly and the blocking disappeared.
consequence: The incident made priority inheritance a standard consideration in real-time system design.

title: A Database Index Can Make a Query Slower
subject: Database Systems
statement: Adding an index can slow a query when its predicate matches many rows, because random row fetches through the index can cost more than a sequential scan of the table.
short: More indexing is not always faster indexing.
long: More indexing is not always faster indexing. Optimizers use selectivity estimates to decide between an index plan and a scan; stale statistics can make the wrong choice.
proof: A scan reads pages sequentially, whereas an index plan pays an index descent and often one random access per matching row, so a large match set makes the index plan more expensive.
consequence: Index design must follow workload and selectivity rather than the assumption that indexes always help.

title: The High Cost of a Branch Misprediction
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: On a deeply pipelined processor a single branch misprediction can waste more than a dozen cycles, because every younger speculative instruction must be squashed and fetched again from the correct path.
short: One wrong guess can throw away a pipeline full of work.
long: One wrong guess can throw away a pipeline full of work. Branch predictors therefore aim for very high accuracy, and compilers arrange likely paths to be the fall-through path.
proof: When a branch resolves incorrectly the front end discards the speculative instructions and restarts from the resolved target, paying refill and pipeline latency before useful work resumes.
consequence: Misprediction penalties explain why branch prediction is a first-order performance concern.

title: Cache Misses Can Cost More Than Arithmetic
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A main-memory cache miss can stall a core for hundreds of cycles, far longer than the arithmetic it feeds, so data movement rather than computation dominates many kernels.
short: Moving data can be more expensive than operating on it.
long: Moving data can be more expensive than operating on it. The roofline model captures this by comparing attainable arithmetic throughput with memory bandwidth and operational intensity.
proof: Measured memory latencies exceed single-cycle arithmetic latencies by orders of magnitude, and the roofline bound shows when bandwidth rather than compute limits performance.
consequence: Improving locality often yields larger speedups than reducing instruction counts.

title: Little's Law for Queueing Systems
subject: Operating Systems
statement: In a stable queueing system the long-run average number of items in the system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time an item spends there.
short: Occupancy equals arrival rate times average residence time.
long: Occupancy equals arrival rate times average residence time. The identity requires no assumptions about the arrival distribution or service discipline beyond stability and the existence of the averages.
proof: Over a long interval the total time spent by all items equals the area under the occupancy curve, and dividing both sides by the interval length gives L equals lambda times W.
consequence: Little's law relates latency, throughput, and concurrency in servers, networks, and operating-system queues.
